sections.name: 村落的定义与内涵
sections.content_zh:
第一节 村落的定义与内涵

作为世界上最重要的文明古国之一，中国拥有悠久的文明历史，创造过包括农耕文明在内的灿烂辉煌的文化。

在长江流域，湖南道县玉蟾岩出土了距今约1万年的人工栽培稻标本，成为研究水稻起源最早的实证。同时出土的还有当时被捕获的天鹅、鸳鸯等鸟类的骨头和猕猴桃、梅等果实标本，尤其是世界上最早的陶器遗存物证，表明了当时的先民已经从采集渔猎转向农业耕作。在浙江余姚的河姆渡遗址，出土了距今7000多年的稻谷遗存和农业工具，表明当时原始稻作农业已进入耜耕阶段；而大量的干栏式建筑遗存，则直接开启和印证了今天广大南方地区包括西南少数民族住宅形制与居住形式在内的先声与源流，说明中国南方的传统村落已经初步形成。在黄河流域，距今7000年的仰韶文化，以无与伦比的彩陶器形形成了中国历史上著名的彩陶时代。这一时期的先民运用刀耕火种的方法和土地轮休的耕作方式，开始了粮食作物粟以及蔬菜的种植。河南渑池出土的半地穴式的方形建筑，则已经构筑起了远古村落的基本格局。黄河中下游地区，距今4000多年的龙山文化出土的大量胎骨紧密、漆黑光亮的黑陶，表明陶器的制作工艺在原来彩陶的基础上有了进一步的发展；而大量石器、骨器和蚌器的出土，则表明当时的先民已经开始了以农业为主而兼营狩猎打鱼、蓄养牲畜的生产方式，见证远古村落中居民的生活丰富多彩与文明的演进过程。

今天，虽然经历过无以计数的天灾人祸，各个极具地域风格与民族特色的传统村落仍然有不少遗存。它们遍布辽阔广袤的中华大地，给我们的物质生活与精神生活带来深远重大的影响，有已经被列入《世界遗产名录》的宏村和西递、开平碉楼与村落、福建土楼，有被列入《中国世界遗产预备名单》的山陕古民居、江南水乡古镇、苗族村寨、侗族村寨、藏羌碉楼与村寨，有自2012年以来先后共5批列入《中国传统村落名录》的6819个村落。这些都是人类文化的宝贵财富，也是中华民族的重要文化遗产。在这类名单之外的更多普通而历史悠久的传统村落，更是数不胜数，它们如同一颗颗灿烂的星辰，散落在中华大地。只要我们离开城市，传统村落的气息就扑面而来。甚至在现代都市中，我们也能够感受到传统村落文化的存在。可以说，每一个中国人的血液中都流淌着传统村落文化的基因。亲近传统村落，就是在寻找我们的文化之根。守护住了传统村落，就是留住了中华民族可供安放的乡愁。

那么，在这片960万平方千米的土地上传承了上万年源远流长且凝聚着中华民族智慧和汗水的中国传统村落，究竟有着怎样的文化内涵和文化特质？其基本的文化内核是什么？由于受到传统文史哲研究体制与框架的制约，在过去相当长的时间里，其被弃而不问，故鲜而有闻，或闻而不详。叶舒宪先生在论及中国文化的大传统与小传统时说："几百万、上千万平方公里的山河大地也可以当作一部大书来看和读。"其实，成千上万的中国传统村落，何尝不是一部部鲜活的并正在续写的中华民族文明史？

何谓村落？《辞海》中只给了两个字的注解："村庄。"《辞源》中给了六个字的注解："乡人聚居之处。""村落"是个汉语词汇，有关"村落"的称谓，很早就出现在中国古代文献中。如《三国志》："入魏郡界，村落齐整如一，民得财足用饶。"晋代崔豹《古今注》："四顾荒郊，村落绝远。"《北史》："吏人如丧亲戚，城邑村落营斋供……"唐代张守节作《史记正义》，注《史记·五帝本纪》"一年而所居成聚"时，言："聚，在喻反，谓村落也。"又注《史记·秦本纪》："筑冀阙，秦徙都之。并诸小乡聚……""万二千五百家为乡。聚犹村落之类也。""村落"一词，在魏晋以降的古代文献中出现的频率就更高了，在此不必一一赘述。

广义上的村落常常被理解为"乡村""农村"，即指以农业生产为主体的广大聚居地域；狭义上的村落就是乡人聚居聚落，属于自然村，有一定的边界特征。鉴于此，我们认为，村落作为人类生产、生活、居住和进行政治、经济、文化等活动的一类场所，它至少包括两个层面的内容：一是作为实际存在的聚落，它首先是物质实体空间，体现为明显的聚合性，具有一定的地域范围，是自然要素与人文因素共同作用而形成的地域综合体，包括空间构成的房屋、道路、景观、设施、工具和土地等可视性内容；二是作为社会群体的活动单元，它也是非物质社会空间，体现为聚族群体性和血缘延续性的特质，具有一定的社会活动范围，是血缘关系、亲缘关系与地缘关系高度重合的社会单元，包括关系构成的组织、制度、语言、风俗、道德、宗教、经验和技术等不可视性内容。换言之，村落就是物质实体空间和非物质社会空间高度重叠的地域空间，它是农林渔牧业人群长期生活、聚居、繁衍的边界相对明晰的社会单元。

村落作为建立在血缘和地缘基础上的小型聚落，村落有自身的范围与活动空间，具有封闭性、保守性、宗族性和地域性特点，它包含于乡村，但不能等同于乡村。因为乡村的指代更为广泛，通常指非城镇化的地区，包括自然村与行政村，而村落一般具体所指为聚落实体，是乡村的基本单元。村落的发展历程可以映射乡村的变迁，但村落史不能完全等同于乡村史，它们是包含与被包含的关系，是逻辑的内涵与外延关系。不论是施坚雅的"市场理论"、杜赞奇的权力文化网络，还是费孝通的社区论，抑或是贺雪峰、李培林的多元边界论，事实上都认为村落是有界限的，因而不能将村落简单类同于乡村的概念。

通过上述分析，我们可以给"村落"下一个大致的基本的定义，即村落是由古代先民在农耕文明进程中，在族群部落的基础模式上，进而因"聚族而居"的生产生活所需而营造的具有一定规模、相对稳定的基本社会单元。村落与村落文化的内涵虽不尽相同，但关联紧密。"文化"是个舶来词，源自拉丁文"cultura"，这个词原来具有耕种、居住、敬神等多重意义。由此可知，村落和文化的关系是非常紧密的，而且都是农耕文明的产物。村落是基础，文化是内涵。同时，村落与村落原住民是文化载体，文化又因载体而不断传承和衍生。

中国传统村落是中华民族先民由采集与渔猎的游弋生存生活方式进化到农耕文明定居生存生活方式的重要标志，是各民族在历史演变中由"聚族而居"这一基本族群聚居模式发展起来的相对稳定的社会单元，是中国农村广阔地域上和历史渐变中一种实际存在的历史最为悠久的时空坐落。作为社会单元内在结构最为紧密的小群体，中国传统村落的空间形态多样、文化成分多元，蕴含着丰富深邃的历史文化信息。其通过相互关联、内在互动，不断传承内部文化，发挥社会功能，成了社会有机体的重要组成部分，是中国传统文化最根本的基础。从湖南玉蟾岩出土的距今约1万年的人工栽培稻标本来看，中国是世界上少有的拥有上万年历史的农耕文明史大国。以农耕渔猎为基础的村落，因其地理环境、人居条件的差别，逐渐形成了不同地域、不同形态的"村落文化"。这一由基本族群聚居模式发展起来的社会单元，使得村落文化具有聚族群体性、血缘延续性的特质；它承载了中国久远悠长的文明历史，因而极具民族文化的本源性和传承性；村落成员的生产生活以及与之相关的有形或无形的文化形态，从表面化一般形式的呈现到隐性化深层次的内在文化结构与内涵，代表着中国历史的文化传统，体现着"社会人"由单一个体到家庭家族，进而到氏族，最后归属于民族范畴，再直接引申到"国家"概念的文化层面的全部含义。自秦汉以来，按传统的儒学归纳，中国传统村落可以说是"修身、齐家、治国、平天下"人文理想最具基础性和根本性的文化依托。

不同历史时代和不同地域、不同民族所形成的传统村落，承载着大量不同时期、不同地域、不同民族的文化信息，是我国宝贵的物质文化和非物质文化遗产资源，更是世界人类文化遗产极其重要的组成部分。
sections.content_en:
Section 1: Definition and Connotation of Villages

As one of the world's most important ancient civilizations, China has a long civilized history and has created a splendid culture including agricultural civilization.

In the Yangtze River basin, Yuchanyan Cave in Daoxian County, Hunan, has unearthed artificially cultivated rice specimens dating back approximately 10,000 years, becoming the earliest evidence for studying the origin of rice. Also unearthed were bones of birds such as swans and mandarin ducks that were captured at that time, as well as fruit specimens of kiwifruit and plums. Especially, the world's earliest pottery relics indicate that the ancestors at that time had already shifted from gathering and fishing-hunting to agricultural cultivation. At the Hemudu Site in Yuyao, Zhejiang, rice remains and agricultural tools dating back more than 7,000 years were unearthed, indicating that primitive rice agriculture had entered the spade-cultivation stage. The large number of stilt-style building remains directly opened and confirmed the precursor and origin of residential forms and living styles in today's vast southern regions, including ethnic minorities in the southwest, indicating that traditional villages in southern China had already taken initial shape. In the Yellow River basin, the Yangshao culture dating back 7,000 years formed the famous painted pottery era in Chinese history with unparalleled painted pottery forms. The ancestors of this period used the slash-and-burn method and land fallow cultivation to begin planting grain crops such as millet and vegetables. The semi-subterranean square buildings unearthed in Mianchi, Henan, had already constructed the basic pattern of ancient villages. In the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, the large number of black pottery with tight bodies and jet-black luster unearthed from the Longshan culture dating back more than 4,000 years indicates that pottery manufacturing technology had further developed on the basis of painted pottery. The excavation of a large number of stone, bone, and clam tools indicates that the ancestors at that time had begun a production mode based mainly on agriculture while also engaging in hunting, fishing, and livestock raising, witnessing the rich and colorful life of residents in ancient villages and the evolution of civilization.

Today, despite countless natural and man-made disasters, many traditional villages with distinctive regional styles and ethnic characteristics still survive. They are scattered across the vast Chinese land, exerting profound and significant influence on our material and spiritual lives. Some have been listed in the World Heritage List, such as Hongcun and Xidi, Kaiping Diaolou and Villages, and Fujian Tulou. Some have been listed in China's World Heritage Tentative List, such as ancient residences in Shanxi and Shaanxi, water towns in the Jiangnan region, Miao villages, Dong villages, and Tibetan-Qiang watchtowers and villages. Since 2012, a total of 6,819 villages have been listed in the China Traditional Village Directory in five batches. These are precious treasures of human culture and important cultural heritage of the Chinese nation. Beyond these lists, there are countless more ordinary but historically悠久 traditional villages, like brilliant stars scattered across the Chinese land. As soon as we leave the city, the atmosphere of traditional villages greets us. Even in modern metropolises, we can feel the existence of traditional village culture. It can be said that the blood of every Chinese person flows with the genes of traditional village culture. Getting close to traditional villages means seeking our cultural roots. Protecting traditional villages means preserving the nostalgia that the Chinese nation can call home.

So, what kind of cultural connotation and characteristics do China's traditional villages, which have been inherited for tens of thousands of years on this 9.6 million square kilometer land and凝聚 the wisdom and sweat of the Chinese nation, possess? What is their basic cultural core? Due to the constraints of the traditional research system and framework of literature, history, and philosophy, for a considerable period in the past, they were abandoned and rarely heard of, or heard of but not in detail. When discussing the great and small traditions of Chinese culture, Mr. Ye Shuxian said: "Millions or tens of millions of square kilometers of mountains and rivers can also be read as a great book." In fact, are not the tens of thousands of Chinese traditional villages like vivid and continuously written histories of Chinese civilization?

What is a village? In Cihai (Sea of Words), it is given only a two-character annotation: "village." In Ciyuan (Source of Words), it is given a six-character annotation: "place where country people gather." "Village" (cunluo) is a Chinese vocabulary term, and the appellation related to "village" appeared very early in ancient Chinese documents. For example, in Records of the Three Kingdoms: "Entering the boundary of Wei Commandery, villages were neat and uniform, and the people obtained sufficient wealth and use." In Cui Bao's Gujin Zhu (Ancient and Modern Notes) of the Jin Dynasty: "Looking around at the desolate suburbs, villages are extremely far away." In History of the Northern Dynasties: "Officials and people mourned as if losing relatives, cities and villages held vegetarian offerings..." When Zhang Shoujie of the Tang Dynasty wrote Shiji Zhengyi (Correct Meaning of Records of the Grand Historian), annotating "in one year the place became a settlement" in Annals of the Five Emperors, he said: "Settlement, pronounced zai-yu-fan, means village." He also annotated Annals of Qin: "Built Ji Que, Qin moved the capital there. Merged various small townships and settlements..." "Twelve thousand five hundred families form a township. A settlement is like a village." The term "village" appeared even more frequently in ancient documents after the Wei and Jin dynasties, which need not be enumerated one by one here.

In a broad sense, villages are often understood as "countryside" or "rural areas," referring to vast inhabited areas with agricultural production as the main body. In a narrow sense, a village is a settlement where country people gather, belonging to a natural village with certain boundary characteristics. In view of this, we believe that as a place for human production, life, residence, and political, economic, and cultural activities, a village includes at least two levels of content: First, as an actually existing settlement, it is first a material entity space, reflecting obvious aggregation, with a certain geographical range, and is a regional complex formed by the interaction of natural elements and human factors, including visible content such as houses, roads, landscapes, facilities, tools, and land that constitute the space. Second, as an activity unit of social groups, it is also a non-material social space, reflecting the characteristics of clan-group aggregation and blood lineage continuity, with a certain range of social activities, and is a social unit where blood relations, kinship relations, and geographical relations highly overlap, including invisible content such as organizations, systems, language, customs, morality, religion, experience, and technology constituted by relations. In other words, a village is a geographical space where material entity space and non-material social space highly overlap; it is a social unit with relatively clear boundaries where people engaged in agriculture, forestry, fishing, and animal husbandry live, gather, and reproduce for a long time.

As small settlements established on the basis of blood lineage and geography, villages have their own scope and activity space, with characteristics of closure, conservatism, clan nature, and regionality. They are included in the countryside but cannot be equated with the countryside. Because the countryside refers more broadly, usually to non-urbanized areas, including natural villages and administrative villages, while a village generally specifically refers to a settlement entity, which is the basic unit of the countryside. The development process of villages can reflect the changes of the countryside, but village history cannot be completely equated with rural history; they are a relationship of inclusion and being included, a logical relationship of connotation and extension. Whether it is Skinner's "market theory," Duara's cultural nexus of power, Fei Xiaotong's community theory, or He Xuefeng and Li Peilin's multiple boundary theory, in fact, all recognize that villages have boundaries, and therefore villages cannot be simply equated with the concept of countryside.

Through the above analysis, we can give a rough and basic definition of "village": a village is a relatively stable basic social unit of a certain scale created by ancient ancestors in the process of agricultural civilization, on the basis of clan and tribal patterns, and further due to the needs of production and life of "living together as a clan." Although the connotations of village and village culture are not entirely the same, they are closely related. "Culture" is a borrowed word, derived from the Latin "cultura," which originally had multiple meanings such as cultivation, residence, and worship of gods. From this, it can be seen that the relationship between village and culture is very close, and both are products of agricultural civilization. The village is the foundation, and culture is the connotation. At the same time, villages and village indigenous inhabitants are cultural carriers, and culture is continuously inherited and derived through carriers.

Chinese traditional villages are an important symbol of the evolution of the Chinese nation's ancestors from a nomadic survival lifestyle of gathering and fishing-hunting to a settled survival lifestyle of agricultural civilization. They are relatively stable social units developed by various ethnic groups from the basic clan settlement pattern of "living together as a clan" in historical evolution, and are the oldest time-space settlement that actually exists in the vast rural areas of China and in historical gradual change. As small groups with the tightest internal structure among social units, Chinese traditional villages have diverse spatial forms and pluralistic cultural components, containing rich and profound historical and cultural information. Through interrelation and internal interaction, they continuously inherit internal culture and perform social functions, becoming an important part of the social organism and the most fundamental foundation of traditional Chinese culture. Judging from the artificially cultivated rice specimens dating back approximately 10,000 years unearthed at Yuchanyan Cave in Hunan, China is one of the few countries in the world with a history of agricultural civilization of more than 10,000 years. Villages based on agriculture, fishing, and hunting, due to differences in geographical environment and living conditions, have gradually formed "village cultures" of different regions and forms. This social unit developed from the basic clan settlement pattern endows village culture with the characteristics of clan-group aggregation and blood lineage continuity; it carries the long and distant civilization history of China, and therefore is highly original and inheritable in ethnic culture; the production and life of village members and the related tangible or intangible cultural forms, from superficial general formal presentation to hidden and deep internal cultural structure and connotation, represent the cultural traditions of Chinese history, embody the full meaning of "social persons" from individual to family and clan, then to clan, finally belonging to the ethnic category, and then directly extending to the cultural level of the concept of "nation." Since the Qin and Han dynasties, according to traditional Confucian induction, Chinese traditional villages can be said to be the most basic and fundamental cultural support for the humanistic ideal of "cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and pacifying the world."

Traditional villages formed in different historical eras, different regions, and different ethnic groups carry a large amount of cultural information of different periods, regions, and ethnic groups. They are precious material and intangible cultural heritage resources of China, and an extremely important part of the world's human cultural heritage.

sections.name: 村落的由来与村落的形成及其特征
sections.content_zh:
第二节 村落的由来与村落的形成及其特征

一、文明的起源与村落的产生

村落作为农林渔牧业人群长期生活、聚居、繁衍的边界相对明晰的聚落空间和社会单元，它的起源并不是与人类的起源同时发生的，它明显是人类进化和人类文明起源时期的产物。

从距今1500万年的云南开远森林古猿到170万年前的元谋人，再到后来的蓝田人、北京人、丁村人，及至距今约3万年的北京"山顶洞人"，我们可以发现，人类从灵长类古猿经过漫长的进化而来，属于群居型动物，会制造和使用工具。这是体格相对弱小的人类在面对大自然中的凶猛动物和弱肉强食的自然法则而得以生存所特有的能力。人类进化的过程，为我们提供早期村落产生的两条线索。一是群居作为动物性本能，在人类进化过程中得到了最大限度的释放，特别是到了智人阶段，人类为了有效减少单一个体的生存困难，更是发展出了共同防御、共同生存发展的族群观念，基于血缘的聚众而居开始发生。只是，由于人类起源后在很长一段时间内完全过着采集和渔猎的经济生活，为了获取食物，需要频繁迁徙，因此并未形成长期的、固定的、规模化的居住点，物质实体空间不明显，居住方式主要是洞居、穴居和巢居。二是由于生存欲望的驱动，人类开始积极改造自己的生存方式与生存环境，因此发展出大量与生产生活有关的物质和非物质文化，包括工具、器皿、衣物、建筑和制作它们的经验、技术，以及语言、制度、道德秩序和原始信仰等。由此，动物性聚众本能开始向社会性聚居意识转变，基于血缘的原初社会组织便应运而生。氏族组织的产生，使得人类的群居行为具有了较为强烈的社会意义，地域空间上的单一的、松散无序的居民点，开始与作为社会单元的氏族组织重合，因此具有村落文化内涵和功能特征的聚落开始产生。

稻作（粟作）农业是人类食物链环节中可靠的重要一环。特别是伴随着距今1万年左右人工栽培稻和家禽动物的驯化成功，人类开始从依赖大自然的纯采集、狩猎的掠夺式经济生产方式过渡到以人工生产为主的农耕畜牧经济，使不确定的、不断迁移的居民点开始固定下来，人类从"居无定所"的迁徙流动生活方式逐步走向定居生活。定居把人类固定在土地之上，推动了农业的发展，而农业的发展又稳定并扩大了定居生活，人类社会便不断进步。正是在这一相互依存、相互促进的关系中，人类早期村落得以形成，并在规模上不断发展和扩张。带有鲜明农耕文化性质的村落，不仅其居住房屋以群团做有序排列，而且聚合性、防御性、组织性特征鲜明，很多村落都有环壕，环壕之内明显区分为生活区、墓葬区，环壕之外则为农作区。这种早期村落的发展趋势，无论是在粟作系统的黄河流域，还是在稻作系统的长江流域，都可以得到充分反映。以两湖（湖南、湖北）地区以及环洞庭湖的澧阳平原考古所见为例，从湖南道县玉蟾岩约1万年前的人工栽培稻标本出土到北面澧县彭头山遗址9000年前的稻作农业遗存，从彭头山文化的八十垱遗址到皂下文化的临澧胡家屋场遗址，再到城头山遗址7000年前的环壕农业聚落，及至鸡鸣城和距今4000余年的以鸡叫城为中心而形成的聚落群，不仅证明了村落的形成与农耕文明的发展相辅相成，而且说明了人类农耕文明发展的基础与关键是村落。粟作系统的黄河流域，其演变情况大致与此类同。

原始社会后期，村落开始分化，出现巨型聚落和普通聚落两类，以政治性、军事性为特征的城郭应运而生。从北到南，由西而东，早期中华大地上遍布的规模大小不同、形态特征各异的聚落，既证明了这样的事实，又表明最初的城郭是孕育并诞生于村落的。因为早期村落中所产生并形成的物质与非物质的文化形态，包括建筑、工具、组织、制度、道德秩序和精神信仰等，都是城郭构造的基本形态来源。刘易斯·芒福德就曾指出："城市的建筑构造和象征形式，很多都以原始形态早已出现在新石器时代的农业村庄中了……房舍、圣祠、蓄水池、公共道路、集会场地——此时尚未形成专门化的集市——这一切最初都形成于村庄环境之中；各种发明和有机分化都从这里开始，后来才逐渐发展成为城市的复杂结构。……组织化的道德、政府、法律、正义，这类事物都起源于村庄社会的长老会议。"从黄河流域仰韶文化中晚期的聚落到龙山文化时期的聚落，再到两湖地区考古所见的城头山、鸡鸣城等一系列城址和环壕聚落，乃至新近被列入《世界遗产名录》的良渚古城遗址，都是典型例证。"一年而所居成聚，二年成邑，三年成都"，由村落发展为城郭，再到出现以城郭为中心的村落簇拥依附现象，都明白无误地表露出了村落是认识和肯定中国远古文明历史的关键物证。正是这一物证充分证明了一个事实：伴随着私有制的出现，阶级产生，早期人类社会从氏族进化为部落，部落又发展到部落联盟；原有建立在氏族组织基础上的村落，开始向群体体系发展，并形成以城郭为中心聚落的地缘一体化趋势；而从地缘体到跨地缘体的形成，则意味着早期中国以国家形态开始出现，中华大地便逐步从分散走向统一，这是从血缘到地缘进而再到文明的重组与整合。

二、国家的出现与村落的行政化

按照马克思的观点，国家的实质是一个阶级统治另一个阶级，因而它的出现意味着跨地域、跨血缘、跨部落的社会关系、经济关系和政治关系的建立。国家要维系和巩固这种关系，其前提和基础是对土地与人口的全面掌控，因为二者关系到国家的人丁强弱和经济收入的多寡，是"维持统治阶级的生活条件和统治条件"。正因如此，在国家出现之后，村落作为早期人类社会最基础的地域单元、生产生活单元和社会单元，便开始具有了国家层面的意义。无论是先秦的"井田制""授田制""乡遂制"，还是秦汉的"郡县制""乡亭里制"，都充分表明了这一点。国家体制下的村落，虽然受到了来自国家的严格管控，但管控并不意味着村落发展的停滞，反而更凸显出了村落存在的重要性和必然性。考古显示，即使在实施集中城居制的秦汉时期也不同程度地散布着不同形式、不同类型的乡野聚落。马王堆三号墓出土的《地形图》《驻军图》中分别自名为"××里"的有43处和41处，均分散在地形复杂的山川地区，这不仅说明村落广泛存在，而且表明其被纳入了国家的行政管辖范围。

承接秦汉国家对村落的国家认同和实际掌控，"村"这一概念在东汉也随之出现。东汉魏伯阳的《周易参同契·鼎器妙用章》中载"得长生，居仙村"。这里的"村"即指乡野聚落。到东晋南朝时期，文献中有关"村"的记载多了起来，不少乡野聚落开始以"村"为名，并大有取代其他称谓的趋势。《三国志·魏书十六·郑浑传》载："入魏郡界，村落齐整如一，民得财足用饶。"可见，"村"作为一种名称和地域概念，在南北朝时期已被广泛接受。类似的表达在南北朝相关文献中举不胜举，据统计，仅《水经注》就出现了名"村"的聚落19处。

到隋唐，国家对村落的行政管控更为明显，介入程度也愈为加深。村落甚至被纳入了国家行政治理体系之中。在唐代，村落不再只是社会生产生活的空间，还成了国家的行政对象。这一标志性的转变，在于唐代国家在村落中设置村正以行使里正的职责，首次于行政和法律层面肯定了村落的地位。《通典·食货三·乡党》云："在邑居者为坊，别置正一人……在田野者为村，别置村正一人……"正是由于唐代的行政介入，不仅城乡分野得到国家层面的确认，而且"村"作为地域概念，也基本取代了其他称谓，成为专指乡野聚落的专有名词。日本僧人圆仁所著《入唐求法巡礼行记》中出现的56个村名，即可见一斑。

"村坊分治"措施的提出，在承认了村落合法性的同时，增强了国家权力对村落的影响与控制。当然，这种国家权力向地方社会的渗透，可能并不如以往学者们想象中的强烈，或许用"若隐若现"来形容更为妥当。不少学者一般认为我国古代"皇权不下县"，如马克斯·韦伯提出了"有限官制论"，我国社会学家费孝通先生也持类似的观点。事实上，从汉唐国家与村落社会的互动情况来看，国家权力不仅下渗到了县以下的地方社会，而且在一定程度上还体现为制度性介入。只是这种渗透和介入并非以"设置国家机构"的方式实现，而更多的是通过国家在基层的代理人体现的。譬如，汉唐时期的里长、村正，或为村落社会的父老、耋老等，到明清时期，则为所谓的乡绅。国家视野下，村落作为最基础的生活单元和最基本的社会单元，以其聚族群体性、血缘延续性和地缘一体性的特质，不仅得以继续发展，而且在与国家的互动关系中起到了增强民族的内在凝聚力与族群心理认同的作用，这对维系和巩固国家的稳定、繁荣和发展与以族群文化为基础构建起来的国家文化认同和凝聚功能等方面，起到了至关重要的作用。也许正因如此，国家与村落之间事实上有着"共同体"式的关联。

三、村落共同体的形成

"共同体"作为一个学术概念，在社会学领域最早由德国社会学家斐迪南·滕尼斯于1881年提出，他在《共同体与社会》一书中首次将共同体分为血缘共同体、地缘共同体和精神共同体三类，认为"血缘共同体作为行为的统一体发展为和分离为地缘共同体，地缘共同体直接表现为居住在一起，而地缘共同体又发展为精神共同体，作为在相同的方向上和意义上的纯粹的相互作用和支配"。按此，作为"聚族而居"的社会单元，中国村落是血缘关系优先的社会，因而属于"血缘共同体"。费孝通曾指出我国乡土社会"血缘是稳定的力量。在稳定的社会中，地缘不过是血缘的投影，不分离的"。斐迪南·滕尼斯与费孝通的总结无疑是十分精到的，但他们的这一理论尚有需要完善之处。他们的共同缺陷在于将"村落""共同体"关系仅局限在村落内部血缘族群与地缘之间，而事实上，血缘共同体的分布也有其地缘性，在一定的地域范围内，因血缘关系派生的村落从一个发展到多个，就会形成地缘共同体。不仅在理论上，而且从前揭考古遗存方面，都表明地缘共同体会形成地缘文化，而地缘文化在国家的统一之下又会上升为精神共同体，就本质而言，这就是国家精神或文化共同体。中国历史上，秦始皇统一六国的伟大意义正是在于成功创立三公九卿制度，废除分封，代以郡县，将地缘共同体统一于国家意志之下，整合成了国家文化共同体。

由此看来，对于所谓的村落共同体，我们必须从两个层面予以审视。一方面，从村落本体而言，村落共同体是指村民在共同生存的生活环境和经历的基础上形成的具有向心力或同心力的组织或合体。这个共同体具有共同的文化传统、价值观念、风俗习惯、行为规范和高度相似的心理、意识、信仰，以及共同的成员感和归属感。另一方面，从国家视野来看，作为地域单元和社会单元的村落，既是高度自治的共同体，又是国家的基层社会组织，故而国家与村落之间有着"共同体"式的关联。村落与国家的关系，不只是简单的赋税劳役方面的输出，而是在村落与国家的长期互动之中形成了一种具有普遍意义的内化于心、外化于行的家国认同。张之洞曾引用《尚书》说："爱其土物，乃能爱其乡土，爱其本国，如此则为存心良善，方能听受祖考之教训。是知必爱国敬祖，其心乃为善，若反是，则为不善也。""修身、齐家、治国、平天下"，更不只是国家对村落个体的期待，而明显带有村落个体对国家的人文理想。正是通过这种相互关联、内在互动，历朝历代无数村落社会中的个体，通过世代相继的身体力行、忠实践行，使村落社会不断传承自身内部文化，发挥社会功能，成了中国传统社会有机体的重要组成部分。

从历史发展的逻辑来看，中国村落共同体的性质，在先秦就初步形成，唐宋以降直至明清，不断完善、越发紧密，而并非如日本学者柳田节子所认为的，中国在宋代的村落，才形成地缘性的村落共同体。

事实上，从内在文化结构看，其"共同性"突出表现在4个方面。

首先是村落的宗族化发展。中国古代先民聚族而居的历史极其久远，以实体宗族的形态出现于村落，应当是在尊儒学、重纲伦礼教的两汉时期，唐宋以降不断巩固，宋代强化，尤显突出于明清，直至今日，仍是村落的一个显著特征。弗里德曼就曾说："宗族和村落明显地重叠在一起，以致许多村落只有单个宗族。"民国《歙县志·舆地志·风土》载："邑俗旧重宗法，聚族而居，每村一姓或数姓；姓各有祠，支分派别，复为支祠，堂皇闳丽，与居室相间。"不仅村落的居民姓氏体现为一至两个明显的主姓，而且形成了以族规、家训和家法等为多维伦理的儒家价值体系，构建了基于血缘的共同价值准则。

其次是村民互助体系的形成。历史文献显示，村落成员在盖房、借款、节庆礼仪和耕作、水利疏浚等方面，普遍存在相互帮忙、互相道贺、生产互助的道义成分与关系。元代王祯《农书·锄治篇》云："其北方村落之间多结为锄社，以十家为率，先锄一家之田，本家供其饮食，其余次之，旬日之间，各家田皆锄治……间有病患之家，共力助之。故苗无荒秽，岁皆丰熟……名为锄社。"南方，尤其是长江流域主要稻作区域的四川、湖北、贵州、湖南、江西各省各地，村落邻户之间则一直保存着"帮工"传统，一家有事，户户"帮工"，插秧收禾两季，"帮工"蔚然成风，越忙越帮。正是这种互助体系强化了村落成员之间的集群意识，使村落自然生成为基于村落成员高度互相依赖的生活共同体。

再次是村民信仰的同质化。作为一个封闭的、独立的、功能完备的基本社会单元，村落不仅有着明显的村落边界，而且基于这一范围产生并形成了高度一致的神明信仰，学术界称之为"祭祀圈"或"信仰圈"。中国村落文化研究中心收藏的数以千计的明清造像发愿文所录载的每一项内容，都有"××土地"的惯例，这就充分表明作为管理一方土地的神灵，"土地公"具有地域边界的意义。直至今天，湖南等地的村落社会，逢人去世都要去当地土地庙行"告知"仪式，即便没有了庙，也要在原来的土地庙址旁祭祀。正是这种共同的神明信仰使超越宗族的庙宇修葺和共同祭祀活动成为常态，不仅起到了整合村域内同宗同族内部的不同阶层的作用，而且以修建庙宇和拜祭宗族的神明的形式整合了同一地域的不同姓氏族群于同一信仰之下。杜赞奇曾在考察中国华北村庄的宗教时明确指出："在晚清时期，许多村庄除以村庙为中心的宗教组织之外，再无其他全村性的组织。所有村民被自然而然地包括在宗教组织之中，而非本村人则排斥在该组织之外。"有些村落的空间布局甚至明显受到了某种宗教或信仰的影响。

最后是村落治理的乡约化。所谓乡约，是邻里乡人互相劝勉、共同遵守的公约。根据现有的文献史料看，乡约是始于宋代的村落社会中的一种以道德教化为主要目的的制度和民间组织化自发行为。历史上，乡约在村落社会中发挥着积极作用，是村落自治、村落社会保障、村民共同生活和共同进步所形成的一个重要自治制度形式。其制度的产生、形成，源自村落自治或治理的组织。村落族群中，不仅有组织，还设有"约正"一类的执行者。现知中国历史上第一部乡约文本传为北宋熙宁九年（1076年）由蓝田吕氏兄弟制定的《吕氏乡约》。《吕氏乡约》对乡民修身、立业、齐家、交友等行为和迎来送往、婚丧嫁娶等社会性活动做出了规范性要求。这种超越个体利益，建立在群体生命意义之上的互助友爱的道德规范，体现并进一步强化了乡土社会以伦理为本位的共同价值观。宋代以降，全国各地，皆立乡约，知名的如江西的《南赣乡约》、徽州祁门的《文堂乡约》、山西的《雄山乡约》、广东的《沙堤乡约》、福建的《青阳乡约》《惠安乡约》，等等。

事实上，村落共同体的性质还体现于通婚圈和村落武装防卫等方面。关于前者，中国历史上的"舅表婚"事例就比较典型。这种婚姻制度赋予舅舅对外甥女有优先纳娶为媳妇的特殊权利。尽管这种婚姻制度带来诸多弊端，如人口生育质量低下等，但在传统中国村落社会中起到维系血缘共同体的作用。湘桂黔边境的苗族地区和部分侗族地区，直至晚清都仍然流行着这种"舅霸姑婚"的制度，就充分说明了这一点。关于后者则更为突出。历史上的很多村落，如魏晋时期的坞壁，宋代陕北、四川、湖南南部等地的堡寨，都以武装防卫为主要功能。晚清时期，为应对包括白莲教在内的各类动乱，在保甲基础上出现的地方武装组织，以及后来华北地区出现的红枪会，都体现了村落的这种共同防御功能。湖南地方的团练，成了与"太平天国"武装抗衡的国家重要军事力量。有学者甚至认为，武装自卫组织更能体现基层共同体的内聚特征，并更能强化这种内聚特征。不过，需要指出的是，这种依靠武装自卫组织所体现出的村落内聚力，主要出现于中国历史社会动荡时期，因而并不具有长期性和稳定性的特点。晚清的"湘军"在击败"太平天国"之后，尽管在当时一度成了代表国家的武装部队，但使命一结束即行被解散。不过，由此可以反观，作为"共同体"的村落与国家之间的关系也是非常显然和深刻的。

中国村落共同体形成的过程，也是村落社会发展为自给自足的封闭世界的过程。除田赋徭役、战争动乱等因素之外，传统意义上的村落群体，一方面是极少与外界发生关系的，另一方面，村落共同体实际上是服从于国家共同体的，甚至是国家共同体的重要组成部分，因而形成了与城市截然不同的经济形态、社会形态、社会形态和意识形态。从古代社会史来看，相比城郭与市镇，宋元明清时期的村落发展不仅滞后，而且继续承受着唐以来包括城市的扩张带来的生活资料的掠夺式占有、小农经济的局限和村落人口的增加在内的各方面压力。正是各种因素和压力交织在一起，到清代晚期，社会矛盾激化，农民揭竿而起，加之西方列强的入侵，使得村落人口的流动性陡增，生产生活空间的封闭性得以打破，宋元以来形成的村落共同体也渐趋弱化，包括村落在内的乡村社会开始向近现代转型。

四、村落的现代转型

吉尔伯特·罗兹曼指出："所谓走向现代化，指的是从一个以农业为基础的人均收入很低的社会，走向着重利用科学和技术的都市化和工业化社会的这样一种巨大转变。"从时间上来说，中国现代化的意识及其实践大致产生于鸦片战争前后。从洋务运动、戊戌变法、辛亥革命到新文化运动、新民主主义革命，再到社会主义革命和改革开放，这一系列运动和实践使包括村落在内的传统社会发生了较大变化：以人力和畜力为主的生产方式逐渐被批量化、规模化、标准化的机械化生产取代，生产的效率和质量得到明显提高，自给自足的小农经济渐趋瓦解。这种社会现实冲击了以农耕文明为基础的村落，在越靠近城市和交通越发达的地区，村落现代化的程度就越高，历史社会曾形成的"村落共同体"的许多功能已经趋于弱化，甚至有的村落共同体本身已经解体，但是乡约、信仰等诸多方面依然呈现出十分顽强的生命力。

这个过程经历了三个时期。第一个时期是1840—1949年。这一时期的村落开始被动地、缓慢地进行着现代化的转型。通商口岸、大型市镇等工商业相对发达和交通便利地区的周边村落，铁路发达的天津、潍坊、唐山等地的周边村落和长江三角洲地区、珠江三角洲地区的村落加快了粗犷农业的精细分工和适应商业化的转变。在此基础上，建构在农耕文明基础上的文化传统、道德价值取向观念、思维方式、宗教信仰等都发生了一定程度的变化，村落内部的同质性被降低。第二个时期是1949—1978年。这一时期的村落受到了来自国家权力的全面深刻的介入，行政权力由上而下地触及了乡土社会的最基层，村落与外界的关系被高度趋同化，村落自主性大大降低甚至消失了。集体化改造、人民公社建立和"破四旧"运动等，虽然加强了对乡村社会的控制，但弱化了村落的传统性、共同性和自主性。第三个时期是1979年至今。1979年之后，我国实行改革开放，村落去集体化，虽然国家计划经济观念不同程度地实际存在，但国家除了牢牢把握土地的国有化（哪怕是以集体土地之名）外，已经交还了村民生产的主动权和决定权。村落重新焕发新的活力。20世纪90年代之后，村落被进行着"大拆大建"的现代性改造。在这个过程中，具有浓郁农耕文明特征的以伦理为本位的传统价值体系在村落中逐渐或正在不断消解，村落共同体基本瓦解。不论出于何种目的，"大拆大建"带来了村落社会形态、经济形态和文化形态的根本性改变。

通过对中国村落发展的历史性脉络及其变迁背后的显性逻辑与隐性逻辑进行梳理，从中至少可以得出如下几点认识。

第一，村落作为定居生活的产物，它的发展、变迁不仅与中国传统农耕社会的历史演变密切相关，而且是国家与乡村之间的某些历史性和重要的互动关系的体现。在中国历史上，国家合法地垄断了全国范围内的所有资源，但由于社会网络具有过滤国家试图控制社会的某些行为的能力，因此国家对资源的垄断实质上是有限的，它往往需要通过下发不同的行政命令或是制定符合实际的法律法规，不断调适其与村落社会之间的关系，使底层社会为争夺生存生活资源而发生的行为与活动限制在国家的可控范围内。尽管这种变化是缓慢的，是若隐若现的，但不能否认村落在保持整个国家的稳定中所起到的重要作用。无论是两汉魏晋的"散村化"、唐代的"行政化"，还是历史时空下的"村落共同体"，抑或是近代以来的现代化转型，都充分体现了村落对于稳定古代社会既有社会秩序、维系国家与乡村的良性互动关系等方面的积极价值。

第二，历史上，历朝历代关于基层社会的行政编制和田赋徭役制度，虽然在很大程度上影响着村落的变迁，但村落作为一个实际存在的生产生活的聚落空间和相对稳定的社会单元，它的变迁是拥有自身内里逻辑的，除土地有限与人口膨胀之间的矛盾推动以外，还包括宗族关系、宗教信仰、道德观念和乡规民约等因素的作用。村落的历史变迁，不能片面地归因于乡村制度，还要关注制度文化以外的相关文化因素和经济、技术与社会的作用，以及自然地理等诸多因素。

第三，村落是建立在农耕文明发展的基础之上的。土地是农耕文明不可或缺的依赖要素。然而，在传统农耕社会向现代工业社会转型的过程中，村落逐渐失去了依托的土壤，社会发展的客观事实使农村城镇化不可避免，村落在经济、社会和文化形态上正在发生千年不遇的深刻变局。村落将何去何从？村落会终结吗？如果按照发展的规律，发展是事物的本质，任何一种文化现象，一旦丧失社会功能，缺乏变化、创新和发展的潜能，很快就会被历史湮灭或同化，村落当亦是如此。但是，我们要充分意识到，对一个历史悠久的文明古国来说，村落的现代转型是可能的，这种转型应该建立在对传统的批判性继承的基础之上，而非"推倒重来"或全盘西化。要守护村落，振兴乡村，关键在于重塑乡土价值，发挥文化的"活态"效应。

Section 2: Origins of Villages, Their Formation and Characteristics

I. Origins of Civilization and the Emergence of Villages

As a settlement space and social unit with relatively clear boundaries where people engaged in agriculture, forestry, fishing, and animal husbandry live, gather, and reproduce for a long time, the origin of villages did not occur simultaneously with the origin of humanity. It is clearly a product of the period of human evolution and the origin of human civilization.

From the Kaiyuan forest ape in Yunnan 15 million years ago to the Yuanmou Man 1.7 million years ago, then to the Lantian Man, Peking Man, and Dingcun Man, and finally to the "Upper Cave Man" in Beijing about 30,000 years ago, we can see that humans evolved from primate apes through a long process, are social animals, and can make and use tools. This is the unique ability of relatively weak humans to survive in the face of fierce animals in nature and the law of the jungle where the strong prey on the weak. The process of human evolution provides us with two clues to the emergence of early villages. First, gregariousness as an animal instinct was maximally released in the process of human evolution. Especially at the stage of Homo sapiens, in order to effectively reduce the survival difficulties of individuals, humans developed the ethnic concept of common defense and common survival and development, and gathering based on blood lineage began to occur. However, for a long time after human origins, humans lived a gathering and fishing-hunting economic life. To obtain food, they needed to migrate frequently, so they did not form long-term, fixed, and large-scale settlements. The material entity space was not obvious, and the living methods were mainly cave dwelling, rock shelter dwelling, and nest dwelling. Second, driven by the desire for survival, humans began to actively transform their survival methods and living environment, thus developing a large amount of material and non-material culture related to production and life, including tools, vessels, clothing, architecture, and the experience and technology of making them, as well as language, institutions, moral order, and primitive beliefs. As a result, animal gregarious instinct began to transform into social settlement consciousness, and the original social organization based on blood lineage emerged. The emergence of clan organization gave human gregarious behavior a relatively strong social meaning. The single, loose, and disorderly settlements in geographical space began to coincide with clans as social units, thus settlements with village cultural connotations and functional characteristics began to emerge.

Rice (millet) agriculture is a reliable and important link in the human food chain. Especially with the successful domestication of artificially cultivated rice and poultry animals around 10,000 years ago, humans began to transition from a predatory economic production mode of pure gathering and hunting dependent on nature to an agricultural and pastoral economy based on artificial production, making uncertain and constantly migrating settlements begin to settle down. Humans gradually moved from a nomadic lifestyle of "no fixed abode" to a settled life. Settlement fixed humans on the land, promoting the development of agriculture, and the development of agriculture in turn stabilized and expanded settled life, and human society continued to progress. It is in this interdependent and mutually promoting relationship that early human villages were formed and continuously developed and expanded in scale. Villages with distinct agricultural cultural characteristics not only had their houses arranged in an orderly manner in groups, but also had distinct characteristics of aggregation, defense, and organization. Many villages had moats, with living areas and burial areas clearly distinguished inside the moats, and farming areas outside the moats. This development trend of early villages can be fully reflected both in the Yellow River basin of the millet system and the Yangtze River basin of the rice system. Taking archaeological findings in the Two Lakes (Hunan and Hubei) region and the Liyang Plain around Dongting Lake as examples, from the excavation of artificially cultivated rice specimens about 10,000 years ago at Yuchanyan Cave in Daoxian County, Hunan, to the rice agricultural remains 9,000 years ago at the Pengtoushan site in Li County to the north, from the Bashidang site of Pengtoushan culture to the Linli Huajiawuchang site of Zaoxia culture, then to the moated agricultural settlement 7,000 years ago at the Chengtoushan site, and finally to the settlement group centered on Jijiaocheng about 4,000 years ago, this not only proves that the formation of villages and the development of agricultural civilization complement each other, but also shows that the foundation and key to the development of human agricultural civilization is the village. The evolution in the Yellow River basin of the millet system is roughly similar.

In the late primitive society, villages began to differentiate, appearing as two types: giant settlements and ordinary settlements, and city walls with political and military characteristics emerged as the times required. From north to south, from west to east, settlements of different sizes and morphological characteristics spread across early China, which both proves this fact and shows that the earliest city walls were nurtured and born from villages. Because the material and non-material cultural forms produced and formed in early villages, including architecture, tools, organizations, institutions, moral order, and spiritual beliefs, are the basic morphological sources of city wall construction. Lewis Mumford once pointed out: "Many of the architectural constructions and symbolic forms of the city already appeared in primitive form in Neolithic agricultural villages... houses, shrines, cisterns, public roads, assembly grounds—at this time not yet specialized marketplaces—all these initially formed in the village environment; various inventions and organic differentiations began here, and later gradually developed into the complex structure of the city... Organized morality, government, law, justice, these things originated from the council of elders in village society." From settlements in the middle and late Yangshao culture in the Yellow River basin to settlements in the Longshan culture period, then to a series of city sites and moated settlements such as Chengtoushan and Jijiaocheng found archaeologically in the Two Lakes region, and even the Liangzhu ancient city site recently listed in the World Heritage List, are typical examples. "In one year it became a settlement, in two years it became a town, in three years it became a capital," from villages developing into city walls, then to the emergence of village clustering around city walls, all clearly show that villages are key material evidence for understanding and affirming the history of ancient Chinese civilization. It is this material evidence that fully proves a fact: with the emergence of private ownership, classes arose, and early human society evolved from clans to tribes, and tribes developed into tribal alliances; villages originally based on clan organizations began to develop toward group systems, forming a trend of geographical integration centered on city-wall settlements; and the formation from geographical entities to cross-geographical entities means that early China began to appear in the form of a state, and the Chinese land gradually moved from dispersion to unification, which is the reorganization and integration from blood lineage to geography and then to civilization.

II. The Emergence of the State and the Administrative Nature of Villages

According to Marx, the essence of the state is the rule of one class over another, so its emergence means the establishment of cross-regional, cross-bloodline, and cross-tribal social, economic, and political relations. To maintain and consolidate these relations, the premise and foundation for the state is comprehensive control over land and population, because both relate to the strength of the state's population and the amount of economic income, and are "the conditions for maintaining the living and ruling conditions of the ruling class." For this reason, after the emergence of the state, villages, as the most basic geographical unit, production and life unit, and social unit of early human society, began to have significance at the state level. Whether it was the "well-field system," "land-granting system," and "township-suburb system" in the pre-Qin period, or the "commandery-county system" and "township-ting-li system" in the Qin and Han dynasties, this point is fully demonstrated. Villages under the state system, although subject to strict control from the state, control does not mean the stagnation of village development, but rather highlights the importance and necessity of the existence of villages. Archaeology shows that even in the Qin and Han dynasties when centralized city residence was implemented, rural settlements of different forms and types were scattered to varying degrees. The "Topographic Map" and "Troop Station Map" unearthed from Tomb No. 3 at Mawangdui respectively have 43 and 41 places named "×× li," all scattered in mountain and river areas with complex terrain, which not only shows that villages existed widely, but also indicates that they were incorporated into the state's administrative jurisdiction.

Following the Qin and Han states' national recognition and actual control over villages, the concept of "village" (cun) also emerged in the Eastern Han Dynasty. Wei Boyang of the Eastern Han Dynasty wrote in Zhouyi Cantongqi · Dingqi Miaoyong Zhang: "Attaining longevity, dwelling in an immortal village." Here "village" refers to rural settlements. By the Eastern Jin and Southern Dynasties period, there were more records about "villages" in literature, and many rural settlements began to be named "village," with a trend of replacing other terms. Records of the Three Kingdoms · Wei Shu 16 · Biography of Zheng Hun records: "Entering the boundary of Wei Commandery, villages were neat and uniform, and the people obtained sufficient wealth and use." It can be seen that "village" as a name and geographical concept was widely accepted in the Northern and Southern Dynasties period. Similar expressions are numerous in relevant literature of the Northern and Southern Dynasties. According to statistics, the Commentary on the Water Classic alone has 19 settlements named "village."

By the Sui and Tang dynasties, the state's administrative control over villages became more obvious, and the degree of intervention deepened. Villages were even incorporated into the state's administrative governance system. In the Tang Dynasty, villages were no longer just spaces for social production and life, but also became administrative objects of the state. This landmark change lies in the Tang state setting up village chiefs (cunzheng) in villages to exercise the duties of li chiefs, affirming the status of villages at the administrative and legal levels for the first time. Tongdian · Shihuo 3 · Xiangdang states: "Those living in towns are wards (fang), each with a ward chief... those living in the countryside are villages (cun), each with a village chief..." It was precisely due to the administrative intervention of the Tang Dynasty that not only was the urban-rural division confirmed at the state level, but "village" as a geographical concept also basically replaced other terms, becoming a proper noun specifically referring to rural settlements. The 56 village names appearing in the Japanese monk Ennin's Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law give a glimpse of this.

The proposal of the "village-ward separate governance" measure, while recognizing the legitimacy of villages, enhanced the influence and control of state power over villages. Of course, this penetration of state power into local society may not be as strong as previously imagined by scholars; perhaps "looming" is a more appropriate description. Many scholars generally believe that in ancient China "imperial power did not extend below the county." For example, Max Weber proposed the "limited official system theory," and Chinese sociologist Fei Xiaotong held a similar view. In fact, judging from the interaction between the state and village society in the Han and Tang dynasties, state power not only penetrated into local society below the county, but also manifested as institutional intervention to a certain extent. It is just that this penetration and intervention were not realized by "setting up state institutions," but more through the state's agents at the grassroots level. For example, the li chiefs and village chiefs in the Han and Tang dynasties, or the village elders and venerable old men in village society, and by the Ming and Qing dynasties, the so-called local gentry. From the state's perspective, villages, as the most basic living unit and social unit, with their characteristics of clan-group aggregation, blood lineage continuity, and geographical integration, not only continued to develop, but also played a role in enhancing the internal cohesion of the nation and ethnic psychological identity in the interactive relationship with the state. This played a crucial role in maintaining and consolidating the stability, prosperity, and development of the country, as well as the national cultural identity and cohesion function built on ethnic culture. Perhaps for this reason, there is in fact a "community"-type connection between the state and villages.

III. Formation of Village Communities

"Community" as an academic concept was first proposed in the field of sociology by German sociologist Ferdinand Tönnies in 1881. In his book Community and Society, he first divided communities into three types: blood community, geographical community, and spiritual community, believing that "blood community, as a unified body of behavior, develops into and separates into geographical community, which directly manifests as living together, and geographical community then develops into spiritual community, as pure interaction and domination in the same direction and meaning." Accordingly, as a social unit of "living together as a clan," Chinese villages are societies where blood relations take priority, and thus belong to "blood communities." Fei Xiaotong once pointed out that in China's rural society "blood lineage is a stable force. In a stable society, geography is but a projection of blood lineage, inseparable." The summaries of Ferdinand Tönnies and Fei Xiaotong are undoubtedly very precise, but their theory still needs improvement. Their common defect lies in limiting the "village" and "community" relationship only to blood clans and geography within the village. In fact, the distribution of blood communities also has its geographical nature. Within a certain geographical range, when villages derived from blood relations develop from one to many, a geographical community will form. Not only in theory, but also from the archaeological remains mentioned above, it is shown that geographical communities form geographical culture, and geographical culture, under the unification of the state, rises to spiritual community. Essentially, this is the national spiritual or cultural community. In Chinese history, the great significance of Qin Shi Huang's unification of the six states lies precisely in successfully establishing the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers system, abolishing enfeoffment, replacing it with commanderies and counties, unifying geographical communities under the national will, and integrating them into a national cultural community.

From this perspective, regarding the so-called village community, we must examine it from two levels. On the one hand, from the village itself, a village community refers to an organization or entity with centripetal force or concentric force formed by villagers on the basis of a common living environment and shared experiences. This community has common cultural traditions, values, customs, behavioral norms, and highly similar psychology, consciousness, beliefs, as well as a common sense of membership and belonging. On the other hand, from the state's perspective, villages, as geographical units and social units, are both highly autonomous communities and the state's grassroots social organizations, so there is a "community"-type connection between the state and villages. The relationship between villages and the state is not simply the output of taxes and corvée, but in the long-term interaction between villages and the state, a universally meaningful national identity internalized in the heart and externalized in behavior has been formed. Zhang Zhidong once quoted the Book of Documents: "Loving one's local products, one can love one's native land, love one's country, and thus have a good conscience, and can listen to and receive the teachings of ancestors. Thus one must love the country and respect ancestors, then one's heart is good; otherwise, it is not good." "Cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and pacifying the world" is not only the state's expectation for village individuals, but clearly carries the humanistic ideal of village individuals toward the state. It is through this interrelation and internal interaction that countless individuals in village society throughout history, through generations of personal practice and faithful implementation, have enabled village society to continuously inherit its internal culture and perform social functions, becoming an important part of the organism of traditional Chinese society.

From the logic of historical development, the nature of Chinese village communities initially formed in the pre-Qin period, and from the Tang and Song dynasties until the Ming and Qing dynasties, continuously improved and became increasingly close, rather than as Japanese scholar Yanagida Setsuko believed that Chinese villages only formed geographical village communities in the Song Dynasty.

In fact, from the internal cultural structure, its "commonality" is prominently manifested in four aspects.

First is the clan-based development of villages. The history of ancient Chinese ancestors living together as clans is extremely long. The appearance of entity clans in villages should be in the Western and Eastern Han dynasties when Confucianism was respected and Confucian ethical codes were emphasized. From the Tang and Song dynasties onward, they were continuously consolidated, strengthened in the Song Dynasty, particularly prominent in the Ming and Qing dynasties, and even today remain a significant feature of villages. Freedman once said: "Lineages and villages clearly overlap, so much so that many villages have only a single lineage." The Republic of China She County Gazetteer · Geography · Local Customs records: "The local tradition values clan law, people live together as clans, each village has one or several surnames; each surname has an ancestral hall, with branches and sub-branches, and branch halls, grand and beautiful, interspersed with residences." Not only do village residents' surnames reflect one or two obvious main surnames, but also a Confucian value system with multi-dimensional ethics such as clan rules, family instructions, and family laws has been formed, constructing common value criteria based on blood lineage.

Second is the formation of villagers' mutual aid systems. Historical documents show that village members generally have moral components and relationships of mutual help, mutual congratulations, and production mutual aid in aspects such as house building, borrowing, festival rituals, farming, and water conservancy dredging. Wang Zhen of the Yuan Dynasty wrote in Nongshu · Chuzhi Pian: "In northern villages, people often form weeding associations, with ten families as a unit, first weeding one family's field, the family provides food and drink, then the others in turn, within ten days all families' fields are weeded... if there is a sick family, everyone helps together. Thus seedlings are not neglected, and years are abundant... called weeding associations." In the south, especially in the major rice-growing regions of the Yangtze River basin such as Sichuan, Hubei, Guizhou, Hunan, and Jiangxi, neighboring households in villages have always maintained the "helping hands" tradition. When one family has an event, every household "helps." During the two seasons of transplanting and harvesting, "helping hands" becomes a common practice, the busier the more help. It is this mutual aid system that strengthens the collective consciousness among village members, making villages naturally become life communities based on high interdependence among village members.

Third is the homogenization of villagers' beliefs. As a closed, independent, and fully functional basic social unit, villages not only have obvious village boundaries, but also based on this scope produce and form highly consistent deity beliefs, which academia calls "sacrifice circles" or "belief circles." Every item recorded in the thousands of Ming and Qing statue dedication vows collected by the China Village Culture Research Center has the convention of "×× land," which fully shows that as the deity managing the land of one area, "Lord of the Land" has the significance of geographical boundaries. Even today, in village societies in Hunan and other places, when someone passes away, they must go to the local Earth God Temple to perform an "announcement" ritual; even if there is no longer a temple, they must sacrifice beside the original Earth God Temple site. It is this common deity belief that makes temple renovation and common sacrificial activities beyond clans become normal, not only playing a role in integrating different strata within the same clan in the village, but also integrating different surname groups in the same region under the same belief in the form of building temples and worshipping clan deities. Duara clearly pointed out when examining religion in North China villages: "In the late Qing period, many villages, apart from religious organizations centered on village temples, had no other village-wide organizations. All villagers were naturally included in religious organizations, while non-villagers were excluded from these organizations." The spatial layout of some villages is even clearly influenced by some religion or belief.

Fourth is the village covenant-based governance of villages. The so-called village covenant (xiangyue) is a convention that neighbors and villagers mutually exhort and jointly abide by. According to existing historical documents, village covenants are a system and spontaneous folk organizational behavior that began in the Song Dynasty in village society, with the main purpose of moral education. Historically, village covenants played a positive role in village society and were an important autonomous system formed by village self-governance, village social security, and villagers' common life and progress. The emergence and formation of this system originated from the organization of village autonomy or governance. Among village clans, there were not only organizations, but also executors such as "covenant directors." The earliest known village covenant text in Chinese history is said to be the Lü Clan Village Covenant formulated by the Lü brothers of Lantian in the ninth year of Xining of the Northern Song Dynasty (1076). The Lü Clan Village Covenant made normative requirements for villagers' self-cultivation, career establishment, family regulation, friendship-making behaviors, and social activities such as visiting, weddings, and funerals. This moral norm of mutual help and friendship beyond individual interests, based on the meaning of group life, embodies and further strengthens the common values of rural society with ethics as the foundation. From the Song Dynasty onward, village covenants were established throughout the country, well-known ones such as Jiangxi's Southern Jiangxi Village Covenant, Qimen's Wentang Village Covenant in Huizhou, Shanxi's Xiongshan Village Covenant, Guangdong's Shadi Village Covenant, Fujian's Qingyang Village Covenant and Hui'an Village Covenant, etc.

In fact, the nature of village communities is also reflected in marriage circles and village armed defense. Regarding the former, the example of "mother's brother cross-cousin marriage" in Chinese history is typical. This marriage system gave the mother's brother the special right to优先 marry his sister's daughter as his daughter-in-law. Although this marriage system brought many drawbacks, such as low population reproduction quality, it played a role in maintaining blood communities in traditional Chinese village society. In the Miao areas on the borders of Hunan, Guangxi, and Guizhou and some Dong areas, this "uncle dominating aunt marriage" system was still popular until the late Qing Dynasty, which fully illustrates this point. Regarding the latter, it is even more prominent. Many villages in history, such as the fortresses (wubi) in the Wei and Jin dynasties, and the fortified villages (baozhai) in northern Shaanxi, Sichuan, and southern Hunan in the Song Dynasty, had armed defense as their main function. In the late Qing period, to cope with various uprisings including the White Lotus Society, local armed organizations emerged on the basis of baojia, and later the Red Spears Society in North China, all reflecting this common defense function of villages. The local militia (tuanlian) in Hunan became an important national military force抗衡 the "Taiping Heavenly Kingdom" armed forces. Some scholars even believe that armed self-defense organizations better reflect the cohesive characteristics of grassroots communities and can strengthen this cohesion. However, it should be pointed out that the village cohesion reflected through armed self-defense organizations mainly appeared in turbulent periods of Chinese history, and thus does not have the characteristics of long-term and stability. The "Hunan Army" in the late Qing, after defeating the "Taiping Heavenly Kingdom," although it once became the armed force representing the country at that time, was disbanded as soon as its mission ended. Nevertheless, from this we can see that the relationship between villages as "communities" and the state is also very obvious and profound.

The process of the formation of Chinese village communities is also the process of village society developing into a self-sufficient closed world. In addition to factors such as land taxes, corvée, wars, and turmoil, traditional village groups, on the one hand, rarely had relations with the outside world; on the other hand, village communities actually submitted to the national community, and were even an important part of the national community, thus forming economic forms, social forms, and ideologies completely different from cities. From the perspective of ancient social history, compared with city walls and market towns, the development of villages in the Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties was not only lagging, but also continued to bear various pressures since the Tang Dynasty, including the predatory occupation of living materials brought by urban expansion, the limitations of small-scale peasant economy, and the increase of village population. It was precisely the intertwining of various factors and pressures that by the late Qing Dynasty, social contradictions intensified, peasants rose up, and coupled with the invasion of Western powers, the mobility of village population increased sharply, the closure of production and living spaces was broken, and the village communities formed since the Song and Yuan dynasties gradually weakened, and rural society including villages began to transform toward modern times.

IV. Modern Transformation of Villages

Gilbert Rozman pointed out: "The so-called moving toward modernization refers to such a huge transformation from a society based on agriculture with very low per capita income to an urbanized and industrialized society emphasizing the use of science and technology." In terms of time, China's modernization consciousness and practice roughly emerged around the Opium War. From the Westernization Movement, the Hundred Days' Reform, the 1911 Revolution to the New Culture Movement, the New Democratic Revolution, then to the Socialist Revolution and Reform and Opening Up, this series of movements and practices caused great changes in traditional society including villages: the production mode mainly based on human and animal power was gradually replaced by batch, large-scale, and standardized mechanized production, production efficiency and quality were significantly improved, and the self-sufficient small-scale peasant economy gradually collapsed. This social reality impacted villages based on agricultural civilization. The closer to cities and the more developed the transportation, the higher the degree of village modernization. Many functions of the "village community" formed in historical society have tended to weaken, and even some village communities themselves have disintegrated, but village covenants, beliefs, and many other aspects still show very tenacious vitality.

This process went through three periods. The first period was 1840-1949. During this period, villages began to undergo modern transformation passively and slowly. Villages around trading ports, large market towns and other areas with relatively developed industry and commerce and convenient transportation, villages around Tianjin, Weifang, Tangshan and other places with developed railways, and villages in the Yangtze River Delta and Pearl River Delta regions accelerated the refined division of rough agriculture and the transformation to adapt to commercialization. On this basis, cultural traditions, moral value orientations, ways of thinking, religious beliefs, etc. built on agricultural civilization all underwent certain changes, and the homogeneity within villages was reduced. The second period was 1949-1978. During this period, villages received comprehensive and profound intervention from state power, administrative power reached the grassroots of rural society from top to bottom, the relationship between villages and the outside world was highly homogenized, and village autonomy was greatly reduced or even disappeared. Collectivization transformation, the establishment of people's communes, and the "destroy the four olds" movement, although strengthening control over rural society, weakened the tradition, commonality, and autonomy of villages. The third period is from 1979 to the present. After 1979, China implemented reform and opening up, villages were de-collectivized. Although the concept of planned economy still exists to varying degrees, except for firmly grasping the nationalization of land (even in the name of collective land), the state has returned the initiative and decision-making power of villagers' production. Villages regained new vitality. After the 1990s, villages underwent "large-scale demolition and construction" modern transformation. In this process, the traditional value system based on ethics with strong agricultural civilization characteristics is gradually or constantly dissolving in villages, and village communities have basically disintegrated. Regardless of the purpose, "large-scale demolition and construction" brought fundamental changes to village social forms, economic forms, and cultural forms.

By sorting out the historical context of Chinese village development and the dominant and hidden logic behind its changes, at least the following understandings can be drawn.

First, villages, as products of settled life, their development and changes are not only closely related to the historical evolution of traditional Chinese agricultural society, but also a reflection of certain historical and important interactive relations between the state and rural areas. In Chinese history, the state legally monopolized all resources nationwide, but because social networks have the ability to filter certain behaviors of the state trying to control society, the state's monopoly of resources is essentially limited. It often needs to issue different administrative orders or formulate practical laws and regulations to continuously adjust its relationship with village society, so that the behaviors and activities of grassroots society fighting for survival resources are limited within the state's controllable range. Although this change is slow and looming, it cannot be denied that villages played an important role in maintaining the stability of the entire country. Whether it was the "scattered villagization" in the Han, Wei, and Jin dynasties, the "administrativization" in the Tang Dynasty, the "village community" in historical time and space, or the modern transformation since modern times, all fully demonstrate the positive value of villages in stabilizing the existing social order of ancient society and maintaining the benign interactive relationship between the state and rural areas.

Second, historically, the administrative organization of grassroots society and the land tax and corvée systems of various dynasties, although greatly affecting village changes, villages, as an actually existing settlement space for production and life and a relatively stable social unit, have their own internal logic of change. In addition to the contradiction between limited land and population expansion, it also includes factors such as clan relations, religious beliefs, moral concepts, and village rules and conventions. The historical changes of villages cannot be one-sidedly attributed to the rural system, but also need to pay attention to relevant cultural factors beyond institutional culture, the role of economy, technology, and society, as well as natural geography and many other factors.

Third, villages are built on the basis of the development of agricultural civilization. Land is an indispensable dependent element of agricultural civilization. However, in the process of transformation from traditional agricultural society to modern industrial society, villages gradually lose the soil they rely on. The objective fact of social development makes rural urbanization inevitable, and villages are undergoing profound changes unseen in a thousand years in economic, social, and cultural forms. Where will villages go? Will villages end? If according to the law of development, development is the essence of things. Any cultural phenomenon, once it loses social function and lacks the potential for change, innovation, and development, will soon be annihilated or assimilated by history, and villages are no exception. However, we must fully realize that for a country with a long civilization history, the modern transformation of villages is possible. This transformation should be based on the critical inheritance of tradition, rather than "tearing down and rebuilding" or total Westernization. To protect villages and revitalize rural areas, the key lies in reshaping rural values and发挥 the "living" effect of culture.

sections.name: 中国村落的特征
sections.content_zh:
第三节 中国村落的特征

人们定居下来以后，为了生存，必然会在一定的范围内进行生产生活和繁衍，在生产生活的过程中不断积累相关的经验，耕种以谋生，建房以居住，交流以相处。日积月累，不断发展，于是生发出相应的文化。概而言之，所谓传统村落文化的范畴，即是指在传统农耕社会中，人们在群居的基础上进行的系列生产生活的过程中所形成的一切物质文化和非物质文化的总和。也就是说，传统村落文化不仅包括有形的建筑文化，而且应该包括生活在传统村落中的"人"，以及由"人"所创造、传承的一切有形的和无形的文化形态。

有形的显性的文化形态，大多体现在传统建筑中，甚至隐性的文化也有在建筑中予以体现和反映的。以长江中游的湖南地方为例，如湘中的府第式建筑，往往是以一家人或一个家族为一个整体的大院落，其建筑从空间布局到功能体现忠实地遵循着传统汉文化的礼乐秩序，甚至制度文化意义重于实际居住功能的需求。如双峰曾国藩的家府，就是儒家居住等级与制度文化的典范。"中为堂，左为尊，右为次"，"东阶为主，西厢待客"，没有丝毫的僭越或者疏忽，可谓"秩序井然"。而湘南地区郴州一带聚族而居的村落，往往是一栋栋独立的住宅，此接彼连，整体上形成气势恢宏的村落。虽然每一个住宅同样体现了礼乐秩序的传统精神，但从大的格局来看，单个住宅之间既相对独立，又维系在一个族群的大框架系统之中，与祠堂等公共建筑相匹配，在"慎终追远""长幼有序、尊卑有别"的儒家伦理文化的基本体系之下，独立的空间布局便于营造出相对宽松的人际关系和生存理念，个体的主观独立愿望在客观的空间布局中基本可以得到尊重，与湘中的大宅院把个体（人）完全淹没于隐性的制度文化之中形成明显差别。这种差别，不仅仅体现在建筑文化上，也反映在建筑的壁画上，湘中和湘南呈现出两种完全不同的基调。湘中府第式庄园建筑上的壁画，多能见到以人伦秩序教化为主题内容的庄重严肃的题材，如同家训，成教化、助人伦的劝诱功能已超出了作为绘画艺术自身应当具备的审美愉悦。即便是应当使人轻松的戏剧题材，也蒙上了些许沉郁的威仪。而在湘南，富有个性化的艺术表达则非常突出和典型。正襟危坐的家训式场景描绘很少见，而纯粹欣赏性的山水楼台、花鸟人物和雅士偏好的松、竹、梅、兰题材则成为主流。从绘画的技法看，湘中地区的壁画技法讲究规整严谨，无一不呈现出正统文化的气息，令观者不由得端正严肃、敬而畏之。湘南地区的壁画则并无太多的技法讲究和制约，笔随意走、画由兴出，所以信笔而行，是技法依我，而不是我就技法，其凸显的是文人意趣与情致，往往令观者赏心悦目、神而往之。而与湘中、湘南相对应的湘西南、湘西北少数民族建筑，则多为依山傍水、就地取材的干栏式。它们错落于青山绿水、茂林修竹之间，与之浑然一体、亲切和谐，没有丝毫的矫情和富贵逼人的气息，展示出朴实无华却不乏热烈豁达的民族情怀。其壁画更富灵动浪漫的精神气象与神秘奇异色彩，呈现的是与湘中、湘南不同的建筑文化和建筑艺术精神，可令观者深刻领悟到人—建筑—自然三者间最为真切友好的关系。

村落生活中的无形文化更是比比皆是，比如：端午吃粽子和中秋吃月饼体现的是民俗文化；清明扫墓体现的是宗族文化；过年时的祭祖祭天体现的是祭祀文化；春天播种，夏天除草，秋天收获，冬天收藏体现的是生产文化。村落中的家法族规与乡规民约更是礼仪文化的集结地，如明代大儒王阳明《南赣乡约》云："故今特为乡约，以协和尔民。自今凡尔等同约之民，皆宜孝尔父母，敬尔兄长，教训尔子孙，和顺尔乡里。死丧相助，患难相恤，善相劝勉，恶相告戒，息讼罢争，讲信修睦。务为良善之民，共成仁厚之俗。"该乡约中详细规定了人们的行为规范：孝敬父母、尊重长辈、和睦乡邻、戒恶行善、忠厚仁义等。人们正是秉承着这些行为规范代代相传，生生不息，积淀成深厚的文化内涵。真所谓"小村落，大文化"！

中国村落及其文化呈现出鲜明的个性特征，主要表现在四个方面。

一、村落的活态性特征

"活态"是传统村落文化最突出的特征之一。所谓"活态"，是指传统村落文化呈现独特的生命力，延续数百年甚至上千年而依然发挥着固有的功能，至今仍是传统村落中原住民生活的一部分，如村落的古井依然流水潺潺，为村民生活用水提供方便；池塘依旧发挥着生态调节的功能；还有小桥、古树，风景犹在；祠堂、古塔等建筑虽然改变了原始功能，但在居民心中依然是神圣之所，意义未泯；传统的方言依然是村落中交流的主要方式；祖宗的灵位依旧立在神龛上面，被恭敬地供奉着；街道古巷里村落历史的足迹清晰可辨；各种故事、历史传说依然回荡在村落的上空。所以，传统村落被誉为"活化石""活态博物馆"。

费孝通说："祖先们在这地方混熟了，他们的经验也必然就是子孙们所会得到的经验。时间的悠久是从谱系上说的，从每个人可能得到的经验说，却是同一方式的反复重演。同一戏台上演着同一的戏，这个班子里演员所需要记得的，也只有一套戏文。他们个别的经验，就等于世代的经验。经验无需不断累积，只需老是保存。"又说："当一个人碰着生活上的问题时，他必然能在一个比他年长的人那里问得到解决这问题的有效办法，因为大家在同一环境里，走同一道路，他先走，你后走；后走的所踏的是先走的人的脚印，口口相传，不会有遗漏。"费孝通揭示了传统村落中两个很重要的文化现象：经验与传承。在传统村落中，世世代代累积的经验就是很重要的村落文化。而这种经验的累积，人们并不是用文字的方式记录下来，而是通过口传和不断重复践行的方式传承下来。

简而言之，传统村落文化虽然传承了数百年甚至上千年，但依然发挥着固有的功能。我们从现有的村落原住民的生产生活中，穿越时空的隧道，依然能感受到数百年甚至上千年前他们的祖先生活的情形。

城邑中的精英文化，往往是由文化精英们通过文字记录的方式传播的，并保存在典籍中；传统村落中原住民更多的是用口口相传、代代相承的方式，在言传身教的行为中传递自己的文化。

相对而言，城邑文化趋于静态，而村落文化是动态的；城邑文化是文字的，村落文化是口语的。在传统村落社会，人们既是文化的创造者，又是传承者和践行者；不仅表现为"知"，而且鲜明地突出"行"，"知"规范"行"，"行"实践"知"。知行合一的活态，正是传统村落文化的突出表现。传统村落中这种"活态"的文化，显示出了强大的生命力，成为中华文化中最具象征性的民族文化。因而，研究和保护好这种"活态"的文化，意义十分重大。这种"活态"文化在历史中数千年了，我们不仅有责任让这种"活态"文化活在当下，而且有义务让其活向未来，成为永远。然而，到了当今世界，在现代工业化和城镇化的进程中，绝大多数传统村落面临着极其严峻的情势。如何保持传统村落文化的"活态"，已经成了当前人类学、社会学、历史学等多学科研究的全新的重要课题，并且这种课题的研究很难以某一单一学科独立地、相对完整地完成。所以，多学科的交叉介入研究，将成为一种必需。

二、村落的血缘性特征

村落的初期形态，最早可以追溯到远古时期的部落生活，并延续数千年而不绝。在其发展历程中，不论是哪种类型的村落形态，也不论村落的形态历经了多少变迁，血缘性一直都是村落文化的重要特征。

在农耕生活的初始时期，人类的生产能力极为低下，仅凭个人几乎很难生存，所以必须依靠群体才能谋生，而最可靠的则是人类与生俱来的血缘关系形成的群体，最有效的是以血缘关系为基础的生活方式。可以想见，人类最早的群体应该是以血缘关系为纽带的氏族。恩格斯指出："一定历史时代和一定地区内的人们生活于其下的社会制度，受着两种生产的制约：一方面受劳动的发展阶段的制约，另一方面受家庭的发展阶段的制约。劳动越不发展，劳动产品的数量、从而社会的财富越受限制，社会制度就越在较大程度上受血族关系的支配。"在远古时代，生产力极其低下，单靠个人的独立生活是不可想象的，只有依靠血缘亲族团体才能生存下去。这时，人们的血缘关系与地位显得尤为重要和突出，它支配着人们的一切。"全盛时期的氏族制度……其前提是生产极不发达，因而……部落始终是人们的界限，无论对另一部落的人来说，或者对他们自己来说，都是如此：部落、氏族及其制度，都是神圣不可侵犯的，都是自然所赋予的最高权力，个人在感情、思想和行动上始终是无条件服从的。"在远古部落时期，血缘关系是最强有力的联系纽带。摩尔根在谈到部落联盟建立条件时说："氏族所体现的亲属感情、各氏族的同宗关系，以及他们的方言仍能相互理解，这三者为联盟提供了重要的因素。"在远古时期的部落内，血缘关系可以说是最根本的关系，而没有任何血缘关系的人几乎很难在一个部落内立足。

到了西周时期，血缘关系进一步引申出以家族为主的宗法制。在远古时期的部落社会为了生存而自发形成的以血缘为基础的群体关系，到了"西周，不仅没有采取过破坏氏族的改革，反而经过'维新'，把旧的氏族机关和氏族制度大量移用到阶级社会中，这就不能不给血缘关系的保存留下很大余地"。

"族者，凑也，聚也。谓恩爱相流凑也。上凑高族，下至玄孙，一家有吉，百家聚之，合而为亲，生相亲爱，死相哀痛，有会聚之道，故谓之族。"一个家族长期居住在同一个地方，动辄数代至十数代甚至数十代，于是，在长期的生产生活过程中，就慢慢形成了"聚族而居"的以家族宗法制为中心的村落社会结构。

家族宗法制是中国古代社会独特的社会结构与制度。中国原始社会中以婚姻和血缘关系组合而成的家族制度，在阶级社会中发展为维护剥削阶级世袭特权的家族宗法制。商代奴隶制在血缘关系基础上形成种族奴隶制国家，周代"封诸侯、建同姓"把家族宗法组织作为奴隶制国家的组织形态。此后，封建制虽然取代了奴隶制，但是家族宗法制的社会组织并没有改变。最直接的原因是适应于奴隶制的家族宗法制并没有妨碍于封建制，恰恰相反，家族宗法制又继续适应甚至更加适应封建制。战国秦汉以来的乡、里、聚、邑、连、闾组织或伍、什编制，以及里正、父老、廷椽、啬夫等基层属吏，仍然代表着社会广泛存在的家族宗法制组织的统治。历代封建王朝不断更迭，家族宗法制却基本上以不变应万变（形式上和部分的"质"有所衍变，但其社会"细胞"的"内核"基本不变）。家族宗法制始终是中国古代直到民主革命前中国社会结构的基本"细胞"。中国封建社会的生产方式、社会组织形式、阶级关系和阶级斗争特点、上层建筑，无不受到家族宗法制的制约和影响。家族宗法制的稳定性、顽固性和不变性，是中国封建社会长期延续的重要原因。

一边保持着家族或氏族组织，一边又以家族共居，组成一个村落的情况，在我国少数民族中更为普遍。如云南基诺族村寨一般包括数个具有血亲或姻亲关系的父系大家族；傈僳族的村落组成，一般分为三种形式，一是以一个氏族内的一个大家族单独组成，二是由同一氏族内的两个或多个大家族联合组成，三是由几个不同氏族的家族混合组成；在傣族中，有时一个村寨就只属于一个家族，有时一个村寨由几个家族和一些零星户组成；在湘、桂、黔三省边界相连的广大地区，侗族、苗族的村落，不少是以房亲或者房族为构建形态的，一个寨子或好几个寨子都是由同族同姓的房亲、房族组成的。少数也有外姓杂住其间，但外姓居民的几房在形成上也是由其内在房亲构成的。由此可见，地缘关系和血缘关系是并存的。

"聚族而居"的生活方式凸显了村落中的血缘关系，尤其是在人类社会的早期，血缘关系起着很重要的维系作用。在中国传统社会，小农经济一直是长达数千年的经济格局与形式，血缘关系也一直在传统社会尤其是在传统村落中起着不可替代的作用，并因此形成了以父系血缘为基础的家族宗法制和亲属关系。

费孝通说："我们的格局……好像把一块石头丢在水面上所发生的一圈圈推出去的波纹。每个人都是他社会影响所推出去的圈子的中心。被圈子的波纹所推及的就发生联系。每个人在某一时间某一地点所动用的圈子是不一定相同的。"费孝通在这里很形象、生动、深刻地指出了中国传统社会中以血缘为中心所形成的"这种丢石头形成同心圆波纹的性质"的差序结构，在传统社会中，这种"血缘圈"发挥了重要的作用。

三、村落的地域性特征

中国幅员辽阔，南方和北方纬度差别相当大，气候不同，地质内在构造与地貌特征都不尽相同。因而，传统村落文化呈现出鲜明的地方特色。"十里不同风，百里不同俗"，正是这种地域性特征的鲜活说明。一个村落的文化，往往与其所在的环境息息相关，不同的地域有不同的地形海拔、土质水分、光照温度、日月潮汐、风霜雨雪等影响因素，物种作物的生长发育与土壤、水质、气温、气压、湿度、植被等都有密切的关系。所以，地域不同，不仅影响村落的形成，而且会形成不一样的文化。俗话说，"一方水土养一方人"——一方具有自身独特生活方式的人。从这个基础出发，我们也可以说，一方水土滋生一方文化。比如，天井是传统村落中常见的建筑。在我国南方建筑中，天井一般南北方向开口狭窄，东西方向狭长，这样可以为建筑提供充足的自然采光，同时强烈的太阳光也不会直接射透天井。而在北方，天井南北方向开口比较大，成为人们晒太阳的理想场所。同样是天井，南北地域的不同直接导致了不同的天井建筑样式与建筑空间，以至形成不同的文化。

民间常有"天赋地造"之说，这在村落建筑材料上反映得尤为突出。不同的地域生产不同的建筑材料，因而人们常常因地制宜地选择当地适当的材料来构建各种建筑。比如，产石地区多石构，不仅柱梁墙是石质材料，就连能遮阳挡雨的"瓦"也是天然的"石片瓦"，而非人工烧制的陶瓦。产木地区多干栏式建筑，产竹地区搭竹楼，黄土高原多窑洞。也有同时使用竹木材料的，南方地区由于多雨潮湿，所以多采用干栏式结构，而北方地区却多采用抬梁式结构。概而言之，不同地域、不同民族所兴建的传统村落，是不同地域的不同原住民祖先因地制宜，依据当地所特有的自然物产条件与气候光照温度条件，以当地的材料结合当地的建筑工艺和智慧所营造出来的，有着鲜明浓郁的地域特征和民族个性。

不仅仅是建筑不同，饮食习惯也明显不同，通常说"南甜、北咸、东辣、西酸"，虽不尽准确，但大致反映出不同地方的人们饮食习俗的不同。"鲁菜""粤菜""湘菜""川菜""徽菜""淮扬菜""浙菜""闽菜"这"八大菜系"，显示出了更加清晰的地方差异性。

即使像小搬运这样的习俗，各地在挑、担、抬、背、扛、提、搭、推、驮等方式上也有明显的不同。同样是搬运泥沙，有的习惯于肩挑，有的习惯于头顶，有的习惯于背运，有的习惯于手提等，千差万别，各具传统习惯、习俗的特色。

地域性是传统村落文化在空间形态上所显示的特征。地域性特征还突出地反映了传统村落文化的多样性。因而，我们在认识、研究传统村落文化时不能不充分考虑到其地域特征，否则很容易抹杀地域村落的文化形态与个性，也就意味着丢失村落文化的多样性和丰富性。

四、村落的封闭性特征

有人曾经对越南的一个村庄做出这样的描述："浓密的竹林掩映着典型的越南村庄，荆棘篱笆环绕着村舍。村民们居住在绿竹屏蔽之后，就像居住在神话故事中的魔圈里面。周围的田野提供了他们所需要的物产，他们躲在自己造就的保护圈内，不愿与陌生人打交道，甚至不愿意与政府打交道。比如给政府交税吧（这是他们与政府的主要联系），他们就按一个整体由社区统一上交。村庄是这片土地的主宰，是这个国家的支柱，但他们又保持着内部自治和地区范围的自给自足的经济。"这虽然是对越南村落的描述，但是与过去传统社会中的中国传统村落的生活形态有基本的一致性。

由于大多数村落位于乡野僻静之地，加上古代社会道路交通欠发达等要素的制约，村落与外部社会缺少交往，信息较为闭塞。再加上在以小农经济为主体的传统社会，农业生产的自给自足性强，无须与外部社会进行过多的物质交换，从而导致了村落事实上往往成了一个比较独立的、半封闭型的、鸡犬相闻而不相往来的"小国寡民"社会。村落的封闭性主要表现在如下三个方面。

其一，人口流动少。"乡土社会是安土重迁的，生于斯、长于斯、死于斯的社会。不但是人口流动很小，而且人们所取给资源的土地也很少变动。"在传统社会，在一个地方出生的人，往往就在这个地方长大、结婚、生子、变老，一直到死去；人们很少流动，即使外出，老了，也要叶落归根；死了，即使千里万里，也要把棺材运回来，葬在故土里。所以，在没有发生历史变故或自然变故的情况下，一个村落自形成之日起，就在很大程度上一直是几个姓氏，很少发生变动。房子、土地、山林乃至墓地，都是一代一代地传下去的，不会有太大的变动。

其二，土地依赖与生产的封闭性。马克思论述法国农民的时候说："小农人数众多，他们的生活条件相同，但是彼此间并没有发生多种多样的关系。他们的生产方式不是使他们互相交往，而是使他们互相隔离。这种隔离状态由于法国的交通不便和农民的贫困而更为加强了。他们进行生产的地盘，即小块土地，不容许在耕作时进行分工，应用科学，也就没有多种多样的发展，没有各种不同的才能，没有丰富的社会关系。每一个农户差不多都是自给自足的，都是直接生产自己的大部分消费品，因而他们取得生活资料多半是靠与自然交换，而不是靠与社会交往。一小块土地，一个农民和一个家庭；旁边是另一小块土地，另一个农民和另一个家庭。一批这样的单位就形成一个村子。……广大群众，便是由一些同名数简单相加而形成的，就像一袋马铃薯是由袋中的一个个马铃薯汇集而成的那样。"马克思的"马铃薯之喻"生动反映了小农社会独立、封闭的生产关系。考诸中国传统村落，长期以来，农民的生产无不是独立自封的状态。费孝通说："乡下人离不了泥土，因为在乡下住，种地是最普通的谋生办法。"向土地求生，是小农社会中乡下人谋生最直接、最简单的方式，他们的生产对象就是土地，"土地是他们的命根子"。由于土地有限，生产力低下，人们要谋生，必须在土地上花费大量的精力，以致他们没有更多的时间和精力从事多样性的生产，也无财力改善生产工具和生产条件。因而，在土地不增加的前提下，只有不断地在土地上付出更多的时间和精力，对土地付出的劳力越多，人们对土地的依附就越紧密，他们只能日复一日、年复一年地在土地上谋生，因而，完全"被土地所囿住"。向土地求生的生产理念，早已经深入村落原住民的骨髓里，以致现在跟随子女进入城市居住的不少乡民，都试图在城市小区的周边寻找适宜土地，播撒生产的种子，有些甚至把土挑到房顶，自己"制作"小型耕地，达到播种的目的。所以，在乡下人的脑海里，似乎只要有土地，他们的第一个想法就是播种，似乎也只有在土地里播种生产他们才觉得踏实可靠，他们的生产观念完全被局限在土地上了。

其三，生活独立与封闭性。乡下人在土地上播种，依靠土地谋生，生产的目的是自我谋生，所有的产品最终都是为了满足自己的生活，生活所需也基本上由自己生产。"几千年来都是个体经济，一家一户就是一个生产单位。"从生产到消费，是一条完整的封闭的生产生活链，这种建立在以家庭为单位的自给自足基础之上的生产方式，没有分工，相对独立而没有彼此的依赖，本质上是封闭的。再者，在一个相对平和的村落社会中，每个家庭都可以自食其力，平时的生产生活一般不需要他人的帮助，只在偶然的和临时的状态中（如婚丧）才求助于人。生活上，以家庭为单位绝对独立的这种自食其力，客观上不仅形成了人际关系的封闭，而且封闭了人们的思想。

生产的脆弱性，则从根本上限制了小农扩大生活交往的条件，并促使其易于产生保守的心理而排斥外在世界。这是因为交换往往对劳动效率较高的生产者有利，劳动效率高的、不直接从事生活资料生产的人，往往参与交换的积极性高、需求旺盛。而小农由于劳动效率较低，他们参与集市交换往往是不划算的。因此，从根本上说，小农是不愿意拿辛勤劳作获得的生活资料来参与交换的，他们总是最大限度地自我满足家庭需求，只有在迫不得已时才参与少量的交易行为。

另外，在传统村落社会中，村落相对保持孤立状态，村落与村落之间的接触本来就不多，不仅很难有产品交换发生，而且其他相关信息的传播也是相当有限的。正如费孝通所指出的，"乡土社会的生活是富于地方性的。地方性是指他们活动范围有地域上的限制，在区域间接触少，生活隔离，各自保持着孤立的社会圈子"。一般来说，在生于斯、长于斯、死于斯的乡土社会，个人是可以在自己的"一亩三分地"上自食其力生活的，但这也并不意味着乡民就不需要伙伴。事实上，在重大节庆、婚丧和农忙等偶然性的、临时性的状态之中，仍是需要其他乡民一起协助的。但是，总体上而言，在传统中国，几乎每个村落都拥有一个相对完整的生产生活系统，除了基本的徭役、兵役和诉讼等，村落几乎很少与外部世界特别是朝廷发生直接接触。
