In terms of artifacts, the most typical feature of the Longshan culture is black pottery, especially eggshell black pottery mainly distributed in Shandong, characterized by thinness, hardness, luster, and blackness, so the Longshan culture is also called the "Black Pottery Culture." In terms of settlements, the most significant feature of the Longshan culture is settlement differentiation, with settlements divided into two types: giant settlements and ordinary settlements. The former generally appear as central settlements, with a certain number of sub-central or ordinary settlements attached around them. Such settlements are generally regarded by the archaeological community as cities, because they reflect relatively strong political and military characteristics. Some scholars have summarized the new changes in single-site settlements during the Longshan culture period, believing there are at least four aspects of change: first, the upgrading of settlement surrounding ditch scale; second, the upgrading of settlement moat scale; third, the rise of various city sites, including two types: moat cities and castles; fourth, the increase in the number and scale of double-settlement, multi-settlement sites, and city sites, such as the Haojiatai Site in Yancheng, the Guchengzhai Site in Xinmi, and the Wangchenggang Site in Dengfeng of the Henan Longshan culture, and the Dinggong Site and Yaowangcheng Site of the Shandong Longshan culture. In terms of settlement nature, most giant settlements during the Longshan culture period already belonged to city-wall type settlements, beyond the category of villages, and strictly speaking do not belong to our discussion object. However, to better understand the evolutionary path and change characteristics of prehistoric settlements, it is still necessary to introduce representative and typical city-wall settlements.

The Haojiatai Site, located on the terrace northeast of Shicao Zhao Village, east of Yancheng City, Luohe City, Henan Province, has a total area of 65,000 square meters. The Haojiatai settlement is rectangular in plane, with an area of more than 30,000 square meters, dating back about 4,600 years, and is currently the earliest important city site discovered archaeologically in the Henan Longshan culture. The east wall, north wall, and four city corners of the settlement city site are relatively well preserved. There is an 8.8-meter-wide gap in the middle of the east city wall, possibly the location of the city gate. Nearly 30 house sites, more than 500 ash pits, more than 110 tombs, as well as wells, pottery kilns, and ash ditches were discovered inside the city. The house sites are located in the southwest of the site, regularly arranged in rows. The houses were built on elevated earthen platforms, with interior floors higher than exterior, and mostly used adobe for building walls, with occasional wattle-and-daub walls. The row houses face northeast to southwest, with each house having one door on the south wall, with varying door widths between 0.6-0.75 meters, and all exterior doors have thresholds. The living areas vary in size; for example, the largest room of the Haojiatai phase III culture house site is 18.49 square meters, and the smallest is nearly 9.63 square meters. The interior floors are generally paved with loess, solid and flat. There are stove sites inside the houses, and daily living utensils were also found, with strong traces of life. The tomb form is rectangular vertical pit earth burial, without burial implements, and most have no grave goods.

The Guchengzhai Site, located around the Guchengzhai villager group, Dafanzhuang Village, Quliang Township, 35 kilometers southeast of Xinmi City, Henan Province. The site is large in scale, with Neolithic sites inside and outside the city reaching 2.7 million square meters. The city site was built on a terrace on the east bank of the Zhen River, rectangular in plane, with the existing south, north, and east city walls and two relatively opposite north and south city gate gaps. The three city walls are overall well preserved without any shortage. There is a 34-90 meter wide moat around the city site, with complete city defense facilities, covering an area of nearly 180,000 square meters, and is a relatively typical city-wall settlement of the Henan Longshan culture era. The cultural layers of the site include the Yangshao culture, Longshan culture, Erlitou culture, Erligang culture, Yinxu culture, and Han culture, among which the remains from the Longshan culture era are the richest. A large area of rammed earth building complexes from the Longshan culture era was discovered in the northeast of the city, including two large house sites, one as the main building and the other as an auxiliary building. The main building should belong to a palace-style building, rectangular in plane, facing east from west, 28.4 meters long from north to south and 13.5 meters wide from east to west, with corridors on the south, north, and east sides, covering an area of 383.4 square meters, basically completely preserved, and is a typical early palace-style building. The rammed earth building site has 6 rows of post holes or plinths arranged from north to south, dividing the house into 7 rooms. The auxiliary building is located to the north of the main building, only 7.4 meters apart, composed of three wall foundation trenches, numerous post holes, doorways, and a gatekeeper's room, with a width of 4 meters, belonging to a corridor-style building. According to relevant research results, these two buildings should be a combination of the main hall and corridor, which is the earliest known large building in China with courtyard (siheyuan) characteristics, and it is this architectural pattern that laid the basic pattern of later palace-style buildings in China.

The Dinggong Site, located east of Dinggong Village, Changshan Town, Zouping County, Shandong Province, is on the piedmont plain south of the Lubei Plain. Except for a small amount of Dawenkou culture and Yueshi culture, the cultural layers are mainly Longshan culture, late Shang, and Han culture, with scattered Eastern Zhou and Song dynasty cultural remains. The site covers an area of about 180,000 square meters, with a total excavation of more than 2,000 square meters, exposing nearly 100 house sites, more than 1,600 ash pits, and nearly 100 tombs from various periods. In addition, more than 5,000 relics including pottery kilns, wells, and stone, bone, shell, pottery, and bronze artifacts were seen. Particularly important is the discovery of Longshan culture pottery fragments suspected to be inscribed with characters. The city site is rounded square in plane, with relatively regular city walls on all sides. The Longshan culture period city wall is about 25 meters wide, and the moat is 30-40 meters wide. The house sites have two types: semi-subterranean and ground-level, with the latter more numerous. In form, the vast majority are square or rectangular, with circular ones fewer. The former has a smaller area, generally small houses of less than 10 square meters; the latter has a larger area, with the largest exceeding 50 square meters.

The Yaowangcheng Site, located 16.7 kilometers southwest of Rizhao City, Shandong Province, with its west and south sides close to the Nanxinzhuang River. The site is about 825 meters long from north to south and 630 meters wide from east to west, with a total area of more than 520,000 square meters. The cultural layer is mainly Longshan culture, including Dawenkou culture, Yueshi culture, Shang-Zhou, and Han cultural remains. House sites, tombs, and pottery, stone, and bone artifacts were unearthed from the site. City walls were discovered at the site. The northern city wall runs northwest-southeast, with the main wall about 300 meters long and 26-28 meters wide, with a gap of about 10 meters wide in the middle section, definitely the location of the city gate. A moat with an opening width of nearly 30 meters was found outside the wall, running roughly parallel to the city wall. The west city wall runs along the edge of the third terrace on the east bank of the Nanxinzhuang River, slightly north by east, with a wall width roughly equivalent to the north wall. The east city wall is basically parallel to the west city wall. According to archaeological survey reports, the Yaowangcheng city wall is nearly 500 meters long from north to south and about 300 meters wide from east to west, with the city site area including the city wall being nearly 150,000 square meters. The house sites have two types: rectangular and circular, with wall foundations, stove sites, and doorways, and the living surfaces are well preserved. The rectangular house sites generally have an area of 12-15 square meters, with doorways located in the south by east. The walls are 20-25 centimeters thick, with two construction methods: one using rammed earth; the other using adobe staggered masonry, with gaps filled with gray-yellow clay, and finally plastered with yellow mud inside and outside. The circular house sites have basically the same construction method as rectangular ones, digging circular foundation trenches on earthen platform bases, with rammed earth and buried columns inside the trenches. From 1995 to 2004, Shandong University, in collaboration with the University of Pittsburgh, conducted archaeological surveys in the southeastern coastal area of Shandong, concluding that Yaowangcheng was one of the cores of the southeastern coastal area of Shandong, belonging to a large settlement group standing north-south with Liangchengzhen.

II. Major Prehistoric Settlement Sites in the Yangtze River Basin

The Yangtze River Basin refers to the vast area through which the main stream and tributaries of the Yangtze River flow. The main stream flows through 11 provinces and regions: Qinghai, Tibet, Yunnan, Sichuan, Chongqing, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Anhui, Jiangsu, and Shanghai, spanning the abdomen of China; the tributaries extend north and south, involving provinces and regions such as Gansu, Shaanxi, Henan, Guizhou, Guangxi, Guangdong, Fujian, and Zhejiang, with a basin area of 1.8 million square kilometers. Like the Yellow River Basin, as an area rich in natural geographical resources, the Yangtze River Basin is also a source of the origin and development of Chinese civilization. Not only is agriculture relatively developed, but the settlements formed and changed along with agricultural development are also extremely concentrated and rich. Compared with the settlement sites in the Yellow River Basin, although the settlements in the Yangtze River Basin show certain similar features in macro appearance due to the consistency of early humans' survival and life demands, after all, the natural geographical conditions have great differences, with different natural environments and climatic conditions, so there are relatively obvious differences to a large extent and in micro aspects. This also fully confirms that the origin of Chinese civilization has been a pattern and cultural characteristic of pluralistic integration since ancient times.

(1) Paleolithic Residential Sites

1. Baise Basin, Guangxi

The Baise Basin is located in the western part of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, spanning Baise City, Tianyang County, and Tiandong County from west to east. The main body of the basin is distributed northwest-southeast, belonging to a long and narrow basin with a total area of about 800 square kilometers. The You River traverses the entire basin from west to east. It is precisely because of the pleasant climate, open terrain, and rich natural resources that it is suitable for human habitation and activities, so it has been an important area for human activities since the Paleolithic Age. The archaeologically discovered Baise Basin is also the area where Paleolithic sites are most concentrated in Lingnan Guangxi. Since the first discovery of Paleolithic sites in the Baise Basin in 1973, more than 100 Paleolithic sites have been discovered in this area to date, with tens of thousands of Paleolithic artifacts excavated and collected over the years. The entire Paleolithic site community is mainly distributed on the high platforms on both banks of the You River in Guangxi, especially in the upper reaches where the terrain is open, the site distribution is most dense, obviously being the main area of human activity in the Baise Basin. Some scholars, based on the distribution of Paleolithic sites, believe that there are at least 4 site clusters and 12 site groups in the Paleolithic sites of the Baise Basin, all showing very obvious artificially organized states. It is worth noting that among the Paleolithic remains discovered in the Baise Basin, there is a large batch of typical large cutting tools - hand axes. These hand axes are similar to the Acheulean stone tools popular in Africa and Eurasia, so the Baise Basin is also regarded by the international academic community as a major area for early human migration and cultural exchange. In addition to the discovery of similar stone tools in the Baise Basin, they have also been found in the Luonan Basin and Liangshan in Hanzhong in the Yellow River Basin.

2. Liyang Plain, Hunan

Since the 20th century, Hunan has discovered a large number of Paleolithic sites in the four river basins of Xiang, Zi, Yuan, and Li. According to incomplete statistics, there are more than 300 sites to date, especially concentrated in the western Yuan River basin and the northwestern Li River basin. The latter is the area most concerned by the academic community, and the sites seen also have certain representativeness and typicality. The Paleolithic sites in the Li River basin are concentrated in the Liyang Plain in the middle and lower reaches, located on the northwest bank of Dongting Lake in Hunan, surrounded by mountains on the west, south, and north sides. The climate here is warm and humid, with rich land and water resources and open terrain, suitable for human survival and habitation. Archaeological discoveries show that at least 500,000 years ago, there were traces of human activities in the Liyang Plain. The typical site is the Huzhuashan Site in Jinshi, where a batch of stone artifacts belonging to the South China gravel stone tool cultural tradition was discovered, including gravel points. In addition, sites such as Jigongdang, Wuyashan, and Shiligang were successively discovered. The Jigongdang Site is a middle Paleolithic site, and the unearthed stone tools also belong to the southern gravel industry tradition. Contemporary sites include Dashengmiao in Shimen, Zhangjiatan, and Hongqi in Li County. The cultural age of the Wuyashan Site is in the late Paleolithic, with stone tool assemblages including choppers, hand-axe-like tools, large points, points, scrapers, and stone hammers. Sites of the same nature include Hushan, Huashan, Zhujiashan, and Jinya. The Shiligang Site is a cultural site of the transition from Paleolithic to Neolithic in the Li River basin, with an area of nearly 40,000 square meters, in which rice phytoliths were also discovered, which is of great significance for us to explore the origin of agriculture and the origin of human settlements in Hunan. Roughly 10,000 years ago, the Liyang Plain entered the Neolithic Age. Archaeological discoveries show that not only did agriculture originate and develop in this area, but humans also began to enter relatively stable settled life. Typical sites include the Pengtoushan Site and the Bashidang Site.

3. Shuiyang River Basin, Anhui

The Shuiyang River is a tributary on the south bank of the Yangtze River, located in southeastern Anhui Province. Since the 1980s, a large number of Paleolithic sites have been discovered on both banks of the Shuiyang River, forming a certain community phenomenon. Representative sites include the Chenshan Site and Guanshan Site in Xuanzhou, and the Maozhushan Site in Ningguo. The Chenshan Site in Xuanzhou was excavated in 1988, covering an area of 100 square meters, with 78 various stone artifacts discovered. Surveys suggest that this stone tool site is very large, should be hundreds of thousands of square meters. The Guanshan Site was excavated in 1993, covering an area of about 200 square meters, in which when clearing the upper cultural layer, an ancient human living surface was also discovered within a 25-square-meter area. The Maozhushan Site in Ningguo is only 0.5 kilometers from Guanshan, excavated in 1997, with the existing remains area only 3,000 square meters. Among them, a ring composed of 1,167 stone tools with a blank area in the middle was discovered, which should be a trace of early human life. The stone tool types include choppers, scrapers, pointed choppers, and stone balls. This series of discoveries all indicates that human activities in the Shuiyang River area were relatively frequent and reflected a certain degree of organization.

4. Han River Basin and Yangtze River Coast, Hubei

The middle and lower reaches of the Han River have the Jianghan Plain, located in the central and southern part of Hubei Province, starting from Yichang in the west to Wuhan in the east, connected to the Dongting Lake Plain in the south, and is the area with the most concentrated resource elements in Hubei. The climate here is pleasant, the land is fertile, and water resources are abundant, making it the main area of early human activities in Hubei. According to archaeological evidence, there are nearly 100 Paleolithic cultural sites discovered in the Han River basin and along the Yangtze River in Hubei. Typical ones include the Xuetangliangzi Site in Yun County, the Shilongtou Site, the Huangjiawo Site, the Jigongshan Site, and the Zhangnaodong Site. The Xuetangliangzi Site in Yun County, dating back about 800,000 years, has successively discovered 2 early human skull fossils and more than 300 stone tools, mainly made of gravel raw materials. The Shilongtou Site belongs to the early Paleolithic category, roughly equivalent to the Peking Man period, with few stone tool types, mostly choppers. The Huangjiawo Site, dating back 100,000-50,000 years, belongs to the middle Paleolithic, with an area of about 10,000 square meters and relatively rich stone tool types, including choppers, scrapers, hand picks, hand axes, and notched tools. The Jigongshan Site is a late Paleolithic cultural site, with an area of about 1,000 square meters. The fact that tens of thousands of stone artifacts and stone materials were unearthed indicates that the Jigongshan Site may have been a stone tool manufacturing site for early humans. The irregular blank area composed of several large stone tool assemblages discovered in the middle of the site may, like the ring remains discovered at the Maozhushan Site in Ningguo, Anhui, belong to the living surface of early humans. The Zhangnaodong Site is a rock-shelter cave, a late Paleolithic cultural site, located on the second terrace of the Zhangnao River, Longtan Township, Zhongba, Fang County, Hubei, with more than 2,000 stone artifacts discovered, including choppers, scrapers, and points. These Paleolithic sites not only indicate that the Han River basin in Hubei had rich human activities as early as the Paleolithic Age, but also help us understand the origin of settlements in the Yangtze River Basin.

(2) Neolithic Settlement Sites

Roughly equivalent to the Yellow River Basin, after entering the Neolithic Age, about 10,000 years ago, agriculture began to rise and develop in the Yangtze River Basin, and the residential sites formed since the Paleolithic Age began to develop toward settlement, scale, and density. As the main area for the origin of rice agriculture, the Yangtze River Basin, due to its fertile land and abundant water resources, achieved relatively good agricultural development. The rise and development of rice agriculture not only initially solved the food problem of early humans, but also fixed humans within the regional area on the land, making settled life a norm. Because agriculture differs from the production and lifestyle of gathering, fishing, and hunting - the former is cultivated on the land, requiring long-term care by humans. It is precisely due to the long-term demand for agricultural cultivation that sites originally for short-term activities gradually developed into long-term fixed residential sites, which over time became settlements. Overall, the settlement nature of various residential sites in the Neolithic Age began to become increasingly obvious. However, since agricultural cultivation was still extensive, belonging to the nature of shifting agriculture, residential sites or settlements still had migratory characteristics - that is, when the land resources within a regional area were exhausted, humans had to seek elsewhere to re-establish residential sites or settlements. The development of early settlements in vast areas of China, including the Yangtze River Basin and the Yellow River Basin, all reflected such characteristics. To some extent, the rapid development or dense distribution of settlements was, on one hand, the result of agricultural development and population expansion, and on the other hand, possibly the cause of land resource exhaustion. This section intends to introduce typical and representative settlement sites within the Yangtze River Basin in conjunction with archaeological excavation materials, in order to better understand the situation and appearance of settlement development and changes in this region.

1. Early Neolithic Settlement Sites

Archaeological discoveries of early Neolithic settlement sites in the Yangtze River Basin include the early Neolithic Xianrendong remains and Diaotonghuan cultural remains in Wannian, Jiangxi, the Yuchanyan cultural remains in Dao County, Hunan, and the first phase cultural remains of Dingshishan in Yongning, Guangxi. The middle Neolithic is typified by the Pengtoushan culture type, Zaoshi lower layer culture type, Chengbeixi culture type, and Kuahuqiao culture type. These cultural types also fully show that after the origin of rice agriculture, after the long development of the early and middle Neolithic Age, it gradually rose to become the main sector of the social economy. However, compared with after the middle Neolithic, especially the late Neolithic, agricultural development during this period was still limited. Although fixed residential sites or settlement sites all had certain agricultural characteristics, their numbers were not large and the settlement scale was still relatively small. Nevertheless, from these early human remains, the settlement forms they showed were roughly the same, reflecting that the artificially organized form was becoming increasingly fixed and clan communes began to form.

(1) Xianrendong Remains and Diaotonghuan Cultural Remains in Wannian, Jiangxi

The Xianrendong remains and Diaotonghuan remains are two early Neolithic remains, located in a small intermontane basin in the limestone hilly area of Dayuan Township, Wannian County, Jiangxi Province. The basin is about 4 kilometers long from east to west and 1 kilometer wide from north to south, with the two sites only 800 meters apart. The Xianrendong remains are a cave site, located at the foot of Xiaohe Mountain in the northern part of the basin, with the cave entrance facing southeast, about 3 meters above the water surface. The cave entrance is 5.75 meters high and about 18.9 meters wide, with a cave depth of 40 meters, which can be divided into four branch caves of different sizes in the north and south. The northern branch cave has a small entrance leading to the outside, obviously being a residential site for early human life. The Diaotonghuan remains are a rock shelter site, located on a small hilltop in the western part of the basin. Because the two are close in distance, comparable in age, and similar in unearthed artifacts, they are considered to belong to the same ethnic group. The excavators even believe that the Diaotonghuan Site was a temporary camp and slaughterhouse for the original inhabitants living in Xianrendong to hunt in this area. After multiple excavations, the Xianrendong Site has discovered artificial artifacts such as pottery, stone tools, bone tools, and shell tools, as well as animal bones, and more than 20 fire remains and several ash pits. Among them, the discovery of pottery has attracted extensive attention from the academic community at home and abroad. Because the invention and use of pottery in prehistoric society largely meant the emergence of agriculture and the beginning of human settled life, the unearthed pottery from Xianrendong dating back 20,000 years can not only explain the transformation of early human production and social behavior, but also indicate that pottery was manufactured and used 10,000 years or even earlier before the emergence of agriculture. The Diaotonghuan Site also unearthed the world's earliest wild rice and cultivated rice phytolith specimens. This series of discoveries all indicates that humans began to move from the Paleolithic Age to the Neolithic Age, and began the emergence of agriculture and settled life.

(2) Yuchanyan Cave Remains in Dao County, Hunan

The Yuchanyan Cave remains, commonly known as Toad Cave, is located in Baishizhai Village, Shouyan Town, Dao County, Hunan Province, and is an early Neolithic remain dating back about 12,000 years. The cave was discovered in the lower part of a limestone remnant hill, about 5 meters above the ground, with a spacious cave hall at the entrance part. According to archaeological excavations, the original landform of Yuchanyan Cave was high in the west and low in the east. When early humans chose it as a residential address, in order to expand living space for easier habitation and life, they paved gravel on the uneven ground, and in some areas paved gray-white and gray-yellow lime-like accumulations. In the cave site, burning ash piles and artificial artifacts such as pottery, stone tools, bone tools, horn tools, tooth tools, and shell tools, as well as aquatic and terrestrial animal bones, were discovered. These remains are all concentrated in the western part of the cave, which not only indicates that the west was the main living area for people, but also reflects that early human settlements had preliminary functional zoning. Among the stone tools, primitive agricultural production tools such as hoe-shaped tools, stone hammers, and sub-waist axe-shaped tools were discovered. Among them, the hoe-shaped tool uses a flat and long gravel as raw material, struck into a tool on one end and both sides on a single face, with the using part being the end edge, possibly bound to a curved handle for digging soil. The unearthed pottery fragments are also one of the earliest evidence of pottery manufacturing discovered in China, dating back about 18,000 years. Most importantly, rice husks were discovered in the cave site. Electron microscope analysis and identification show that these rice husks include both wild rice and artificially cultivated rice. The discovery of this series of tools, pottery, and rice remains all indicates that primitive rice agriculture existed in the Yuchanyan area as early as 10,000 years ago. Of course, it should be pointed out that the existence of agriculture does not mean that early humans fully entered agricultural production and life. In fact, in early human society represented by Yuchanyan, although agriculture began to appear, people's economic life was still dominated by gathering, fishing, and hunting, supplemented by agriculture.

(3) Pengtoushan Culture Type

Named after its first discovery at the Pengtoushan Site in Li County, Hunan Province in 1985, the Pengtoushan culture dates back 9,000-8,000 years, mainly located northwest of Dongting Lake in the Yangtze River Basin, concentrated around Dongting Lake and in the lower reaches of the four rivers of Xiang, Zi, Yuan, and Li, especially richest in the Liyang Plain. The altitude here is generally below 50 meters, with flat terrain, crisscrossing dikes and embankments, fertile land, and mild climate, suitable for human production, life, and habitation. Archaeological excavations show that the cultural remains represented by the Pengtoushan Site are currently the earliest known early Neolithic culture in the Dongting Lake area, closely related to the Zaoshi lower layer culture and Chengbeixi culture. Currently, more than 10 Pengtoushan culture sites have been discovered around Dongting Lake. In addition to the Pengtoushan Site, there are the Lijiagang Site, Bashidang Site, Xialiajiawan Site, Xiaojiagang Site, Huangmagang Site, Caojiawan Site in Li County, and the Jinjigang Site in Linli County, among which the Pengtoushan Site and Bashidang Site are the most typical.

The Pengtoushan Site, located on a low slope on the north bank of the Li River about 12 kilometers west of the county seat of Li County, Hunan Province, in the Liyang Plain, covers an area of about 60,000 square meters. The site was discovered in 1984 and excavated in 1988, with an exposed area of 400 square meters. Two architectural remains were discovered, respectively a ground-level building with post holes and a small semi-subterranean building; 18 tombs were cleared, with small and shallow tomb pits, mostly secondary burials, with pottery grave goods ranging from 1-4 pieces; 15 ash pits were cleared, mostly irregularly circular or oval in plane, with锅底-shaped bottoms. Among the unearthed relics are artificial artifacts such as stone tools and pottery. Most stone tools are chipped stone tools, while pottery is simple and primitive in manufacture, made by the primitive coiling method, with charcoal fragments mixed in the pottery body. According to observations by archaeological excavators, the pottery fragments from the site also contain a large amount of carbonized rice husks and grains. From the chipped stone tools, polished stone axes, complete buffalo bones, and rice remains discovered at the Pengtoushan Site, the economic life of Pengtoushan began to transition from gathering, fishing, and hunting to agricultural production, but still dominated by the former, with a certain scale of rice cultivation and livestock breeding.

The Bashidang Site, located in Wufu Village, Mengxi Town, about 20 kilometers north of the county seat of Li County, Hunan Province, on the slope on the north bank of the Cen River, a tributary of the Li River, slopes from northwest to southeast, covering an area of about 30,000 square meters, with an excavation area of more than 1,200 square meters. A large number of relics from the Pengtoushan culture period were discovered at the site, including pottery, stone tools, bone tools, wood tools, and more than 100 types of plant and fruit pit remains. In addition, tens of thousands of complete carbonized rice grains and rice were unearthed. After detection and identification by agricultural experts, they are considered to be rice with characteristics of both indica, japonica, and wild rice, being primitive ancient cultivated rice of small-grained indica type in the differentiation period. The north side of the settlement uses a section of ancient river channel as a protective enclosure, with earthen walls and moats surrounding the east, south, and west sides, forming a closed irregular rectangular living area, reflecting a certain degree of planning and defensiveness. The earthen wall and moat are the most important discoveries at the site. This site is currently the earliest early settlement with moats and earthen walls discovered archaeologically in China. Its discovery has important academic value for us to understand the external form and economic and social forms of early settlements. More than 10 houses were discovered at the site, including semi-subterranean buildings, but most are rectangular or square ground-level buildings, including stilt-style (ganlan) and platform-style. There are stove pits inside the houses, with strong traces of life. More than 100 tombs are scattered around the residential area, without a dedicated burial area, with pottery grave goods in the tombs. The discovery of this settlement site indicates that settlements with moats and earthen walls in the Yangtze River Basin had already formed in the early Neolithic Age and had a certain scale.

(4) Zaoshi Lower Layer Culture Type

The Zaoshi lower layer culture is named after the excavation of the Zaoshi Site in Shimen, Hunan Province. The Zaoshi Site was first discovered in the early 1960s, but was initially only considered a Shang Dynasty site. Later, with two excavations in 1977 and 1981, exposing an area of 1,100 square meters, and the discovery of Neolithic cultural remains different from the early Daxi culture remains in this region in the lower layer of the site, it attracted the attention of the archaeological community. Archaeologists speculated that this might represent a new "culture." Later, with the successive discovery of same-type cultural remains, the archaeological community formally proposed the name of this culture type. Like the Pengtoushan culture, the Zaoshi lower layer culture is mainly distributed around the Dongting Lake area, but comparatively, its distribution area is wider, including not only the lower reaches of the four rivers of Xiang, Zi, Yuan, and Li, but also extending to the middle reaches, especially concentrated on the north bank of the Li River within Li County and Linli County. Currently, more than 30 Zaoshi lower layer culture sites have been discovered in this area, spread over eight or nine counties and cities around Dongting Lake. Among them, sites with obvious settlement characteristics include the Hujiawuchang Site and Fenshanbao Site.

The Hujiawuchang Site, located in the northwest of Linli County, Hunan Province, north of the Li River, at the western edge of the Dongting Lake Plain, covers an area of more than 7,000 square meters. It was first excavated in 1986, exposing an area of 160 square meters, basically square in plane. Two red-burnt earth houses were discovered at the site. The houses are rectangular ground-level buildings with doorways and post holes, possibly with columns set up to support the interior roof; the houses have a certain height and the interior is relatively spacious. There is also one tomb, with chipped and polished stone tools unearthed, as well as a large number of distinctive pottery. The pottery is made by the clay-slab coiling method. Except for a very small amount of coarse clay red pottery and black pottery, the exterior of the pottery has a thin and delicate red pottery skin. The forms include ring-footed plates, double-eared jars, high-necked jars, and plate-mouthed jars. Plain-surfaced pottery accounts for a certain proportion, but most have simple decorations such as incised patterns, cord patterns, stamped patterns, impressed patterns, and applique patterns. The discovery of these remains indicates that early human production and life underwent significant changes, not only accumulating relatively rich survival and life experience, but also further enhancing aesthetic consciousness.

The Fenshanbao Site, located at Qianlianghu Farm, 35 kilometers west of Yueyang City, Hunan Province, on a low and gentle small terrace in the lake and marsh area of East Dongting Lake. The site was discovered during the 1985 cultural relics survey, with an area of more than 40,000 square meters, and was excavated in 1990, exposing an area of 149 square meters. Remains such as residential sites, ash pits, and tombs, as well as a large number of relics, were discovered at the site. The house sites are similar in form, nearly rectangular in plane, with house foundations roughly north-south oriented, and well-preserved living surfaces, generally with similarly formed fire pits. The fire pit is located in the southeast corner, circular, and the excavators believe that the fire pits seen at the site may be unrelated to diet. The stone tools include choppers, stone discs, scrapers, burins, stone axes, and whetstones by form. The unearthed pottery is all hand-made, uneven in thickness, with coiling traces, mainly charcoal-tempered red pottery, generally decorated with red slip, with a surface layer, and the walls are mostly polished, with decorations, mainly simple geometric patterns; the main vessel types include jars, ring-footed plates, and bowls, in large quantities and diverse forms. In terms of cultural relations, the Fenshanbao Site has a certain relationship with the Hujiawuchang Site, with roughly comparable ages, and also has some connection with the Chengbeixi culture, but there are also differences, reflecting the characteristics of unity and diversity of early human culture.

(5) Chengbeixi Culture Type

The Chengbeixi culture is named after its first discovery at the Chengbeixi Site in Yidu, Hubei Province. The Chengbeixi Site was discovered in 1973 and excavated twice in 1983 and 1984. In addition to discovering that the upper layer is Shang Dynasty cultural accumulation, the lower layer is a Neolithic cultural layer, which is different from contemporary cultures discovered in the same regional area. With the increase of same-type archaeological discoveries, archaeologists proposed the naming of "Chengbeixi culture." Among the Neolithic cultural remains in Hubei, the Chengbeixi culture has the earliest age, from 6500 BCE to 5000 BCE. This type of culture is mainly distributed in the hilly zone between the western Hubei mountains and the Jianghan Plain, that is, along the Yangtze River between the eastern part of the Three Gorges and the Jianghan Plain. Although this regional area has many high mountains and gorges, the gorges are relatively wide, with gently sloping hills on both banks of the Yangtze River, good soil quality in front of the mountains, and large-area terraces, suitable for human survival and habitation. To date, more than 10 Chengbeixi culture type sites have been discovered archaeologically. The Chengbeixi Site is representative of rich cultural relics, but most sites including it have not discovered house sites. However, if the clustering characteristic of houses is used as a main criterion for judging settlement formation, then there are not many sites with settlement characteristics in the Chengbeixi culture type. Although some sites have cleared house sites, there are only 1-2 of them. For example, the Chayuandian Site discovered 2 house foundations, and the Wangjiadu Site discovered 1, neither with strong settlement nature. Although many sites have unearthed rich pottery, stone tools, and other remains, reflecting frequent early human activities in this regional area, after all, a settlement is a regional space where material entity space and non-material social space highly overlap, a social unit with relatively clear boundaries. Therefore, many sites seen in the Chengbeixi culture type cannot strictly be attributed to the category of settlements.

(6) Kuahuqiao Culture Type

The Kuahuqiao culture is named after the excavation of the Kuahuqiao Site in Xianghu Village, Xiaoshan District, Hangzhou City, Zhejiang Province, dating back 8,000-7,000 years. The Kuahuqiao Site is located on the shore of Xianghu in the southwestern part of Xiaoshan, south of Kuahuqiao, with low hills on both north and south sides, covering an area of more than 30,000 square meters, with an exposed area of more than 1,000 square meters. Four ruined house sites, more than 20 ash pits, and one tomb were discovered at the site. One identifiable house is a rectangular ground-level building, with remaining walls 30-40 centimeters high and 35 centimeters wide, the walls built of gray-white soil with wooden stakes buried in the middle, and burnt earth surfaces remaining inside; among them, there is a square ash pit with a "well"-shaped wooden frame, preserving a whole pit of acorns. The unearthed relics include artificial artifacts such as pottery, stone tools, bone tools, and wood tools, as well as animal bones, plant stems and branches, and more than 1,000 carbonized rice grains, rice, and rice husks, and a dugout canoe. Most pottery is daily utensils, with forms including cauldrons, round-bottomed jars, double-eared jars, straight-mouthed bowls, ring-footed plates, and ring-footed bowls, among which double-eared jars and ring-footed plates belong to painted pottery. Pottery spinning wheels and thread wheels were also seen, the latter still attached with fibrous thread ends. The stone tools are all polished, mainly including axes, adzes, chisels, hammers, grinding stones, and grinding sticks, with relatively exquisite manufacture and fully polished surfaces. The bone and horn tools are mainly agricultural, fishing-hunting, textile, sewing, and living utensils, such as plows, arrowheads, harpoons, awls, needles, daggers, spoons, whistles, and forks. Wood tools are also mostly used for fishing-hunting, textile, construction, and production tools, the most typical being dugout canoes, shovels, paddles, ladders, dustpans, and wooden bows. This series of discoveries all indicates that the Kuahuqiao people had primitive rice agriculture, but obviously also had an economic life of gathering, fishing, and hunting. However, from the large number of agricultural production tools and rice remains unearthed, agriculture may have risen to a dominant position in the economic life of the Kuahuqiao people. We can consider the Kuahuqiao Site an early settlement with relatively obvious agricultural characteristics. Its production and life were not only very active but also extremely rich, reflecting that the economic form and social structure of early humans in the lower Yangtze River region underwent certain changes. It can be affirmed that as an early Neolithic cultural remain in the lower Yangtze River region, the discovery of Kuahuqiao is of great significance for us to understand the early settlement origin and forms in this regional area.

The Zoumaling-Tunzishan Site: Zoumaling is located in Dongsheng Town, Shishou City, Hubei Province, and is a late Neolithic settlement site. The site is located along the Yangtze River, only 4 kilometers north of the Yangtze River, belonging to the transition zone from low hills to plains, with a superior geographical location. The site is irregularly rectangular in plane, with a total area of about 80,000 square meters and an excavation area of 1,200 square meters. Tunzishan is located on a low hill only 50 meters northeast of Zoumaling but connected to it, with an area roughly equivalent to Zoumaling. It has not been excavated yet, but archaeological surveys have found large areas of red-burnt earth house site-type accumulations. Surveys found that Zoumaling-Tunzishan should be a double city site. Because surveys found city moats and walls enclosing both according to the terrain, the site obviously presents an irregular "8" shape. Archaeological surveys also found that settlement sites of different scales exist around the double city site, reflecting that the double city site may be the central settlement in this regional area. From the excavation situation of Zoumaling, a total of 4 house sites, 2 pottery kilns, 109 ash pits were discovered, 19 tombs were cleared, and the unearthed relics are very rich. The phase I house sites are rectangular ground-level buildings with foundation trenches, wooden columns supporting grass-mixed mud walls, with living surfaces rammed and trimmed, facing south. There is 1 phase II house site, a single-room house site, irregularly rectangular, with an area of about 8 square meters, composed of post holes, thresholds, and living surfaces, with the living surface being gray-white clay with hard soil quality. No house sites were found in phase III. The phase IV house site is a crank-shaped multi-room ground-level building with wattle-and-daub walls. The west side is a large room, and the east side is two or more small rooms, with an 85-centimeter-wide doorway between the large and small rooms. The small room is located east of the house site, and 4 pottery vessels inverted on the living surface were discovered in its northwest corner: a dou (stemmed vessel), jar, bowl, and cup; there are 2 ash layers, and the small room may belong to a kitchen or dining place. A large number of pottery fragments were found inside the house site, and 17 spinning wheels and 8 stone tools were also seen, including 6 stone axes.

(2) Qujialing Culture Settlements

The Qujialing culture is named after its first discovery at the Qujialing Site in Jingshan County, Hubei Province, dating back 5,500-4,600 years, succeeding the late Daxi culture and preceding the early Shijiahe culture. The Qujialing Site is located between two small rivers, the Qingmudang River and its tributary the Qingmu River, at the southern foot of Dahong Mountain, situated on an oval-shaped mound with gentle terrain, covering an area of about 400,000 square meters, with an exposed area of nearly 1,000 square meters. The site has discovered ash pits, tombs, and 2 large-area red-burnt earth remains, as well as distinctive pottery, including painted pottery, painted-decorated pottery, and painted pottery spinning wheels. The distribution of the Qujialing culture is centered on the Jianghan Plain in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, extending northward across the Tongbai Mountains to the Nanyang Basin in southwestern Henan, with cultural influence reaching central Henan and even the banks of the Yellow River, northwestward along the Han River to the Wudang Mountain area; westward directly to the Three Gorges; southward ending at the southern bank of Dongting Lake, with influence reaching central Hunan; eastward to the Huanggang and Huangshi area, bounded by the Dabie Mountains to the northeast. This culture spans the three provinces of Hubei, Hunan, and Henan. To date, archaeology has discovered nearly 1,000 sites in this regional area, and we only select one or two important ones for introduction.

The Jimingcheng Site, located at the junction of Longchuanzui Village and Wangjiachang Village, Shizikou Town, Gongan County, Jingzhou City, Hubei Province, sits on a narrow plain, only 2 kilometers south of a river, located in the connecting zone between the Jianghan Plain and the Dongting Lake Plain. Jimingcheng is irregularly oval in plane, slightly trending from northeast to southwest, with obvious turns at the southeast and southwest corners. The maximum north-south distance is about 500 meters, east-west about 400 meters, with an area of about 150,000 square meters. The city site is well preserved, with only the northeast part missing. The city wall has a perimeter of about 1,100 meters, with a top width of about 15 meters and a bottom width of about 30 meters. There is a moat outside the city wall, with a perimeter of about 1,300 meters. Three city gate remains were discovered at the site, namely the east gate, west gate, and north gate. The east gate is about 12 meters wide; the west gate is located south of the west city wall, 11-12 meters wide; the north gate is located west of the city wall, 14 meters wide. Cultural relics such as pottery were also unearthed from the city site. This site is of great significance for us to understand the social development level and early settlement forms in the Jianghan region.

The Jijiaocheng Site, belonging to the middle Qujialing culture, is located in Cennan Township, about 12 kilometers north of Li County, Hunan Province, in the central Liyang Plain. The settlement site is nearly square in plane, with rounded corners, 400 meters long from east to west and about 370 meters wide from north to south, covering an area of nearly 150,000 square meters, with an exposed area of 190 square meters. The west and north city walls are well preserved. The southern section of the west wall is about 60 meters wide, with a residual height of 4-5 meters; the western section of the north wall is 40-60 meters wide, with a residual height of 2-3 meters, with a gap in the middle of the north wall, possibly the location of the city gate; the east wall only retains the northern and southern sections, about 40 meters wide, with a residual height of 3-4 meters; the south wall has been destroyed. Jijiaocheng has moats and a city moat. A conical earthen platform was discovered at the site, with a bottom diameter of nearly 10 meters and a height of about 1.5 meters. In the center of the platform top, there is a red-burnt earth pile about 2.5 meters in diameter and about 1 meter thick, level with the top surface of the platform, with a large amount of broken pottery fragments remaining, located under the city wall, possibly related to sacrificial activities held during city wall construction, roughly belonging to the late Qujialing culture. Archaeological excavations also show that the construction of the Jijiaocheng city site was continuous, experiencing several stages: middle Qujialing culture, late Qujialing culture, and early Shijiahe culture, indicating that this was an early settlement with a large time span and continuous use. Moreover, a settlement community formed around Jijiaocheng, with nearly 40 settlements closely clustered within an area of only 20 square kilometers, reflecting an obvious trend of geopolitical integration. These discoveries indicate that Jijiaocheng, as a regional central settlement, already had the role and significance of geopolitical integration.

The Huanglianshu Site, also known as the Longshangang Site, is located on a sloping terrace west of Huanglianshu Village, Taohe Township, Xichuan County, Henan Province, backed by a 50-meter-high earthen mound to the southeast and adjacent to the Huangling River to the northwest, at the confluence of the Dan River and Huangling River. The existing area of the site is about 200,000 square meters, with the Neolithic remains accumulation range about 140,000 square meters, and cultural accumulation thickness of 1-4.2 meters, including remains from the Neolithic Age, Western Zhou, Han, Song-Yuan, Ming-Qing periods, dominated by Neolithic remains, containing remains from the Yangshao culture, Qujialing culture, and Shijiahe culture periods. Among them, the Qujialing culture lasted the longest and had the richest relics. There are 25 house foundations, mostly located on the terrace in the southeast of the site, backed by mountains and facing water, facing the Huangling River in front and relying on the loess mound behind. The houses are in a courtyard layout, divided into north and east rows of houses. The north row of houses is northwest-southeast oriented, basically parallel short row houses, with 5 house sites; the east row of houses is northeast-southwest oriented, longitudinally long row houses, with 17 house sites; three small courtyard-style open squares are formed in the middle, with a single large room in the south-central part of the courtyard, with the door facing northeast, possibly the residence of the clan leader or a space for public activities. These houses are divided into single-room and double-room types, among which 8 are double-room and the rest are single-room; the houses are neatly arranged with close spacing, some spacing between 0.3-1.2 meters; the house shape is square or rectangular, dug and built wattle-and-daub buildings, with walls plastered with white lime; there are fire pits, generally one per room; a few houses have white lime floors outside. There are 17 ash pits and 38 tombs, with few grave goods in the tombs, only 4 tombs respectively with one or two pieces of pottery (ding tripods, jars) and rough ornaments, mainly earrings composed of stone beads and pottery rings, stone bracelets, and stone ornaments. Although there are few grave goods, they still reflect that society began to differentiate, possibly with distinctions in status and wealth. The settlement site unearthed 997 production tools and living utensils, the former such as stone axes, stone adzes, stone sickles, stone knives, stone net sinkers, pottery spinning wheels, bone fishhooks, arrowheads, bone awls, horn awls, tooth awls, bone needles, stone mortars and pestles, pottery pestles, and grinding tools; the latter including pottery ding tripods, pottery jars, pottery bowls, pottery vats, pottery basins, and pottery pots. These discoveries all indicate that Huanglianshu was a large settlement with strict social organization and frequent social activities.

(3) Hemudu Culture Settlements

The Hemudu culture is named after its first discovery in Hemudu Town, Yuyao City, Zhejiang Province. It is a late Neolithic culture in the area south of the lower reaches of the Yangtze River, dating back 7,000-5,300 years. Archaeological discoveries show that the Hemudu culture is mainly distributed in the Ningbo-Shaoxing Plain on the south bank of Hangzhou Bay and the Zhoushan Islands. Currently, relatively clear Hemudu culture sites, in addition to the Hemudu Site in Yuyao, include Xiangjiashan, Zhushan, Xiazhuang in Yuyao, Tongjia'ao in Cixi, Baziqiao and Shaxi in Ningbo, Tashan in Xiangshan, Mingshanhou in Fenghua, and Baiquan in Dinghai, with the Hemudu Site being the most typical.

The Hemudu Site, located on a narrow river valley plain on the south bank of Hangzhou Bay, is a transition zone from hills to plains, with terrain gently sloping from southwest to northeast, with Siming Mountain to the south, Cinan Mountain area to the north, and north-south trending low hills to the east. The excavation area of the site is 2,630 square meters, with a total of more than 1,000 wooden components unearthed, including three types: long round logs, pile wood, and wooden boards. Thirteen rows of orderly arranged pile wood were discovered at the site, possibly with more than 6 buildings, among which one connected long house has a depth of about 7 meters, with a 1.3-meter-wide front porch under the eaves, and a width of more than 23 meters. The house remains are mainly arranged in rows, with pile wood driven into the virgin soil, and scattered beams, column logs, and thick boards also seen, with no grass reinforcement or red-burnt earth, all being mortise-and-tenon wooden structures, typical stilt-style (ganlan) buildings. The important components of the wooden building remains are basically northwest-southeast oriented, some nearly north-south, obviously arranged with backs to mountains and faces to water. From the architectural structure, it is clearly different from the semi-subterranean or ground-level buildings in the Yellow River Basin, and the construction techniques are also different. In addition to differences in social organization structure, this is more likely caused by different natural geographical environments. There are 27 tombs, located in the west, north, and northeast of the excavation area. In the first cultural layer, the maximum number of grave goods is 5-6 pieces, with the minimum only 1 piece, mostly pottery, generally with cauldrons and dou vessels, as well as jade and stone; no grave goods were seen in the second cultural layer; in the third cultural layer, no tomb pits are seen, no burial implements, the vast majority have no grave goods, and a few have a small amount of grave goods. One wooden well was discovered, composed of more than 200 pile woods and long round logs, with a circle of nearly circular fence piles on the periphery, about 6 meters in diameter and about 28 square meters in area, and a square vertical shaft on the elevation. Archaeology shows that the animal bones at Hemudu involve 47 species of animals; most test pits have found 20-50 centimeter thick accumulation layers of rice, rice husks, rice leaves, rice stems mixed with wood chips and weaves. After identification, the rice belongs to artificially cultivated rice. Accompanying the rice remains, a large number of agricultural tools were also unearthed, mainly bone plows (bone si), as many as 170 pieces, among which 2 pieces still have wooden handles and rattan for binding remaining on the handle. These discoveries indicate that rice agriculture had not only risen to become the main economic sector of the Hemudu people, but also that rice cultivation had entered the "plow cultivation stage." Moreover, from nearly 10 types of bone textile tools including spinning wheels, yarn winding rods, warp dividing wood, warp beams, machine knives, shuttle-shaped tools, and bone needles, as well as thousands of production and living tools such as stone tools, pottery, and wood tools, the Hemudu people had a relatively developed agricultural economy, while also having livestock and hunting economic activities, reflecting the social structure and development degree of clan communes in the late Neolithic Age of the Yangtze River Basin.

(4) Majiabang Culture Settlements

The Majiabang culture is an archaeological culture represented by the discovery and excavation of the Majiabang Site in Tiandaiqiao Village, Nanhu District, Jiaxing City, Zhejiang Province. It is a late Neolithic culture in the lower Yangtze River region, mainly distributed in the Taihu Lake surrounding area of southern Jiangsu and northern Zhejiang. Currently, there are more than 30 excavated Majiabang culture sites, mainly including the Majiabang Site, Luojiajiao Site in Tongxiang, Chuodun Site in Kunshan, and Luotuodun Site in Yixing, among which the Majiabang Site and Luojiajiao Site are the most typical.

The Majiabang Site, located 7.5 kilometers southwest of the city center of Jiaxing, sits on a plain where three rivers intersect, with the site about 150 meters long from east to west and 100 meters wide from north to south, covering an area of 15,000 square meters, with an excavation area of 213 square meters. One rectangular house site was discovered in the upper cultural layer, with 13 post holes on the east, south, and west sides, and a gate site at the southeast corner. Within the post hole range, there is a layer of yellow-green hard soil surface about 8 centimeters thick, which should be the living surface. Bone arrowheads, bone chisels, etc. were unearthed around the house. A house suspected of being burned was also seen. The lower layer architectural remains are simple, being a pit, with cattle and deer bones discovered, not necessarily residential buildings. The west and northwest of the site are burial grounds, more than 10 meters from the residential area, with 30 skeletons discovered, no tomb pits. Artificial artifacts such as bone tools, stone tools, jade artifacts, and pottery were unearthed. The bone tools are mostly production tools such as bone awls, bone arrowheads, bone chisels, and bone needles, and the stone tools are also tools such as stone adzes and stone axes.

The Luojiajiao Site, located northeast of Shimen Town, Tongxiang City, Zhejiang Province, is about 400 meters long from east to west and 300 meters wide from north to south, with a total area of about 120,000 square meters and an exposed area of 1,338 square meters. 53 ash pits were cleared, with rich archaeological relics and animal and plant remains discovered. The unearthed relics include about 800 complete or restorable pottery, stone, bone, and wood artifacts. Among them, pottery includes daily utensils such as cauldrons, basins, plates, bowls, dou vessels, ding tripods, and pots, as well as spinning wheels; stone tools include axes, adzes, knives, and spinning wheels; bone tools are mainly production tools such as arrowheads, plows, and daggers; among the wood tools, there is a batch of squarely processed mortise-and-tenon wooden building components, with processing methods including fire roasting and axe and adze chiseling. Some wooden components have pin holes on the tenons, and the mortises are divided into penetrating and non-penetrating, all made according to different building needs, aiming to make the wooden components more firmly joined. These discoveries all indicate that wooden buildings generally existed at the Luojiajiao Site.

(5) Shijiahe Culture Settlements

The Shijiahe culture is named after the discovery and confirmation of the Shijiahe Site Group in Tianmen City, Hubei Province, and is a late Neolithic culture type in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River following the Qujialing culture. The distribution area of the Shijiahe culture is roughly equivalent to that of the Qujialing culture, mainly distributed in the area centered on the central Jianghan Plain of Hubei and its surrounding range, with radiation scope including Hubei, southwestern Henan, and northern Hunan, even reaching the Zhengzhou-Luoyang area to the north. To date, archaeology has discovered nearly 1,000 Shijiahe culture sites, especially forming a Shijiahe site group around the Shijiahe Town area of Tianmen.

The Shijiahe Site Group, located about 17 kilometers northwest of Tianmen City, Hubei Province, is in the ridge-shaped plain area of the low hills south of Dahong Mountain, at the confluence of the Shijia River in the east and the Maxi River in the southwest. The site group has more than 30 sites, densely distributed north of Shijiahe Town at altitudes between 30-45 meters. Outside this range, sites are only sporadically distributed, fully reflecting the community nature of the Shijiahe site group. According to archaeological excavations, a "Shijiahe earthen city" was discovered in the area centered on Tanjialing, including sites such as Dengjiawan, Sanfangwan, Tucheng, Huangjinling, and Yangjiawan. The earthen city is located east of Dengjiawan and north of Huangjinling, with residential houses in the north and west of the city and the southwest end outside the city. The earthen city is slightly shoe-shaped in plane, about 510 meters long from north to south and 280 meters at its widest from east to west, covering an area of nearly 1.2 million square meters, with low gullies resembling ring-shaped moats around the city wall. The east and north sections of the city wall are slightly wider, with larger height differences, and the city circle is very complete. There is a gap about 12 meters wide at the north of the east section, possibly the location of the city gate. A large number of mid-late Western Zhou remains were also discovered in the city site, indicating that the city site may have been in continuous use for a long time. Outside the city site, there are small-scale sites scattered around the city, such as Hujiawan, Zhoujiawan, Yanjia Xinchang, and Yanjia Guangling to the north of the city, Kubaishu, Tanjiagang, and Yandouziwan to the west of the city, and Maojialing, Wangjiatai, Aojiaquan, and Zhaguofentou to the northeast of the city. This distribution seems to indicate a master-subordinate relationship between the earthen city and surrounding settlements, with the earthen city being the political power core and surrounding settlements subordinate to this core. It can be seen that the Shijiahe site group is undoubtedly a geopolitically integrated settlement community with the earthen city as the central settlement.

(6) Liangzhu Culture Settlements

The Liangzhu culture is represented by the discovery and excavation of the Liangzhu Site in Yuyao City, Zhejiang Province, dating back 5,300-4,500 years, and is a late Neolithic culture type in the lower Yangtze River region. Archaeological discoveries show that the Liangzhu culture is mainly distributed in the surrounding areas of the Qiantang River basin and Taihu Lake basin, especially dense in the northeast and east of the Qiantang River basin. According to relevant data, there are more than 200 Liangzhu culture sites reported to date, and some scholars estimate even no less than 1,000, such as Fanshan and Yaoshan in Yuhang, Zhejiang, as well as Zhaolingshan in Kunshan, Jiangsu, Caoxieshan in Wuxian, Sidun in Wujin, and Fuquanshan in Qingpu, Shanghai. Among the discovered sites, those with the clearest settlement attributes and certain clustering characteristics are mainly the Liangzhu culture site group in Yuhang, Zhejiang.

The Liangzhu culture site group, located in the northern suburb of Hangzhou City, Zhejiang Province, is mainly distributed in the three towns of Pingyao, Anxi, and Liangzhu in Yuhang City, covering an area of about 34 square kilometers. The site group is located in the border zone between the western Zhejiang mountainous hills and the Hangzhou-Jiaxing-Huzhou Plain, being a hilly valley with dense water networks. To date, more than 100 sites of pure Liangzhu culture and sites containing Liangzhu culture have been discovered in this area. Overall, the Liangzhu culture site group can be roughly divided into three areas: first, about 30 northern sites, with the narrow zone between the north bank of the East Tiao Stream and the remnants of Tianmu Mountain as the main distribution range, concentrated at the foot of the southern slope of Dazhe Mountain hills and the piedmont zone, distributed in two parallel belts; second, the area centered on Mojiaoshan in the southwest of the site group, with more than 50 sites distributed; third, the area centered on Xunshan in Liangzhu Town in the southeast, with more than 20 sites distributed within a 1-kilometer radius, very dense. The types of remains and relics discovered in the site group are very rich, including remains such as residential sites, cemeteries, altars, and handicraft workshops, as well as relics such as production and living tools and sacrificial vessels. The residential sites of the site group are divided by scale, represented by three sites respectively: Mojiaoshan, Yaojiadun, and Miaoqian. Mojiaoshan is a giant rectangular rammed earth platform with an area exceeding 30,000 square meters, with three small mounds on the site, possibly the remains of the main building. Within a 100-square-meter area on the south side, several rows of large column pits were discovered, possibly ritual buildings. Later, in the southeast of the site, not only large-area pit-shaped burnt earth accumulations were cleared, but also remains such as neatly arranged ditch ridges, stone accumulation pits, and ash pits filled with pure soil were exposed. These discoveries all reflect that the Mojiaoshan Site may be a central settlement site.

sections.name: 国家的诞生与村落的蠡测
sections.content_zh:
第三节 国家的诞生与村落的蠡测

村落的不断分化扩张以及群团化不断发展的直接结果，是城市的出现和地缘一体化的形成。而地缘一体化的持续巩固和扩大，则促进了国家的产生。按照马克思的观点，这一发展趋势是私有制演化的产物，也是阶级社会的产物。正如恩格斯在《反杜林论》中所言："随着分配上的差别的出现，也出现了阶级差别。社会分为享特权的和被损害的、剥削的和被剥削的、统治的和被统治的阶级，而同一氏族的各个公社自然形成的集团最初只是为了维护共同利益（例如在东方是灌溉）、为了抵御外敌而发展成的国家。从此也就同样具有了这样的职能：用暴力对付被统治阶级，维持统治阶级的生活条件和统治条件。"国家的实质是一个阶级统治另外一个阶级，因而它的出现意味着跨地域、跨血缘、跨部落的社会关系、经济关系和政治关系的建立。国家要维系和巩固这种关系，其前提和基础是对土地和人口的全面掌控，因为二者关系到国家的经济收入，是"维持统治阶级的生活条件和统治条件"。《诗经》中所谓"普天之下，莫非王土。率土之滨，莫非王臣"即为此意。正因如此，在国家出现之后，村落作为早期人类社会最基础的地域单元、生产生活单元和社会单元，便开始具有了国家层面的意义。

一、早期国家的出现与村落

从考古发现和历史文献记载来看，大致在二里头文化以后，及至商、西周政权的建立，早期中国便开始以国家的形式正式出现。按前揭，国家的实质是一个阶级统治另外一个阶级，村落作为以血缘为纽带的地方力量，显然是被统治的对象，并且还是早期中国严格监管的对象。因为作为地域单位和实际存在的生产生活单元，村落的代名词就是土地和人口，它直接关系到国家的根基与发展。从理论上而言，国家与村落之间，既相互制约、相互牵制，相互牵制，也互为促进、共同发展。但事实上，早期国家形成后的很长一段时间内，国家并没有成为村落发展的助推力，反而制约了村落的发展。其根本原因在于，早期国家的维系和巩固是以统治为前提的。文献记述显示，为了更好地维系国家统治，先秦国家对于土地实行"井田制"，由奴隶和庶民耕种；战国以后改行"授田制"，土地由国家授予，但庶民只有使用权，不能买卖。对于人口，则实行国民化管理，在制度上努力将奴隶和庶民纳入城郭集中居住。秦统一六国后，更是通过设立郡县制，县下建立"乡里"制来加强控制。正是这一系列制度，使早期中国有效地加强了国家与地方社会之间的交流和沟通，但也正因如此，村落的发展空间被大大压缩了。

井田制作为一种春秋以前就存在的土地制度，是早期国家管理和控制社会的一类有效方式。它曾在很长一段时间内影响着包括村落在内的早期中国社会形态的形成与发展。"井田"作为一个专有名词被提出，最早见于《春秋穀梁传·宣公十五年》："古者三百步为里，名曰井田。"文中进一步指出，"井田者，九百亩，公田居一。私田稼不善，则非吏；公田稼不善，则非民。初税亩者，非公之去公田而履亩，十取一也，以公之与民为已悉矣"。大致意思是，井田可以分为公田与私田两个部分，其中公田一份，余者皆为私田。私田分别由八家之民耕种，他们不仅要向国家缴纳足额赋税，而且要共同承担耕种公田的责任。《孟子·滕文公上》记："方里而井，井九百亩。其中为公田，八家皆私百亩，同养公田。公事毕，然后敢治私事。"与《孟子》所载不同的是，《周礼》中的说法，其《地官·小司徒》云："乃经土地而井牧其田野，九夫为井，四井为邑，四邑为丘，四丘为甸，四甸为县，四县为都，以任地事而令贡赋，凡税敛之事。"《周礼》中的"井田"之说，认为井田无"公田""私田"之分。其实，有关于井田制的系列问题，不仅在先秦就存在不同的理解，自清末以来更是引起广泛的争议，有不少学者从不同角度对此进行了不同的论述与讨论，特别是有关其具体形式与内容，更是众说纷纭，莫衷一是。与村落形成有关的，大致有两种看法。以杨宽先生为代表的学者，认为井田制就是春秋时代以前的农村公社制度。它的产生是出于"统一治理和管理水利灌溉的需要"，实行"在河流灌溉的平原地区"，并认为在此基础上形成了作为居住空间的"邑"和"里"。尽管这一观点被普遍接受，但也有学者对此提出了质疑，认为"在井田制下，农民的个人份地直接受自国家而非村社共同体，因此井田制不仅不是典型的农村公社的土地制度……而是属于土地国有制性质的国家授田制，它并非西周时代的土地制度，而是在战国时代的国家授田制的基础上加以增饰而创制出来的一种理想制度"。

上述各种说法，孰是孰非不是我们所要讨论的，可以肯定的是，作为一项土地制度或赋税制度，井田制应该正式形成于西周时期，在夏商时期便已出现。不仅商周的甲骨文、金文和先秦古典文献等历史材料中均有类似内容的表述，而且相关记述都表明它在早期国家社会的形成过程中所起到的重要作用。早期中国，以国家形式的出现，意味着它不再是简单的以血缘为纽带的氏族公社，而是一个跨血缘、跨地缘的国家社会组织。要维系这样一个社会组织，原始公有制显然已经很不适应，于是，井田制作为在一定地域范围内平均分配土地的方式应时而生，并起到了维系和稳定国家的效果。从本质上而言，商与西周国家推行井田或者说井田制的根本目的是征收赋税，因而其出发点是一致的。而要实现这一目的，一方面，要将作为生产资料的土地的效益极大规模地发挥出来，必须对土地进行合理分配，尽可能使国家、土地拥有者、土地耕种者三方或多方获利，并使这种利益有度、平衡。另一方面，则要将作为生产力的国民固定在土地上。《春秋穀梁传》所载"私田稼不善，则非吏；公田稼不善，则非民"虽是对官吏和农户二者的要求，但由于官吏是私田的管理者和督促者，所以"稼田"归根结底是针对农户的，这就在制度层面将农户固定于土地。正是这一逻辑出发点，使井田制作为一项国家的制度，具有了村落变迁层面的意义。其意义突出体现在与井田制配套存在的基层管理制度，即所谓"国野之制"，它们互为因果，共同维系着早期国家的基层社会形态。

"国野之制"，即《周礼》所云的"体国经野，设官分职"。与乡野有关的是"乡遂之制"。在"国"设六乡，《周礼·大司徒》云："正月之吉，始和布教于邦国都鄙……使之各以教其所治民。令五家为比，使之相保；五比为闾，使之相受；四闾为族，使之相葬；五族为党，使之相救；五党为州，使之相赒；五州为乡，使之相宾。""国"即"都鄙"，韦昭注："都，国也。鄙，边邑也。"郑玄注曰："都鄙，王子弟公卿大夫采地，其界曰都，鄙所居也。"都鄙就是当时的都邑或是国都周边范围的固定居民点，集中居住贵族、手工业者、庶人和商人等。都鄙营造形成了集中城居的形式，所谓"凡造都鄙，制其地域而封沟之，以其室数制之"即是证表。"六乡"的设置，则正好于制度设置层面对此进行了巩固，其功能目的，是既便于管理，又可以将农民固定在一定区域范围内的土地上，进而维系国家的稳定。这种做法与早期中国实行的分封制密切相关。"凡建邦国，以土圭土其地而制其域：诸公之地，封疆方五百里，其食者半；诸侯之地，封疆方四百里，其食者参之一；诸伯之地，封疆方三百里，其食者参之一；诸子之地，封疆方二百里，其食者四之一；诸男之地，封疆方百里，其食者四之一。"分封制可能最晚在商代已开始出现，封侯、伯之类，尚不完善，其真正成熟并广泛推行是在周代。周代将土地分封给诸侯，诸侯在封疆内将土地分赐卿大夫，卿大夫再把土地分赐子弟和士。分封，实质上造成了中央与地方之间的分裂，所以"六乡"的设置，也是为了加强中央对分封之地的控制。"国"之外，则于"野"设"六遂"，"以土地之图经田野，造县鄙形体之法。五家为邻，五邻为里，四里为酂，五酂为鄙，五鄙为县，五县为遂，皆有地域，沟树之"。"国"之外的广大区域即为"野"，郑玄注："郊外曰野。此野谓甸、稍、县、都。"简而言之，野即广大乡村地域。文献中所提到的"里"，则是乡村地区的基层组织，并且属于官方认可的有一定边界的居住空间。

很显然，作为春秋之前国家普遍实行的治理制度，特别是在西周时期，井田制和国野制都起到了积极的作用，既促进了中央国家与诸侯国及其地方社会的沟通和交流，又维系了国家的稳定。然而，我们必须思考的是，文献中如此规整的制度是否就一定符合实际呢？按照文献记述来理解，作为自然聚落的村落似乎是难以归入其中的。正是因为有了这一系列文献记述，中国先秦时期或是汉以前的历史时期，被以宫崎市定为代表的日本学者认为是"都市国家"，进入三国以后，才逐渐向被称作"村"的散村演变。国内的侯外庐先生在20世纪30年代也论述了殷周为城市国家的问题，并将中国"城市国家"的起源追溯到殷商晚期，指出古文字"邦""封"同义，"城""国"同义。当然，侯先生并没有否认先秦以前就存在农业型的聚落，相反还认为我国在西周到春秋时期便发生了城市和农村的第一次分裂。也有不少学者认为"都市论"不可靠，至少是不全面的，认为先秦以前百姓完全居住于城郭的说法值得商榷。持这一说法的学者，日本有松本雅明、池田一雄，国内则以侯旭东为代表。笔者以为，造成这种分歧的关键固然与立论的出发点不同有关，但主要在于两个方面：一是对村落内涵缺乏把握，尤其是"都市论者"往往只是将村落理解为一种社会组织，与国家制度联系起来，既忽视了它作为物质实体空间的客观存在，又忽略了它在聚族群体性和血缘延续性这一基础上所形成的语言、风俗、道德、宗教、经验与技术等非物质性内容，因而当先秦文献中有关基层制度的记述语焉不详或是体现为一种行政理想时，通常就自觉排除在国家制度之外还存在实际的生活单元或族群的可能；二是先秦文献中的有关记载多为后人根据自我理解的追述，或者只是统治者为便于管理和控制国家而衍生出的充满主观理想的一种制度，可能并非真正客观的社会现实，而且人们对这类文献的理解通常存在不同程度的差异，还往往忽视了人类学、地理学在解读村落作为社会单元和地域单元方面的积极作用。

基于上述几点，我们认为《周礼》中"体国经野，设官分职"的"国野之制"，制度上虽然非常完整，设置上也极为严密，在"国"设"六乡"，在"野"设"六遂"，但是并不能说明村落就完全被纳入国家的管制范畴，百姓也未必全部集中于城郭居住。因为作为一种国家组织制度，即便是在统一规划的城郭之中，由于人口增长或减少具有不可预计性，尚且难以实现"五家为比，五比为闾，四闾为族，五族为党，五党为州，五州为乡"的"六乡"编排，更遑论在地理条件复杂、族群多样的"野"了。"野"不仅仅是通常意义上城郭的周边地域，还包括那些尚未被统驭的蛮、夷、戎、狄和流民之民等聚居的区域，所以要实现"五家为邻，五邻为里，四里为酂，五酂为鄙，五鄙为县，五县为遂"的"六遂"编排，在当时显然可能并非现实。特别是以井田制进行土地分配的制度，在蛮夷之地，不仅难以适从，而且过于理想，乡野聚落与行政编制的统合也是困难的。相关研究显示，西周时期的里，作为乡村或都鄙地区的基层组织和实际居住空间，是有边界的，并且规模有大小之别。这也表明"五邻为里，四里为酂"可能并不完全符合实际。事实上，殷商甲骨文和青铜器铭文显示，殷商国家以外，尚存有不少未被统驭的方国或部落，如土方、危方、鬼方、微方、羌方、龙方、四邦方、兹方、刀方、大方、盂方、井方、二邦方等，它们都普遍分布在殷代国家的周边。考古也发现，在商周时期，中原王朝核心区域以外的广袤地带，特别是长江流域的成都平原、江汉地区、洞庭湖水系、鄱阳湖水系等普遍存在着乡野聚落。

到春秋战国时期，由于诸侯争霸、列国称雄，相对稳定的国家形式遭到破坏，特别是伴随着奴隶起义、平民暴动和新兴地主阶级的兴起，居民的生产积极性不高，户口逃逸的情况常见，建立在"国野制"基础上的社会形态基本瓦解。所以，为了维系和发展国家的经济利益，战国时期的各国不同程度地兴起变法运动，普遍推行郡县，改"井田"为"授田"，大力发展社会经济。正是由于基层组织的相对宽松，以及土地所有制的变化，"私田"得以出现。私田属于新兴的地主阶级，可以用于租赁，因而一些逃逸的人口，除了在野外自行开辟耕地外，往往通过租赁私田耕种转为佃农。这部分人往往只需向地主付租，而无须承担国家徭役，所以国家对此是严加监管的。睡虎地秦墓竹简《魏户律》记战国晚期魏国的律令云："廿五年闰再十二月丙午朔辛亥，告相邦：民或弃邑居壄（野），入人孤寡，徼人妇女，非邦之故也。"这段话至少说明两个问题，一是除了蛮夷聚落外，城郭外还存在乡野聚落，并且不受制于国家；二是国家对这类由"流邑之民"形成的乡野聚落是持反对态度的，因为这是"非邦之故"。至于为何是"非邦之故"，除了《魏户律》中提到的"入人孤寡，徼人妇女"的理由外，恐怕主要是《管子》中提到的"强耕而自以为落，其民，寡人不得籍斗升"的说法。大意是由于耕作而自发形成的聚落，统治者是难以征收其赋税的。正因如此，在管理手段落后、信息闭塞的早期社会，统治者将百姓集中城居，进行统一管理显然是最佳方式。何休所注的《春秋公羊传·宣公十五年》极具说服力，其云："民春夏出田，秋冬入保城郭。田作之时，春，父老及里正旦开门坐塾上。晏出后时者不得出，莫不持樵者不得入。五谷毕入，民皆居宅。"徐彦的疏指出："古者邑居，秋冬之时入保城郭，春夏之时出居田野。"这段注疏作为后人的追述，虽不能证明集中城居就是先秦时期的普遍形式，但至少在一定程度上反映了哪怕是作为城居，也还存在以下两种情况：一是民居于城郭，耕种则在城郭附近；二是有专人管理，进出时间是受限的。翻检文献资料，我们发现，可能因为田地超越了城居的耕作半径，所以为便于农事而派生出了一种所谓的"庐"，即在就近田处建造的临时性房屋。《诗经·小雅·信南山》云："中田有庐，疆场有瓜。"东汉郑玄笺："中田，田中也，农人作庐焉，以便其田事。"唐孔颖达疏："古者宅在都邑，田于外野。农时则出而就田，须有庐舍，故言中田，谓农人于田中作庐以便其田事。"虽没有直接证据能证明"庐"后来发展成了村落，但从理论上而言，不是没有这种可能。我们在湖南江永勾蓝瑶寨考察时就发现了类似形式、功能的"牛庄屋"。它是旧时居于深山的瑶民为便于农业生产而于平地近田处建起的临时住所，一到开春，瑶民便长住其中，久而久之，就干脆移居平地，形成了村落。2019年10月中国村落文化研究中心团队在湖南郴州发现的一处我国目前所知村落建筑类型中保存最好、规模最大、年代序列最为清楚且仍在活态传承的代头村，也可佐证这一点。因为从村落空间来看，居于盆地中央的居所和位于村落外围两侧、靠近田土一方的牲畜马厩，都说明代头村是为便于农事而建，恰好可以见证历史上因"庐"成"聚"成"衢"的村落生长现象。

由近推远的论证方式虽然不能直证，但也有一定的说服力。因为无论是早期人类，还是现代人类，他们在求生、求存、求便乃至趋利避害等方面的行为和心理上的期盼是相同的，不会因时代变迁而发生很大改变。《史记》中也有关于"一年而所居成聚，二年成邑，三年成都"的说法，虽未必言之凿凿，但结合瑶族地区的牛庄屋与湖南郴州发现的代头村这些活证，便具有说明"庐"可发展为村落的佐证价值。

可以肯定，无论是蛮夷聚落，还是由流邑之民形成的乡野聚落，抑或是为便于农事而出现的"庐"，都使我们有理由认为早期中国以国家的形式出现，并不意味着自然聚落消失或被取而代之，相反呈现出散村化的倾向。可以肯定，于国家和民族视野下的村落，此时不仅得以继续发展，而且作为最基本的生活单元和社会单元，以其聚族群体性和血缘延续性的特质，在增强民族的内聚性与心理认同，避免民族文化的失忆甚至是中华文化的分割、封闭和中断，维系和巩固国家的稳定、繁荣与发展方面，发挥着极其重要的历史作用。

二、商周时期的方国与聚落

从历史视角来看，商周国家的地域范围并非我们今天所理解的现代中国版图与疆界，其核心区域在现今的中原。至于中原以外的广大地区，虽有其势力据点或势力影响，但似乎并未全部被纳入其统驭范围。正如有学者所指出的："从王畿区外围开始，由近及远分布的军事据点是商人控制外服的实体，这些军事组织在驻地屯田。在商都势力强盛期，附近的一部分国族或因商人势力所迫、或因敌族压力而归附。商属地与附属国族联合对抗附近的敌族，这样就形成了一个个的商人势力范围圈。"就此而论，我们当然不能简单地将商周势力范围等同于商周疆域，其核心区域在王畿及其周边范围，王畿以外，其势力影响可能由近及远地逐渐减弱。一般认为，商代的核心区域在今河南中部偏北及河北南部一带，在北纬34°~38°，东界大体在今河南省商丘以西和濮阳迄东一线，南界在淮阳、鲁山一线，西界及于孟津和太行山以东，北界在今河北省邢台、内丘附近。周代的核心区域，西界在今陕西省宝鸡市与甘肃省陇西县之间，大约包括渭南、商洛、汉中、咸阳、宝鸡等几个地区及甘肃省东部几个县，北部与汧陇一带交界，南及汉水以北，即河南、湖北交界地区，东到郑州西南百余里。核心区域以外，特别是那些商周势力不及的范围，往往被先秦经典文献称为"蛮荒"之地，即那些相对落后的酋邦、氏族和部落聚居区域，卜辞中称其为"方"，即方国。

所谓"方"，即人的集合体，一般规模较小，是一定地域范围内的血缘族群。它的形成与史前社会以来的地缘一体化密切相关，小者往往代表着一处或多处聚落，大者则可能包含一个甚至多个聚落群。由于这些区域范围内的"方国"没有文字，并且政治、经济和军事势力大大弱于中原地区的商周国家，所以不仅缺乏相关文献记载，而且长期成为商周国家征伐的对象。有关于此，我们在先秦经典文献中是难以见到的，现存相关历史信息渺薄。所以，我们尤其不能忽视卜辞和钟鼎铭文中的有关表述。因为这类文献史料作为商周时期的文字表达，不仅更贴近历史年代，而且更贴近史实，为我们提供了当时为数不多却弥足珍贵的历史信息，也为我们了解其时的历史状况留下了依稀可辨且难能可贵的线索。从文字描述的表象背后，可以发现商周社会的某些真相，包括商周国家对待方国的态度和立场。所以，我们讨论商周国家体制下的聚落，固然要利用经典文献来解读，但也要重视卜辞和钟鼎铭文。因为只重视前者容易使我们陷进先入为主的偏见，认为商周国家即代表着商周时期的广大区域，而忽略了商周国家核心及疆域以外的广袤地域。

殷代卜辞和钟鼎铭文中所见方国很多，近代以来的不少学者对此进行过系列考证。最早是孙诒让1904年的《契文举例》，其单独列出《方国》一篇，搜集了20多个地名。此后，罗振玉1915年的《殷墟卜辞中所见地名考》，认为殷墟卜辞中有200余个地名；1920年日本学者林泰辅的《甲骨文地名考》一文，对卜辞中的117个地名进行了考释，并绘制有地名示意图《龟甲兽骨地名图》。后来陆续有更多的学者加入其中，包括林义光、丁山、程憬、陈梦家、傅东华、郭沫若、李学勤等，不一而足。尽管他们中有的只是重复前人的考证，并无新绩，甚至有沽名钓誉之嫌，但并不影响这一群体的卓越成就。根据这些研究成果，我们大体可以了解商周时期的方国至少包括两类：一类是商周国家的敌对者，另一类则是依附于商周国家的臣服者。前者如方、危方、鬼方、下危、土方、微方、羌方、龙方、四邦方、兹方、刀方、大方、人方、盂方、井方、二邦方等；后者如井方、亚方、戈方、仓侯、丹伯、去伯、上丝、禾侯、竹侯、宋伯、攸侯等。事实上，这两种分类也并非绝对，因为有些方国与商王朝的关系是时敌时友。从时间上来说，上述方国大多是与商王朝同时期存在的，西周灭商，周王朝成为中原最强大的国家之后，一方面是原商王朝控制的四方诸侯相继归顺，另一方面则是周王朝核心区域及其势力范围之外的地区，仍旧广泛存在尚未被其统驭的方国。按《商代地理与方国》一书的考证，大致而言，上述方国主要分布在商周王朝核心区域的东、西、南、北四方。

文献可考的东部方国，主要分布在今山东除胶东半岛以外的地区，包括淮河附近以及江苏、安徽、河南交界地区，典型的方国有人方、孟方（东方）、林方、旁方、危方、攸侯等。其中人方长期与商王朝为敌，甲骨卜辞显示，商王朝曾屡次对其进行征伐。征伐过程也表明，商王朝核心区域周边还存在不少都邑一类的聚落。例如，可以辨识的有：大邑商，"甲午……步从侯喜征人方……告于大邑商"（《合集》36482）；西周何尊也有铭曰："唯武王既克大邑商，则廷告于天，曰：'余其宅兹中国，自之乂民。'""□□王卜，在商，贞今日于京亡灾。""甲寅王卜，在京，贞今日□[于]亡灾"（《合集》36567）。除此之外，还有雇、杞等几十余处。林方，"庚寅卜，……贞王臿林方亡灾"（《合集》36968/2）。林方原臣服于商，后反叛被灭，其地大概在今安徽境内，郭沫若认为在霍山县东北30里，陈梦家则认为在淮南，属于淮夷之邦。后者观点得到学术界的普遍认可。危方，原臣服于商，如下辞云："癸亥，贞危方以牛其登于来甲申"（《合集》32896、33191/4），类似的表述在《合集》10084/1、8492/1、32229、32897/4、32899/4等中均有体现。但其后来反叛，被商朝镇压，"……小臣墙从伐，半危美……人二十人四……而千五百七十……车二丙，橹百八十三，函五十，夫……于祖乙，用美于祖丁……"（《合集》36481正/3）。攸侯，为商朝封国，"甲戌卜，方，贞攸侯令其呙曰：'毐，若之。'五月"（《合集》5760正/1）。从这里来看，攸侯可能是商王朝征伐东部区域的前沿军事据点，似是戍边的族群聚落。

文献可考的西部方国最多，主要分布在今河南西部，山西西部、南部，陕西渭河流域以及陕西与山西、内蒙古、甘肃的交界地区，较为突出的方国有方、羌方、鬼方、土方、方、马方、巴方、商方、龙方、方、周方、马方、旦方、井方、亚方、戈方、侯等。方，甲骨文作，属武丁时期的敌对势力范围。从卜辞来看，方作为敌对方，曾多次内侵商朝，从卜辞常见的"方出""方伐""方敦"等表述便可窥见一斑。同时，也说明方可能是一个势力比较强劲的方国或族群。"癸巳卜，，贞旬亡。王曰：'土[ ]，其来艰。'气至五日丁酉，允来[艰自]西。……'土方征于我东啚，[ ]二邑；方亦我西啚田。'"（《合集》6057正/1）方的入侵，可能与侵占田地、掠夺人口和牲畜有关。方不仅侵略商王朝，还侵略周边的方国，并且联合土方、方等国一起侵略（《合集》8610正）。对此，商王朝间歇性地进行了反攻和征伐。至于羌方，陈梦家先生认为应该是一个游牧民族，而"羌"则是他们的种姓，后来被商王朝征服，成了商朝的田猎场（《合集》29309、29310）。召方与甲骨文中的"刀方"可能指同一方国，前期与商王朝为敌，商朝曾频繁征伐，似乎说明召方也是西方一个强劲的部落联盟。日本学者岛邦男认为召方位于周朝召公奭所在的召城一带；另有学者则认为这一地区过于偏西，应该在今山西中北部的地区。龙方为附属国，大体位于商王朝西北，与羌方接近，曾参与征伐羌方，卜辞云："贞呼龙氏羌。""勿呼龙氏羌。"（《合集》272反/1）后来龙方也叛服不定，商王朝又对其进行了征伐（《合集》31972/4）。鬼方早期活动范围比较广，包括今山西西北部、内蒙古及陕西北部的广大区域，与商王朝敌对，武丁以后成为附属国，并且为商朝打仗、祭祀、捕获羌人、贡纳人牲与官吏等，卜辞云："贞鬼获羌。""贞鬼不其获羌。""乙巳卜，方，贞鬼获羌。一月。""乙巳卜，方，贞鬼不其获羌。"（《合集》203正/1）西周小盂鼎铭记有康王二十五年周朝征伐鬼方的情况，其云："……伐鬼方……[执酋]三人，获馘四千八百□二馘，俘人万三千八十一人……"由此来看，鬼方可能是一个人口众多、由多个血缘族群组成的部落联盟。周方是殷商时期的西部方国，曾臣服于商王朝，后来灭商，建立周王朝。马方为商敌国（见《合集》6624、6761、5717正），位于山西西北部。旦方与商王朝互有攻伐，武丁时商朝曾派雀、戈、戉等部族前往征伐（《合集》6948正/1、6949正/1、6951反/1、6952正/1），后臣服于商（《合集》10184/1、7891/1、23431/2、33179/4、33180/4）。井方为商王朝附属国，是商王武丁王后妇井的母国，一直与商朝关系密切。有学者认为著名的"后母戊"就是妇井。亚方、戈方、仓侯、丹伯、禾侯都是商王朝的附属国或封国，与商朝的关系密切，有些曾与商朝一起参与征伐其他方国的行动。

文献可考的南方方国，主要分布在河南南部、安徽南部、湖北地区以及江西中北部，方国有zhong方、雇伯、虎方、卢伯、暴侯等。其中zhong方为南方地区势力强劲的敌对国，与商王朝之间曾长期存在互伐。"甲辰卜，宾，贞zhong方其舀，惟戎。十一月。贞zhong方不舀。"（《合补》1981/1）"贞勿登人五千。贞勿伐zhong方。贞王伐zhong方，受又。"（《合集》6541/1）前者反映出zhong方有内侵的可能，后者显示其征伐兵力达到五千人之多，这也表明zhong方是一南方强国。雇伯、虎方、卢伯、暴侯等都是商王朝的属国或封国，听命于商王朝，并参与征伐战争，卜辞和钟鼎铭文都有显示。譬如，虎方，卜辞有"乙亥卜，贞令虎追方"（《合集》20463反/2）等类似表述，1118年在今湖北安陆发现一套周代成王时期的"安州六器"，其中鼎铭有"佳王令南宫伐反虎方之年，王令中先省南国贯行……"（《集成》2751）。考古也在江西樟树发现有商代吴城遗址，考古学家彭明瀚就认为，吴城应该是虎方的中心。吴城年代大致在商代中晚期，属于城郭聚落，总面积4平方千米，可分居住区、陶窑区、冶炼区和祭祀广场等，出土遗物数千件。

可考的北部方国，主要分布在今山西北部、河北北部和辽宁西部，方国有土方、下危、竹侯、宋伯等。土方大概在今山西西北部，是殷商王朝北部的主要敌对国，卜辞云"辛巳卜，争，贞今载王土方，受又。五月。"（《合集》6412/1）妇好是武丁的妻子，商王朝著名的女军事家，曾参与征伐鬼方、羌方和土方等军事行动，包括此条所云"妇好伐土方"在内的众多卜辞和妇好墓出土的青铜器兵器都充分表明了这一点。然而，土方可能是一个势力强劲的方国，人口众多，疆域较大，因为商王朝征伐土方兵力最多达到五千余人，并且是商王亲自参与，可见土方是不容小觑的力量。卜辞云："丁酉卜，，贞今王共人五千征土方受又。三月。"（《合集》6409/1）下危也是商王朝的敌对国，商朝对其有过长期的征伐，一次征伐的兵力曾达到三千人，"……三千……伐下危受[ ]又"（《合集》6523/1）。竹侯、宋伯属于商王朝的附属国，分别被封为侯和伯爵。1973年辽宁喀左县北洞村一号窖藏曾出土有一件竹侯的青铜罍，其名曰"父丁冉亚"，反映出竹侯与商王朝关系的密切。

从上述商周时期的方国来看，我们大体可以得出几点认识。一是商周以国家的形式出现后，特别是殷商时期，其核心疆域主要在黄河中游地区的中原一带，其核心区域及其周边范围以外的广袤地区，普遍存在属于部落或部落联盟的方国。二是方国可能是史前社会聚落群聚化或地缘一体化的结果，因为卜辞显示各个方国不仅普遍分布于商周核心区域的四周，而且有一定的地域范围或势力范围，如龙方大体位于商王朝西北，与羌方接近。三是方国可能仍为基于血缘的族群，由多个氏族或部落组成，属于部落联盟，譬如西周小盂鼎铭文所记周康王征伐鬼方，就俘获了"[执酋]三人""万三千八十一人"，"酋"是首领，"[执酋]三人"便是三个首领。这段记述表明，鬼方可能至少是三个氏族或部落所组成的地域联盟，而且人口众多。四是商周方国之间的互为征伐，或是方国对商周王朝的依附，都体现为对自然资源的争夺，包括田地、人口和牲畜等，卜辞中诸如"侵田""田猎""俘人"等词汇则是较为充分的表述，可资为证。商周国家与周边部落或方国的攻伐战争或联盟，主要是生存驱动，其目的是守护或扩大自身的生存空间。因为史前农业兴起后，虽然成为人类社会经济生活中的主要门类，但在广泛意义上仍属于掠夺性的粗犷式农业生产。特别是生产技术低下和土地资源贫瘠的商周王朝的周边方国，可能依旧是抛荒农业，所以当土地质量下降时，便只有另寻耕地，向外扩张，或是当食物不足，而生产又跟不上时，便只有抢夺。当然，也正是这一系列不断的攻伐和兼并，使早期中国在一定区域范围内实现了不同族群、不同地域之间的频繁互动，从而出现了跨血缘、跨族群、跨地域和跨文化的相互交织，进而逐步推动早期中国走向多元一体的民族国家，直至正式形成"华夏民族"的概念。尽管这种文化上的交融在商周时期更体现为以商周王朝为核心的文化圈，以及商周王朝对周边方国的征伐，但并没有影响这种交融仍表现为统一性与多样性的并存和协调。考古发现的四川三星堆、江西新干大洋洲、湖南宁乡等地的商周遗址、遗物，以及诸多研究成果都表明了文化的多样性与统一性并存。
