Section 3: The Birth of the State and Speculation on Villages

The direct result of the continuous differentiation and expansion of villages and the continuous development of community formation is the emergence of cities and the formation of geopolitical integration. The continuous consolidation and expansion of geopolitical integration, in turn, promoted the emergence of the state. According to Marx's view, this development trend is a product of the evolution of private ownership and also a product of class society. As Engels stated in "Anti-Dühring": "With the emergence of differences in distribution, class differences also emerged. Society was divided into privileged and injured, exploiting and exploited, ruling and ruled classes, and the state, which naturally formed groups of communes of the same clan initially only to safeguard common interests (for example, irrigation in the East) and to resist foreign enemies. From then on, it also acquired the function of using violence against the ruled class to maintain the living conditions and ruling conditions of the ruling class." The essence of the state is the rule of one class over another, so its emergence means the establishment of cross-regional, cross-blood, and cross-tribal social, economic, and political relations. For the state to maintain and consolidate such relations, its premise and foundation are the comprehensive control of land and population, because the two relate to the state's economic income and are "the living conditions and ruling conditions for maintaining the ruling class." The so-called "Under the whole heaven, every spot is the sovereign's ground; to the borders of every spot of ground, every individual is the sovereign's minister" in the "Book of Songs" expresses this meaning. For this reason, after the emergence of the state, villages, as the most basic regional units, production and living units, and social units of early human society, began to have significance at the state level.

I. The Emergence of Early States and Villages

From archaeological discoveries and historical documentary records, roughly after the Erlitou culture, and up to the establishment of the Shang and Western Zhou regimes, early China began to formally appear in the form of a state. As mentioned above, the essence of the state is the rule of one class over another, and villages, as local forces bonded by blood, are obviously the objects of rule, and also the objects of strict supervision in early China. Because as regional units and actually existing production and living units, villages are synonymous with land and population, which directly relate to the foundation and development of the state. Theoretically, between the state and villages, they both restrict and check each other, and also promote and develop together. But in fact, for a long time after the formation of early states, the state did not become a driving force for village development, but instead restricted village development. The fundamental reason is that the maintenance and consolidation of early states were premised on rule. Documentary records show that to better maintain state rule, pre-Qin states implemented the "well-field system" for land, cultivated by slaves and commoners; after the Warring States period, they switched to the "land-granting system," where land was granted by the state, but commoners only had usage rights and could not buy or sell. For population, they implemented nationalized management, institutionally striving to incorporate slaves and commoners into concentrated residence in cities. After Qin unified the six states, it further strengthened control by establishing the commandery-county system, with the "xiang-li" (village-ward) system established below counties. It is precisely this series of systems that enabled early China to effectively strengthen exchanges and communication between the state and local society, but also for this reason, the development space of villages was greatly compressed.

The well-field system, as a land system that existed before the Spring and Autumn period, was an effective way for early states to manage and control society. It influenced the formation and development of early Chinese social forms, including villages, for a long time. The term "well-field" as a proper noun was first seen in the "Guliang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals - Duke Xuan, Year 15": "In ancient times, 300 paces made a li, called well-field." The text further points out, "Well-field consists of 900 mu, with public field accounting for one. If private field crops are not good, it is the fault of officials; if public field crops are not good, it is the fault of the people. The initial tax per mu means not removing public fields but taxing per mu, taking one-tenth, because the relationship between public and private is already fully understood." Roughly meaning, well-field can be divided into two parts: public field and private field, with one part being public field and the rest being private fields. Private fields are respectively cultivated by eight families, who not only must pay sufficient taxes to the state but also jointly bear the responsibility of cultivating public fields. "Mencius - Duke Wen of Teng, Part I" records: "A square li makes a well, a well consists of 900 mu. Among them is public field, eight families each have 100 mu of private field, and jointly cultivate public field. After public affairs are completed, then dare to attend to private affairs." Different from what is recorded in "Mencius," the statement in "Rites of Zhou" in its "Offices of Earth - Minor Minister of Instruction" says: "Then demarcate land and well-pasture its fields, nine men make a well, four wells make a yi, four yi make a qiu, four qiu make a dian, four dian make a xian, four xian make a du, to manage land affairs and order tributes, all matters of tax collection." The "well-field" theory in "Rites of Zhou" holds that well-field has no distinction between "public field" and "private field." In fact, regarding a series of issues about the well-field system, not only were there different understandings in the pre-Qin period, but since the late Qing dynasty it has aroused widespread controversy, with many scholars discussing it from different angles, especially regarding its specific form and content, with diverse opinions. Related to village formation, there are roughly two views. Scholars represented by Yang Kuan believe that the well-field system was the rural commune system before the Spring and Autumn era. Its emergence was out of "the need for unified governance and management of water conservancy irrigation," implemented "in plain areas with river irrigation," and believed that on this basis, "yi" and "li" as living spaces were formed. Although this view is generally accepted, some scholars have questioned it, believing that "under the well-field system, farmers' individual plots were directly received from the state rather than the village commune, so the well-field system is not only not a typical rural commune land system... but belongs to the state land-granting system of state-owned land nature. It was not the land system of the Western Zhou period, but an ideal system created based on the state land-granting system of the Warring States period."

Which of the above statements is right or wrong is not what we want to discuss. What can be affirmed is that as a land system or tax system, the well-field system should have formally formed in the Western Zhou period and already appeared in the Xia and Shang periods. Not only do historical materials such as Shang and Zhou oracle bone inscriptions, bronze inscriptions, and pre-Qin classical documents have expressions of similar content, but related records all indicate its important role in the formation process of early state society. In early China, the emergence of the state form meant it was no longer simply a clan commune bonded by blood, but a cross-blood, cross-regional state social organization. To maintain such a social organization, primitive public ownership was obviously no longer suitable, so the well-field system, as a way of evenly distributing land within a certain regional area, emerged as the times required and played a role in maintaining and stabilizing the state. Essentially, the fundamental purpose of Shang and Western Zhou states implementing well-fields or the well-field system was to collect taxes, so their starting points were consistent. To achieve this purpose, on one hand, to maximize the benefits of land as a means of production, land must be reasonably distributed, as much as possible enabling the state, land owners, and land cultivators to profit, and making such interests measured and balanced. On the other hand, the national population as productive forces must be fixed on the land. The record in the "Guliang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals" that "if private field crops are not good, it is the fault of officials; if public field crops are not good, it is the fault of the people" is a requirement for both officials and farmers, but since officials are the managers and supervisors of private fields, "farming fields" ultimately targets farmers, which institutionally fixes farmers on the land. It is precisely this logical starting point that gives the well-field system, as a state institution, significance at the level of village changes. Its significance is prominently reflected in the grassroots management system that exists in conjunction with the well-field system, the so-called "guo-ye system" (capital-countryside system), which are cause and effect for each other, jointly maintaining the grassroots social form of early states.

The "guo-ye system" is what "Rites of Zhou" calls "delimiting the capital and organizing the countryside, establishing officials and dividing duties." Related to the countryside is the "xiang-sui system" (township-district system). In the "guo" (capital), six xiang (townships) are established. "Rites of Zhou - Grand Minister of Instruction" says: "On the first day of the first month, begin to harmonize and proclaim teachings to the states and capital districts... making each teach the people they govern. Order five families to form a bi, making them mutually guarantee; five bi to form a lü, making them mutually receive; four lü to form a zu, making them mutually bury; five zu to form a dang, making them mutually rescue; five dang to form a zhou, making them mutually aid; five zhou to form a xiang, making them mutually respect." "Guo" means "du-bi" (capital-district). Wei Zhao annotated: "Du means guo (capital). Bi means border town." Zheng Xuan annotated: "Du-bi are the fiefs of royal sons, dukes, ministers, and grand masters; their boundaries are called du, and bi is where they reside." Du-bi were the fixed residential points around the capital city or national capital at that time, concentrating nobles, artisans, commoners, and merchants. The construction of du-bi formed the form of concentrated urban residence, as evidenced by the saying "whenever constructing du-bi, delimit their territory and seal with ditches, regulate according to their number of rooms." The establishment of "six xiang" exactly consolidated this at the institutional level, with its functional purpose being both convenient for management and fixing farmers on land within a certain regional area, thereby maintaining state stability. This practice was closely related to the enfeoffment system implemented in early China. "Whenever establishing states, use the earth gui to measure their land and regulate their domains: dukes' lands have boundaries of 500 li square, with half for their sustenance; marquises' lands have boundaries of 400 li square, with one-third for their sustenance; earls' lands have boundaries of 300 li square, with one-third for their sustenance; viscounts' lands have boundaries of 200 li square, with one-fourth for their sustenance; barons' lands have boundaries of 100 li square, with one-fourth for their sustenance." The enfeoffment system may have begun to appear as late as the Shang dynasty, with enfeoffed hou and bo, but it was not yet perfect; its true maturity and widespread implementation was in the Zhou dynasty. The Zhou dynasty enfeoffed land to vassals, who within their fiefs bestowed land to ministers and grand masters, who then bestowed land to their sons, brothers, and shi (knights). Enfeoffment essentially caused division between the central and local governments, so the establishment of "six xiang" was also to strengthen central control over enfeoffed lands. Outside the "guo," "six sui" (districts) were established in the "ye" (countryside), "using maps of land to organize fields, creating the method of county-district forms. Five families form a lin, five lin form a li, four li form a cuan, five cuan form a bi, five bi form a xian, five xian form a sui, all have territories, with ditches and trees." The vast area outside the "guo" is "ye." Zheng Xuan annotated: "Outside the suburbs is called ye. This ye refers to dian, shao, xian, and du." In short, ye is the vast rural area. The "li" mentioned in documents is the grassroots organization in rural areas and belongs to officially recognized residential spaces with certain boundaries.

Obviously, as a governance system universally implemented by states before the Spring and Autumn period, especially in the Western Zhou period, both the well-field system and the guo-ye system played positive roles, promoting communication and exchange between the central state and vassal states and their local societies, while maintaining state stability. However, we must consider whether such regular systems in documents necessarily conform to reality. Understood according to documentary records, villages as natural settlements seem difficult to be classified into them. Precisely because of this series of documentary records, the pre-Qin period or the historical period before the Han dynasty in China was considered by Japanese scholars represented by Miyazaki Ichisada as "city-states," and only after entering the Three Kingdoms period did it gradually evolve toward scattered villages called "cun" (village). Domestic scholar Hou Wailu also discussed in the 1930s the issue of Yin and Zhou being city-states, tracing the origin of Chinese "city-states" to the late Shang dynasty, pointing out that ancient characters "bang" and "feng" are synonymous, and "cheng" and "guo" are synonymous. Of course, Mr. Hou did not deny the existence of agricultural-type settlements before the pre-Qin period; on the contrary, he believed that the first division between city and countryside occurred in China from the Western Zhou to the Spring and Autumn period. Many scholars also believe that the "city-state theory" is unreliable, or at least incomplete, believing that the claim that people before the pre-Qin period completely lived in city walls is questionable. Scholars holding this view include Matsumoto Masaaki and Ikeda Kazuo in Japan, and Hou Xudong domestically. The author believes that the key to causing this divergence is certainly related to different starting points of argumentation, but mainly lies in two aspects: first, lack of grasp of village connotation, especially "city-state theorists" often only understand villages as a social organization linked to state institutions, both ignoring their objective existence as material entity spaces and neglecting the non-material content such as language, customs, morality, religion, experience, and technology formed on the basis of clan clustering and blood continuity. Therefore, when records about grassroots systems in pre-Qin documents are vague or reflect an administrative ideal, they usually consciously exclude the possibility of actual living units or ethnic groups existing outside state institutions; second, relevant records in pre-Qin documents are mostly later retrospections based on self-understanding, or just institutions full of subjective ideals derived by rulers for convenient management and control of the state, possibly not truly objective social reality, and people's understanding of such documents usually has varying degrees of difference, often neglecting the accumulated contributions of anthropology and geography in interpreting villages as social units and regional units.

sections.name: 秦汉统治制度下的村落
sections.content_zh:
第一节 秦汉统治制度下的村落

大一统国家建立之后，为了巩固统治，维系国家的稳定，制定和推行一系列符合自身利益的统治政策成了国家治理的必需。这些统治政策的主要内容，大多关系到人口、土地、赋税和文化等问题。而村落作为承载这些内容的主要载体，便因此不同程度地受到影响，甚至改变发展的进程轨迹。大致来看，先秦国家体制下，百姓大都集中居住于封闭的城郭或里邑之中，到秦汉时期，由于社会稳定，特别是郡县制的推行导致社会相对宽松，先秦以来国家体制之外原有的零星的、少量的散居现象渐趋增多。文献和考古显示，全国各地不同程度地散布着不同形式、不同类型的乡野聚落的情况开始发生重要的变化，初步形成了城居与散居并存的格局，城邑与乡村的分野越来越明显。这些变化固然与人类社会自身发展的内里逻辑有关，但很大程度上也是国家政策推行的结果。

一、乡里制度与村落

所谓乡里制度，是指古代中国县级以下的各级基层行政区划的制度，是古代中国管控与治理乡村社会的关键制度。历史上，乡里制度虽因朝代不同而各有兴废，但作为一项成功的治理制度，仍以不同名称或不同形式被以后历朝历代沿袭，在国家治理体系中发挥重要的作用。

乡里制度到底起源于何时，学术界尚无确切定论，但从文献记载来看，乡里制度的萌生比较早。《文献通考》有详细之载述："昔黄帝始经土设井，以塞争端。立步制庙以防不足。使八家为井，井开四道而分八宅。凿井于中，一则不泄地气，二则无费一家，三则同风俗，四则齐巧拙，五则通财货，六则存亡更守，七则出入相司，八则嫁娶相媒，九则无有相贷，十则疾病相救，是以情性可得而亲，生产可得而均。均则欺凌之路塞，亲则斗讼之心弭。既牧之于邑，故井一为邻，邻三为朋，朋三为里，里五为邑，邑十为都，都十为师，师七为州。夫始分于井则地著，计之于州则数详，迄乎夏殷不易其制。"按这一说法，乡里之制在黄帝时期便已产生，然而由于《文献通考》一书是宋人所著，所以其文献记载的真实性不高。一般认为，乡里制度在商周时期便广泛出现，传世文献和金文中常见有"乡""里"等字眼。《逸周书·商誓》载："王若曰：告尔伊旧何父……及百官里居献民……予亦来休命尔百姓里居君子。"《尚书·酒诰》载："越在百姓里居，罔敢湎于酒。"这两条文献所载"里居"即是居住单元，而非表示距离和长度。《周礼》中亦记载有"乡遂之制"，还有乡老、乡师、乡大夫和乡士等职官。"乡遂"一词中："乡"，是国人居住之地，即指城郭及周边的近郊范围；"遂"，则为野人居住之地，指边远农村地区。在"国"设六乡，"令五家为比，五比为闾，四闾为族，五族为党，五党为州，五州为乡"。在"野"设"六遂"，"五家为邻，五邻为里，四里为酂，五酂为鄙，五鄙为县，五县为遂"。

《周礼》所述虽为后人的追述，更体现为一种理想，可能与实情并不完全相符，但对照金文中有关"乡""里"的表述，可以肯定的是，"乡"和"里"作为一种地域组织形态或居民居住空间，在西周时期是客观存在的。西周中期的九年卫鼎铭记："唯九年正月，既死霸庚辰，王在周驹宫，各庙，眉敖者肤卓事见于王，王大……遹舍裘卫林里。……矩迺众濂羚令寿商众意，曰：'顜，履付裘卫林里，则乃成封四封，颜小子俱惟封，寿商'。……卫用作朕文考宝鼎，卫其万年永宝用。"（《集成》2831）铭文的大致意思是"林里"作为贵族"矩"的一块领地，其间有树林，后来出售给了裘卫，四面以土垄封以为界。这应该就属于乡村地域的"里"。与此不同，西周中期的簋铭文载："王曰：'，命汝成周里人，众诸侯、大亚，讯讼罚。……'拜稽首，对扬王休命……"（《集成》4215）此处所言"成周"是西周的都城洛邑，"里人"则是里的管理者，这里的"里"，显然是城区范围内的居住空间或组织。可见，里也并非仅限于"野"，在"国"亦有。被公认为西周时期文献的《逸周书·作雒解》亦云"俘殷献民，迁于九里"，孔晁注"九里，成周之地"。此处的"九里"应不是指地名，而是表明有许多个基层居民组织的"里"。《史记·燕召公世家》云"召公巡行乡邑，有棠树，决狱政事其下"，是指召公于乡邑中处理政务。上述文献表明，"乡里"不仅仅是一个居住空间，更是西周时期国家管控下的乡村地缘形态与基层组织机构。

作为一种制度，乡里之制的定型可能在春秋战国时期。由于春秋战国于形式上而言仍属于东周，所以各诸侯国的诸多制度仍然都沿袭了西周以来的内容，特别是国野之制。其中齐国的国鄙之制最为典型。《管子·小匡》云："管子对曰：'昔者圣王之治其民也，参其国而伍其鄙，定民之居，成民之事，以为民纪……'桓公曰：'参国奈何？'管子对曰：'制国以为二十一乡，商工之乡六，士农之乡十五。公帅十一乡，高子帅五乡，国子帅五乡，参国故为三军……制五家为轨，轨有长。十轨为里，里有司。四里为连，连有长。十连为乡，乡有良人。三乡一帅。'桓公曰：'五鄙奈何？'管子对曰：'制五家为轨，轨有长。六轨为邑，邑有司。十邑为率，率有长。十率为乡，乡有良人。三乡为属，属有帅。五属一大夫，武政听属，文政听乡，各保而听，毋有淫泆者。'"《管子》所载固然不能被完全视为春秋时期诸国的历史事实，但至少是齐国当时的状况。国鄙之制从内容来看，"国"与"鄙"分别设置，与《周礼》所记"国""野"分治在形式上类似，在内容上却不同，当是对周代国野之制的改进。《管子·立政》云："分国以为五乡，乡为之师；分乡以为五州，州为之长；分州以为十里，里为之尉；分里以为十游，游为之宗；十家为什，五家为伍，什伍皆有长焉。"这条文献说明春秋时期的齐国，不仅在西周乡遂之制的基础上进一步完善了乡里制度，而且确立并普及了乡里什伍制度。这种做法的目的，当然还是进一步管控人口，巩固国家统治，使得国家统治管控更加严密，实现"奔亡者无所匿，迁徙者无所容"，"人与人相保，家与家相爱，少相居，长相游，祭祀相福，死丧相恤，祸福相忧，居处相乐"的治理模式。正是这种做法，使春秋时期的齐国呈现"人无非其里，里无非其家"的社会面貌，也促使个人、家庭与乡里组织甚至国家的关系愈加密切，有效解决了家族公社和农村公社解体后基层社会结构涣散的问题。

《左传》中的有关记载，在某种程度上就反映了这类制度在春秋时期推行后深刻影响了人们的生活观念。如《左传·庄公十年》云："十年春，齐师伐我。公将战，曹刿请见。其乡人曰。""乡人"泛指同乡之人，"乡"则具有地域的概念。又《左传·襄公十五年》载："小人怀璧，不可以越乡。"杜注："言必为盗所害。"此处的"乡"明显是一个地域概念。《战国策·秦策一》云："故卖仆妾不出里巷而取者，良仆妾也；出妇嫁于乡里者，善妇也。"大致是说乡里的舆论评价对妇女的嫁娶有很大的影响。诸如此类，都表明伴随乡里之制的广泛推行，地方社会逐步形成了"乡里""乡土"的观念，这是自觉的地域认同。但也正因制度上力图实现"人无非其里，里无非其家"的局面，所以作为自然聚落的村落的自由发展，有可能在当时反而受到过一定程度的制约。

秦统一全国之后，为了巩固国家政权，必须加强对地方社会的控制，尤其是原属于统一之前诸侯国家的广大地域。基于这一逻辑出发点，秦朝吸取了西周的教训，废除了分封制，代以郡县制，将全国分为三十六郡，郡下设县，彻底打破自西周以来的世卿世禄制度。文献记载显示，秦朝不仅于郡下设县，而且对县以下的乡里制度进行了调整。《汉书》载："县令、长，皆秦官，掌治其县。……大率十里一亭，亭有长。十亭一乡，乡有三老、有秩、啬夫、游徼。三老掌教化。啬夫职听讼，收赋税。游徼徼循禁贼盗。县大率方百里，其民稠则减，稀则旷，乡、亭亦如之，皆秦制也。"按这一表述，秦代的乡里制度是乡、亭、里三级制，汉承秦制，无出其右，相比于《管子》中"轨、伍、里、连、乡"的多级制简化了很多，更有利于中央对地方社会的控制。正是由于秦代国家着力健全和统一地方基层政权，地方才普遍建立起了郡县乡里体制，于制度层面较好地消弭了地方分裂势力。但是，与"乡、亭、里"这一传统观点不同的是，有学者根据文献材料对《汉书》中的表述提出了质疑，认为秦汉时期的"亭"并非地方行政机构的名称，甚至认为"十里之亭"的"里"也不是表示"乡里"组织的"里"，而是表距离。后来高敏、朱绍侯等学者还结合竹简等材料从不同层面进行了论证和解读。目前，关于亭的性质基本达成了共识，即认为亭不是一级行政组织，而是乡里组织之外的治安机构，乡里才是基层行政单位。

从文献记载来看，乡里制度的确立和普遍设置，其目的还是实现对全国范围内基层百姓的管控和治理，《汉书》云"三老掌教化。啬夫职听讼，收赋税。游徼徼循禁贼盗"即表露无遗。同书载："凡县、道、国、邑千五百八十七，乡六千六百二十二，亭二万九千六百三十五。"又《续汉书·郡国五》："至于孝顺，凡郡国百五，县、道、邑、侯国千一百八十。"注引《东观书》曰："（桓帝）永兴元年，乡三千六百八十二。"据《续汉书·百官五》注引《风俗通》曰："国家制度，大率十里一乡。"根据上述文献表述，黄今言先生以"十里一乡"为标准，进行了测算，认为西汉如果有6 622个乡，便有66 220个里；东汉如果有3 682个乡，则有36 820个里。按《尹湾汉墓简牍》所记东海郡"县百七十口百六，里二千五百卅四"，"户廿六万六千二百九十"，若按此测算，平均一里大概105户。这一户数与长沙马王堆三号汉墓出土的《驻军图》上所注龙里户数相当。龙里是《驻军图》中户数最多的里，有108户，次者垣里81户、智里68户，较少者如波里17户、资里12户，其他多在40户左右。《驻军图》中可考共41里，每里平均户数在40~50户。湖北江陵凤凰山十号汉墓简牍所载，郑里廪簿共登记25户，即向官府贷粮的户数。如若加上没有贷粮的民户，其户数也未必会多出很多。由此看来，大致可以得出三点认识：一是秦汉时期的乡是里的上级机构，乡统属里；二是里作为户口统计的单位，也是居住空间组织；三是里有大有小，户口数量参差不齐。文献和相关简牍材料所显示的这三个表征，意味着"里"不只是户口统计单位，还体现为一种自然形成的聚落。正因如此，黄今言先生便认为汉代的乡村社会是"一村一聚，往往就是一个'里'，大'聚'有时与里重合"。马新、齐涛等学者更是认为汉代乡村社会是里聚合一，是行政单元与自然聚落的一致。但以侯旭东为代表的不少学者对此提出了不同的看法，他们认为汉代的"里"大部分应是行政编制，不是行政村与自然村的合一。上述这三种观点，无论哪一种，事实上反映了存在的三种情况在汉代社会应该兼而有之。这种社会表象更是充分表明了先秦以来集中城居的理想与现实基本上已全面瓦解。

二、重农抑商政策与村落

我国自古以农立国，早在距今约1万年前的新石器时代便开始进入农业生产阶段。到新石器时代中晚期，农业更是成为社会经济的主要支撑，占据主导地位，成为人们赖以生存的基础。进入阶级社会以后，农业的重要性进一步凸显，农业不仅是人们基本生活资料的主要来源，而且在巩固国家政权、维系国家稳定方面起到积极作用。夏、商、西周时期，井田的出现及井田制度的形成，就充分说明了这一点。文献显示，周族就是以农业发达著称的，其始祖弃"好耕农，相地之宜，宜谷者稼穑焉，民皆法则之。帝尧闻之，举弃为农师，天下得其利，有功"。进入春秋时期，重农成为各诸侯国统治的主要治国思想，如齐国在管仲的建议下，推行了"相地而衰征"的政策，即按照土地好坏等级来征收赋税，以期调动国民对农业生产的积极性，达到"则民不移"的效果。孔子曾指出："道千乘之国，敬事而信，节用而爱人，使民以时。""使民以时"即指国家的统治者要敦促国民按照时令来耕种农作物。春秋晚期"不违农时"甚至成了一项重要的政治主张，是治国理政的根本大事。孟子曾在游说梁惠王时指出："不违农时，谷不可胜食也；数罟不入洿池，鱼鳖不可胜食也；斧斤以时入山林，材木不可胜用也；谷与鱼鳖不可胜食，材木不可胜用，是使民养生丧死无憾也。"春秋以来，井田制逐渐被瓦解，最后被废除，而授田制在此时开始推行。"重农"与"抑商"开始作为国家政策被正式提了出来。其中秦国商鞅变法于此不但翔实，而且最为典型，其变法明确规定："僇力本业，耕织致粟帛多者，复其身；事末利及怠而贫者，举以为收孥。"大意是努力从事农业耕种、纺织工作，并且取得好收成的人，国家要提高其身份，反之，如果从事商业并且懒惰的人，要收为奴隶。《韩非子》中就曾指出，商鞅变法是"以变法易俗而明公道，赏告奸，困末作而利本事"。正因为商鞅变法"重农抑商"取得了显著效果，秦国逐步实现了国富民强，进而为秦始皇统一中国奠定了坚实的物质基础。

秦朝建立后，启用了商鞅的政策，并把韩非子的部分思想引入国家治理，进一步将"重农禁末"发展为"上农除末"的国家政策。秦始皇曾在巡行琅琊时，刻石纪功云："皇帝之功，勤劳本事。上农除末，黔首是富"。为此，秦始皇颁布有七科谪戍条例，即"治狱吏不直者，诸尝逋亡人，赘婿，贾人，尝有市籍者，大父母、父母尝有市籍者"，客观上严厉抑制了商业的发展。

汉代基本承袭了秦代的政策，继续实行"重农抑商"的国策，实行轻徭薄赋、与民休息，发展农业。汉初政论家贾谊曾在劝说汉文帝时说："背本而趋末，食者甚众，是天下之大残也；淫侈之俗，日日以长，是天下之大贼也。残贼公行，莫之或止；大命将泛，莫之振救。……今驱民而归之农，皆著于本，使天下各食其力，末技游食之民转而缘南亩，则畜积足而人乐其所矣。"汉景帝于后元三年（公元前141年）春正月曾下诏云："农，天下之本也。黄金珠玉，饥不可食，寒不可衣，以为币用，不识其终始。间岁或不登，意为末者众，农民寡也。其令郡国务劝农桑，益种树，可得衣食物。"正是由于汉初一系列重农措施的实行，到汉武帝时期，西汉的经济和国力达到了鼎盛。《汉书》载："至武帝之初七十年间，国家亡事，非遇水旱，则民人给家足，都鄙廪庾尽满，而府库余财。京师之钱累百钜万，贯朽而不可校。太仓之粟陈陈相因，充溢露积于外，腐败不可食。"汉武帝时，国家还通过实施盐铁官营、平准、均输等政策，进一步抑制商业的发展，防范商人资本为牟取暴利而对国家经济和社会生活造成诸如贫富两极分化、土地兼并加剧、农业人口流失等问题。汉武帝之后，西汉历代均不同程度地延续和推行了"重农抑商"的政策，昭帝、宣帝时还一度出现了中兴的局面。

东汉以后，国家虽然继续推行"重农抑商"的政策，但力度明显减轻。东汉思想家王符的思想具有代表性。他在《潜夫论·务本》中云："凡为治之大体，莫善于抑末而务本，莫不善于离本而饰末。……夫富民者，以农桑为本，以游业为末；百工者，以致用为本，以巧饰为末；商贾者，以通货为本，以鬻奇为末：三者守本离末则民富，离本守末则民贫，贫则阨而忘善，富则乐而可教。"相比西汉，这一表述中的"本末"已然发生了变化，"本"不仅仅指农业，还包括行业本应遵循的"本"，如百工的"致用"，商贾的"通货"；"末"也未必指"商业"，而是凡违背行业之"本"的都为"末"。当然，王符的表述既非"重商"也不是全面"抑商"，而是主张在"以农为本"的前提下限制生产和经营奢侈品的工商业。正是这样一种思想和相对宽松的政策环境，不仅在一定程度上促进了商业在东汉的发展，而且滋养了农村地区自给自足的小农经济的成长。

"重农抑商""上农除末"政策的提倡和实施，在时间上发生于战国，发展于秦皇时期，完全形成在西汉。作为秦汉国家的一项基本国策，"重农抑商"推行的根本原因，在于农业国家的经济基础是自给自足的小农经济，农业是秦汉国家乃至后世王朝的决定性产业，它的生产状况好坏，是否兴旺发达，直接关系到社会的繁荣稳定和国家的兴衰存亡。所以，历朝历代都把"重农"作为国家经济政策的根本性大事来抓。商鞅就曾说："百人农一人居者王，十人农一人居者强，半农半居者危。故治国者欲民之农也。国不农，则与诸侯争权，不能自持也，则众力不足也。故诸侯挠其弱，乘其衰，土地侵削而不振，则无及已。"国家正因高度认识到农业产业事关国家生死存亡，也正因出台了一系列督促、鼓励和组织农业生产的措施，既确保了财政收入，也将农民紧紧地固定在土地上而不能离开，从而维系了社会的稳定。也正因如此，不仅村落的进一步形成与发展有了制度保证，而且村落与农耕文化紧密地联系在了一起。这突出表现在三个方面：一是"重农"政策有效防止了农业劳动力的流失，特别是减少了农村人口向工商领域的转移，从而为农业生产确保了农民人力资源这一长期稳定的第一生产力要素；二是正因为农民群体的长期存在和不断壮大，作为群体性生产生活空间和社会单元的村落，不仅有了存在的必要性，而且有了生长的必然性；三是围绕农业生产开始形成具有强烈农耕文化特征的风俗习惯，这从汉代画像石上所刻画的各种关于农业题材内容的图像中可以窥见一斑。可以肯定地说，中国传统的村落，不论是形态还是文化内涵，它的形成都与古代中国国家重视农业生产、推行"重农"政策制度密不可分。

三、文化一统政策与村落

文化是社会发展的重要推手，是凝聚一个国家、一个民族内部力量的关键内核要素之一。文化政策作为一个国家发展政策的重要组成部分，既是文化的一种政治表现形态，也是一个国家、一个民族文化利益与文化意志的集中反映和表达。因此，中国古代国家的历朝历代都十分重视文化政策的制定和实施。

秦朝作为中国历史上首个大一统的中央集权制国家，为了消弭战国以来诸侯纷争所导致的文化分裂，增强国家的凝聚力，巩固国家政权的统治，面对统一之后存在的"田畴异亩，车涂异轨，律令异法，衣冠异制，言语异声，文字异形"的情况，采取了一系列对后世影响深远的文化政策。历史上，任何一个王朝在建立初期，都会根据自身的政治、经济形势和政权建设的需要采取相应的文化措施。秦朝作为以法家思想来治国理政的朝代，加之统一之后面对的文化分裂的严峻局面，其在文化政策的制定与实施上都体现出较为强烈的法家特点。

所以，秦朝建立之后，推行了整齐划一的政治与文化政策，即所谓"车同轨，书同文，行同伦"。据史载，秦始皇统一六国之后，便令丞相李斯、中车府令赵高等对文字进行了整理。李斯以秦国文字为基础，参照其他六国的文字，发明了小篆，并刻写范本，在全国范围内传播。《说文解字·叙》中云："丞相李斯乃奏同之，罢其不与秦文合者。斯作《仓颉篇》，中车府令赵高作《爰历篇》，太史令胡毋敬作《博学篇》，皆取史籀大篆，或颇省改，所谓小篆者也。"史载，秦代著名书法家程邈还根据民间流行的更为简化的字体创造了隶书。《说文解字·叙》亦云："秦烧灭经典，涤除旧典，大发吏卒，兴役戍，官狱职务繁。初有隶书，以趣约易……秦始皇使下邽人程邈所作也。"同时，秦朝大力推行法家的治国思想，禁绝《诗》《书》，以吏为师。秦孝公就曾根据商鞅的建议，"燔《诗》《书》而明法令"；后来韩非子更被认为是反对"藏书策，习谈论，聚徒役，服文学而议说，世主必从而礼之"的学士，他指出"夫冰炭不同器而久，寒暑不兼时而至，杂反之学不两立而治"，认为"国平则养儒侠，难至则用介士，所养者非所用，所用者非所养，此所以乱也"。李斯更是斥责儒生"今师今而学古，以非当世，惑乱黔首"，并建议始皇焚书，从而导致了"焚书坑儒"这一文化浩劫的出现。

正是这一系列高压的文化专制主义政策的实施，使得秦代在政治统一的同时初步实现了文化上的一统，不仅有效促进了中央与地方、地方与地方之间的交流互通，而且有利于端正风俗。就此而言，其意义也是有积极的一面的。秦始皇刻石便有整饬稽淫之风的表述，其云："饰省宣义，有子而嫁，倍死不贞。防隔内外，禁止淫泆，男女絜诚。夫为寄豭，杀之无罪，男秉义程。妻为逃嫁，子不得母，咸化廉清。"然而，秦代文化政策的极端，特别是焚书坑儒等反文化行为，造成了严重的后果，不仅激起了民怒，甚至导致了文化传承的断裂和文化多元的消亡。

西汉在文化政策的制定和实施上，吸取了秦代的教训，也避免了秦代的极端。西汉初期，由于社会经济凋敝，"民失作业，而大饥馑，凡米石五千，人相食，死者过半……自天子不能具醇驷，而将相或乘牛车"，所以推行黄老思想，以文法导民，重农桑，与民休息。汉初"与父老约法三章耳：杀人者死，伤人及盗抵罪。余悉除去秦法"。秦法严苛，较为忽视人伦，汉初咎其弊端，重视纲常伦理的建设。汉高祖颁布有尊父的诏令，诏云："人之至亲，莫亲于父子，故父有天下传归于子，子有天下尊归于父，此人道之极也。"

汉初虽以黄老思想为治国思想，但重视恢复儒学，突出表现在三个方面。一是搜集和整理儒家典籍，《汉书·儒林传》云："孝文时，求能治《尚书》者，天下亡有，闻伏生治之，欲召。时伏生年九十余，老不能行，于是诏太常，使掌故朝错往受之。"二是重用儒生，设立官学和博士制度。《汉书·儒林传》载："汉兴，鲁高堂生传《士礼》十七篇，而鲁徐生善为颂。孝文时，徐生以颂为礼官大夫。"三是统治政策部分采纳和吸收儒家思想。汉文帝时，以贾谊、叔孙通为代表的一批儒生受到了重用。《资治通鉴》载："吴公荐洛阳人贾谊，帝召以为博士。……一岁中，超迁至太中大夫。贾生请改正朔，易服色，定官名，兴礼乐，以立汉制。"儒家致力于推行礼制思想，提倡"君尊臣卑"，在强化皇权、维系国家稳定方面具有积极意义。

汉武帝时，更是"罢黜百家，独尊儒术"。汉武帝建元元年（公元前140年），诏云：举"贤良方正直言极谏之士"。丞相卫绾奏："今所举贤良，或治申、商、韩非、苏秦、张仪之言，乱国政，请皆罢。"后来汉武帝又于元光元年（公元前134年）复诏举贤良，于是西汉儒家代表人物董仲舒应诏上"天人三策"，他认为"今师异道，人异论，百家殊方，指意不同，是以上亡以持一统；法制数变，下不知所守"，建议"诸不在六艺之科孔子之术者，皆绝其道，勿使并进。邪辟之说灭息，然后统纪可一而法度可明，民知所从矣"。汉武帝采纳了他们的建议，重视儒家思想，表彰六经，设五经博士（即《诗》《书》《礼》《易》《春秋》），鼓励私学发展，试图以儒家思想为治国理政思想来统驭万民。事实上，汉武帝时所谓"罢黜百家，独尊儒术"也并未出现禁绝百家、学术停顿的局面，而是在"悉延百端之学"的前提下推崇儒学。《史记》中载："至今上（即汉武帝）即位，博开艺能之路，悉延百端之学，通一伎之士咸得自效，绝伦超奇者为右，无所阿私，数年之间，太卜大集。"汉武帝之后，西汉历朝皆尊儒学，以儒家思想为主要治国思想。

东汉在文化政策上延用西汉大一统的风格，推崇儒家思想，基本沿用汉武帝以来的方针与政策。东汉历朝皇帝大多重视儒学，不仅在很大程度上促进了官僚阶层的儒学化，而且逐步使儒学实现了自上而下的民间传播。汉明帝刘庄于永平二年（59年）诏令云："郡、县、道行乡饮酒于学校。皆祀圣师周公、孔子，牲以犬。"这一做法首创了中央和地方官学祭孔子之制，此后，历朝历代直至清代皆祀圣师孔子，祭孔成了一项全国性的重要活动。正是统治者的大力推崇，使东汉社会形成了尊师重道和崇儒好学的社会风气。儒学作为东汉治国的统一思想，在意识形态和价值观念方面逐渐全面侵染整个民间社会，在社会教化和移风易俗方面起到积极作用。同时，通过设立官学，鼓励私学，儒家学说进一步传播，奠定了儒学的价值观念发展为普遍社会价值观的地位。

从秦到汉，文化政策发生了从"崇法"到"崇儒"的改变，其间还经历了西汉初年黄老思想的过渡，体现出了鲜明的阶段性特点。不同阶段的文化政策，对包括乡村社会在内的全社会产生了不同程度的影响，对社会的稳定和国家政权的巩固具有一定的积极作用。特别是汉代统治者改"黄老"为"崇儒"之后，以儒家思想为主导的文化政策，不仅全面渗透到社会的各个阶层，逐渐统一了全社会的思想，而且实现了汉代国家意识形态的合理性建构。可以认为，儒家思想中的所谓"君君、臣臣、父父、子子、夫夫、妇妇"，以及"仁义礼智信"的道德观念和道德规范，于西汉以后便开始在全社会形成内化于心、外化于行的基本传统。由此观之，如果儒家思想作为国家文化大一统治理的形而上的形态，那么，很显然，村落及村落社会就是形而下的忠实的践行者。进一步来看，中华民族"忠孝为本，耕读传家"的文化内核，至迟在汉代以后的村落社会中便生根发芽。正是儒家思想在汉代完成了由上而下的传播，奠定了中国传统乡土社会的文化基调，影响了中华民族特别是汉民族的文化性格和文化精神的定型，有力促进了社会和民族的深度融合。

Section 1: Villages Under the Qin-Han Ruling System

After the establishment of the unified state, to consolidate rule and maintain national stability, formulating and implementing a series of ruling policies in line with their own interests became a necessity of state governance. The main contents of these ruling policies mostly relate to issues such as population, land, taxation, and culture. Villages, as the main carriers of these contents, were therefore affected to varying degrees, even changing the trajectory of their development. Generally speaking, under the pre-Qin state system, most people concentrated in closed city walls or li-yi (ward-settlements). By the Qin-Han period, due to social stability, especially the implementation of the commandery-county system leading to relative social relaxation, the original scattered and small-scale scattered residence phenomena outside the state system since the pre-Qin period gradually increased. Documents and archaeology show that the situation of different forms and types of rural settlements scattered to varying degrees across the country began to undergo important changes, initially forming a pattern of coexistence of urban residence and scattered residence, with the distinction between cities and villages becoming increasingly obvious. These changes are certainly related to the internal logic of human social development, but to a large extent are also the result of the implementation of state policies.

I. Xiang-Li System and Villages

The so-called xiang-li system refers to the system of various grassroots administrative divisions below the county level in ancient China, and is the key system for ancient China to control and govern rural society. Historically, although the xiang-li system rose and fell differently according to dynasties, as a successful governance system, it was still inherited by subsequent dynasties under different names or forms, playing an important role in the national governance system.

There is no exact conclusion in academia about when the xiang-li system originated, but from documentary records, the xiang-li system germinated relatively early. "Wenxian Tongkao" (Comprehensive Examination of Literature) has detailed records: "In the past, the Yellow Emperor first demarcated land and established wells to stop disputes. Set paces and established temples to prevent insufficiency. Make eight families form a well, with the well opening four paths and dividing eight residences. Dig a well in the center, first, not leaking earth qi, second, not costing one family, third, unifying customs, fourth, equalizing skill and clumsiness, fifth, circulating goods, sixth, mutually guarding in life and death, seventh, mutually supervising in coming and going, eighth, mutually matchmaking in marriage, ninth, mutually lending in need, tenth, mutually rescuing in illness. Therefore, emotions can be close, production can be equal. Equality blocks the path of bullying, closeness eliminates the heart of litigation. Since herding in yi, one well becomes lin, three lin become peng, three peng become li, five li become yi, ten yi become du, ten du become shi, seven shi become zhou. Beginning with division in well makes land fixed, counting by zhou makes numbers detailed, and through Xia and Yin this system did not change." According to this statement, the xiang-li system was already produced in the Yellow Emperor period. However, since the book "Wenxian Tongkao" was written by Song dynasty people, the authenticity of its documentary records is not high. It is generally believed that the xiang-li system widely appeared in the Shang and Zhou periods, with words such as "xiang" and "li" commonly seen in transmitted documents and bronze inscriptions. "Yi Zhou Shu - Shang Oath" records: "The King says: Tell you, Yi old He father... and all officials, li residents, and presented people... I also come to gracefully command you, common people, li residents, and gentlemen." "Shang Shu - Wine Proclamation" records: "Among the common people and li residents, none dare to indulge in wine." The "li residents" recorded in these two documents are residential units, not indicating distance and length. "Rites of Zhou" also records the "xiang-sui system," as well as officials such as xiang lao, xiang shi, xiang dafu, and xiang shi. In the term "xiang-sui": "xiang" is the place where guo people (city residents) live, referring to the city walls and surrounding suburban areas; "sui" is the place where ye people (countryside people) live, referring to remote rural areas. In the "guo" (capital), six xiang are established, "order five families to form bi, five bi to form lü, four lü to form zu, five zu to form dang, five dang to form zhou, five zhou to form xiang." In the "ye" (countryside), six sui are established, "five families form lin, five lin form li, four li form cuan, five cuan form bi, five bi form xian, five xian form sui."

Although what is described in "Rites of Zhou" is a later retrospection, more reflecting an ideal and possibly not completely consistent with reality, compared with expressions about "xiang" and "li" in bronze inscriptions, it can be affirmed that "xiang" and "li" as a form of regional organization or residential space objectively existed in the Western Zhou period. The mid-Western Zhou Nine-Year Wei Ding inscription records: "In the ninth year, first month, after the dead brightness, gengchen day, the King was at Zhou Ju Palace, entered the temple, Mei Ao Zhe Fu Zhuo's affairs were seen by the King, the King greatly... Yu gave Qiu Wei Lin Li... Ju then ordered Lian Ling to order Shou Shang and Yi, saying: 'Jie, walk and pay Qiu Wei Lin Li, then form four seals, Yan Xiaozi all only seal, Shou Shang'... Wei made this precious ding for my cultured father, Wei may eternally treasure and use it for ten thousand years." (Collection 2831) The general meaning of the inscription is that "Lin Li" as a fief of the noble "Ju," with woods in between, was later sold to Qiu Wei, bounded on all four sides by earthen ridges. This should belong to the "li" of rural areas. Different from this, the mid-Western Zhou Gui inscription records: "The King said: ', order you to manage Cheng Zhou li people, all vassals, great ya, interrogate litigation and punishment...' bowed and kowtowed, responding and praising the King's gracious command..." (Collection 4215) The "Cheng Zhou" mentioned here is the Western Zhou capital Luoyi, and "li people" are the managers of li. The "li" here is obviously a residential space or organization within the urban area. It can be seen that li was not limited to "ye" but also existed in "guo." The "Yi Zhou Shu - Zuo Luo Jie," recognized as a Western Zhou period document, also says "captured Yin presented people, moved to Jiu Li," with Kong Chao annotating "Jiu Li, place of Cheng Zhou." The "Jiu Li" here should not refer to a place name, but indicate many grassroots residential organizations of "li." "Shiji - Yan Shaogong Shijia" says "Shaogao toured xiang-yi, under a tang tree, decided litigation and government affairs below it," referring to Shaogao handling government affairs in xiang-yi. The above documents show that "xiang-li" is not only a residential space, but also the rural regional form and grassroots organization under state control in the Western Zhou period.

As a system, the finalization of the xiang-li system may have been in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. Since the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods formally still belonged to the Eastern Zhou, many systems of various vassal states still inherited content from the Western Zhou, especially the guo-ye system. Among them, the guo-bi system of Qi was the most typical. "Guanzi - Xiao Kuang" says: "Guanzi replied: 'In the past, sage kings governed their people, three parts their guo and five parts their bi, fixed people's residences, accomplished people's affairs, as people's discipline...' Duke Huan said: 'How about three-part guo?' Guanzi replied: 'Regulate guo into twenty-one xiang, six xiang of merchants and artisans, fifteen xiang of scholars and farmers. The Duke leads eleven xiang, Gaozi leads five xiang, Guozi leads five xiang, three-part guo therefore becomes three armies... Regulate five families as gui, gui has chief. Ten gui as li, li has officer. Four li as lian, lian has chief. Ten lian as xiang, xiang has good person. Three xiang one commander.' Duke Huan said: 'How about five-part bi?' Guanzi replied: 'Regulate five families as gui, gui has chief. Six gui as yi, yi has officer. Ten yi as shuai, shuai has chief. Ten shuai as xiang, xiang has good person. Three xiang as shu, shu has commander. Five shu one grand master, military affairs listen to shu, civil affairs listen to xiang, each protects and listens, without those who indulge.'" What is recorded in "Guanzi" certainly cannot be completely regarded as historical facts of various states in the Spring and Autumn period, but at least reflects the situation of Qi at that time. From the content of the guo-bi system, "guo" and "bi" are separately set up, similar in form to the "guo"-"ye" separate governance recorded in "Rites of Zhou," but different in content, being an improvement of the Zhou dynasty guo-ye system. "Guanzi - Li Zheng" says: "Divide guo into five xiang, xiang has its teacher; divide xiang into five zhou, zhou has its chief; divide zhou into ten li, li has its wei; divide li into ten you, you has its zong; ten families as shi, five families as wu, shi and wu all have chiefs." This document shows that Qi in the Spring and Autumn period not only further improved the xiang-li system based on the Western Zhou xiang-sui system, but also established and popularized the xiang-li shi-wu system. The purpose of this practice was, of course, to further control the population, consolidate state rule, make state rule and control more rigorous, achieving the governance model of "those who flee have nowhere to hide, those who migrate have nowhere to be accommodated," "people mutually guarantee, families mutually love, young live together, old travel together, sacrifices mutually bless, deaths and funerals mutually pity, fortunes and misfortunes mutually worry, residences mutually enjoy." It was precisely this practice that made Qi in the Spring and Autumn period present the social appearance of "people are none other than their li, li is none other than their families," and also made the relationship between individuals, families, and xiang-li organizations and even the state increasingly close, effectively solving the problem of lax grassroots social structure after the disintegration of family communes and rural communes.

Relevant records in "Zuo Zhuan" to some extent reflect that such systems, after implementation in the Spring and Autumn period, deeply influenced people's life concepts. For example, "Zuo Zhuan - Duke Zhuang, Year 10" says: "In the tenth year spring, Qi army attacked us. The Duke was about to fight. Cao Gui requested an audience. His xiang people said." "Xiang people" generally refers to fellow townspeople, and "xiang" has a regional concept. Also "Zuo Zhuan - Duke Xiang, Year 15" records: "A petty man carrying a jade disk cannot cross xiang." Du annotation: "Saying will surely be harmed by bandits." The "xiang" here is obviously a regional concept. "Zhanguo Ce - Qin Ce I" says: "Therefore selling servants and concubines without leaving li-xiang and being taken are good servants and concubines; marrying out a woman within xiang-li is a good woman." Roughly meaning that public opinion evaluation in xiang-li has a great influence on women's marriage. Such examples all indicate that with the widespread implementation of the xiang-li system, local society gradually formed the concepts of "xiang-li" and "xiang-tu" (native land), which is conscious regional identity. But also because the system strived to achieve the situation of "people are none other than their li, li is none other than their families," the free development of villages as natural settlements may have instead been restricted to a certain extent at that time.

After Qin unified the whole country, to consolidate state power, it was necessary to strengthen control over local society, especially the vast areas originally belonging to vassal states before unification. Based on this logical starting point, the Qin dynasty learned the lessons of the Western Zhou, abolished the enfeoffment system, replaced it with the commandery-county system, dividing the whole country into thirty-six commanderies, with counties under commanderies, completely breaking the hereditary official system since the Western Zhou. Documentary records show that the Qin dynasty not only established counties under commanderies, but also adjusted the xiang-li system below counties. "Han Shu" records: "County magistrates and chiefs are all Qin officials, in charge of governing their counties... Generally ten li one ting, ting has chief. Ten ting one xiang, xiang has san lao, you zhi, se fu, you jiao. San lao are in charge of education. Se fu's duty is to hear litigation and collect taxes. You jiao patrols and forbids bandits and thieves. Counties generally are one hundred li square, if people are dense then reduce, if sparse then leave vacant, xiang and ting are also like this, all are Qin systems." According to this expression, the Qin dynasty xiang-li system was a three-level system of xiang, ting, and li. The Han inherited the Qin system, no different, much simplified compared to the multi-level system of "gui, wu, li, lian, xiang" in "Guanzi," more conducive to central control over local society. It was precisely because the Qin dynasty state strove to improve and unify local grassroots political power that localities generally established the commandery-county-xiang-li system, better eliminating local separatist forces at the institutional level. However, different from the traditional view of "xiang, ting, li," some scholars have questioned the expression in "Han Shu" based on documentary materials, believing that "ting" in the Qin-Han period was not the name of a local administrative organization, and even believing that the "li" in "ten li one ting" did not mean the "li" of xiang-li organization, but indicated distance. Later scholars such as Gao Min and Zhu Shaohou also combined bamboo slips and other materials to demonstrate and interpret from different levels. Currently, there is basically a consensus on the nature of ting, that is, ting is not a level of administrative organization, but a public security organization outside the xiang-li organization, and xiang-li is the grassroots administrative unit.

From documentary records, the establishment and universal setting of the xiang-li system aimed to achieve control and governance of grassroots people across the country. "Han Shu" saying "san lao are in charge of education. Se fu's duty is to hear litigation and collect taxes. You jiao patrols and forbids bandits and thieves" reveals this completely. The same book records: "All counties, dao, states, yi: 1,587; xiang: 6,622; ting: 29,635." Also "Xu Han Shu - Jun Guo V": "As for Emperor Shun, all commanderies and states: 105; counties, dao, yi, marquis states: 1,180." Annotation quoting "Dongguan Shu" says: "(Emperor Huan) Yongxing first year, xiang: 3,682." According to "Xu Han Shu - Bai Guan V" annotation quoting "Fengsu Tong": "National system, generally ten li one xiang." Based on the above documentary expressions, Mr. Huang Jinyan used "ten li one xiang" as the standard for calculation, believing that if Western Han had 6,622 xiang, there would be 66,220 li; if Eastern Han had 3,682 xiang, there would be 36,820 li. According to "Yinwan Han Tomb Bamboo Slips" recording Donghai Commandery "counties 170, mouths 106, li 2,534," "households 266,290," if calculated accordingly, average one li is about 105 households. This household number is equivalent to the household number of Long Li noted on the "Garrison Map" unearthed from Han Tomb No. 3 at Mawangdui in Changsha. Long Li is the li with the most households in the "Garrison Map," with 108 households, followed by Yuan Li with 81 households, Zhi Li with 68 households, fewer such as Bo Li with 17 households, Zi Li with 12 households, others mostly around 40 households. There are 41 li verifiable in the "Garrison Map," average households per li between 40-50. According to bamboo slips from Han Tomb No. 10 at Fenghuang Mountain in Jiangling, Hubei, the Zheng Li granary register records a total of 25 households, that is, households borrowing grain from the government. If adding people who did not borrow grain, the household number may not be much more. From this, roughly three understandings can be drawn: first, xiang in the Qin-Han period was the superior organization of li, xiang governed li; second, li as a unit of household registration statistics was also a residential space organization; third, li varied in size, with uneven household numbers. The three characteristics shown by documents and related bamboo slip materials mean that "li" is not only a household registration statistical unit, but also reflects a naturally formed settlement. For this reason, Mr. Huang Jinyan believed that Han dynasty rural society was "one village one settlement, often just one 'li,' large 'settlements' sometimes coinciding with li." Scholars such as Ma Xin and Qi Tao even believed that Han dynasty rural society was li-settlement unity, the consistency of administrative units and natural settlements. But many scholars represented by Hou Xudong put forward different views, believing that most Han dynasty "li" should be administrative establishments, not the unity of administrative villages and natural villages. Whichever of the above three views, in fact reflects that the three existing situations should coexist in Han society. This social appearance fully indicates that the ideal and reality of concentrated urban residence since the pre-Qin period had basically completely collapsed.

sections.name: 国家管控下的乡野聚落
sections.content_zh:
第二节 国家管控下的乡野聚落

秦汉时期，国家大一统，既带来了社会的稳定，也使政治、经济、文化和科技等得以迅速发展，特别是从汉代开始，由于牛耕和铁器的普遍推广，生产力水平大幅提高，农业生产效率得到大幅提升。随着人口的不断增加和农业的兴盛，春秋战国以来形成的山林耕地，在国家授田制之下，被民间占有的量与国家的顷田份地相比已严重不足，不仅难以满足农业生产的需求，而且严重制约了国家整体的经济发展，尤其是使国家经济收入严重不足。因此，汉代推行限田令，并于汉文帝时废除了授田制，国家积极调控土地私有化。也因这一社会背景，民间百姓采伐树林、开辟耕地就有了正当合理的理由。在此基础上，特别是由于耕地私有权扩大、土地兼并、人口流动和豪族势力膨胀等原因，先秦以来形成的乡里制和集中城居的制度，已不能包容和掌握新的乡村内容，脱离国家体制之外的散居现象在秦汉时期进一步凸显，并且在城郭以外的广袤地域形成了不同类型、不同形式的乡野聚落。新型聚落的不断出现，不仅影响国家的徭役赋税，而且明显呈现出人口管控的失控趋势，并将危及国家的安全与稳定。所以，在散居趋势不可改变和乡野聚落普遍存在的现实情境下，国家对乡野聚落的管控就变得势在必行。

一、乡野聚落的类型

考诸文献，发现先秦两汉时期的散居形式名称各异，并且在形成的原因和聚落的性质、形态等方面，皆有一定差异。聚、落、庐、丘等作为村落的早期形态，为我们了解秦汉村落的内容、性质及国家与地方社会的关系提供了一种途径。

（一）聚

"聚"是乡野聚落的早期形态之一。聚之本意为聚拢、聚集，但在中国历史早期，更多的时候可能用于表示聚落。《说文解字》云："聚，会也。从禾，取声。邑落云聚。"清代段玉裁注曰："按邑落，谓邑中村落。"在这里，"聚"即村落。"村落"一词虽是明清时代乡野聚落的泛指词汇，但文献最早可见于《三国志·郑浑传》，其云："入魏郡界，村落齐整如一，民得财足用饶。"三国魏晋时期的"村落"表述，已开始用于指代乡野聚落。《颜氏家训·勉学》记载的一件逸事，可以说明聚与村或是聚与村落之间的渊源关系。其云："吾尝从齐主幸并州，自井陉关入上艾县，东数十里有猎闾村。……及检《字林》《韵集》，乃知猎闾是旧𨜰余聚。"可见，"聚"这一聚落的称谓，可能在魏晋或更早的时期，便开始出现被"村"取代的趋势。到唐代，"聚"也被理解为村落。《史记》载："一年而所居成聚，二年成邑，三年成都。"唐代张守节正义云："聚，在喻反，谓村落也。"

"聚"作为乡野聚落的一种指称，在先秦便出现。《管子·乘马》中载："方六里命之曰暴，五暴命之曰部，五部命之曰聚。聚者有市，无市则民乏。"这里的"聚"似乎不仅是有"五部"规模的"村"，而且是有"市"之"村"。结合南朝佛经《善见律》中"聚落界者，有市，故名聚落界；村界者，无市，名为村"的表述，也大致可以认为《管子》中所云的"聚"指代规模较大的聚落。《管子·侈靡》中也见有"千聚"一词，其载："百盖无筑，千聚无社，谓之陋，一举而取。天下有事之时也。""百盖""千聚"，都意指当时聚落的户数和规模，即户口超百户或千户的聚落。如果缺乏土墙或围墙，又或没有"社"，那么这种聚落是十分简陋的。《史记·苏秦列传》中有"百人之聚"的说法，即聚为百人之多，其云："舜无咫尺之地，以有天下；禹无百人之聚，以王诸侯。"可见，"聚"在先秦常被用来意指聚落及其规模和性质。

相比先秦，秦汉时期"聚"的内涵似乎发生了一定的变化，多用来专称乡野聚落，而非聚落的性质和内容，常见句式为"××聚"。譬如，河南郡的"缑氏刘聚，周大夫刘子邑"，"雒阳有上程聚"，钜鹿郡下曲阳的"鼓聚"，等等，比比皆是。日本学者曾对《汉书》《后汉书》中有关"聚"字的地名进行统计，发现《汉书·地理志》中有"聚"7处，《后汉书·郡国志》中则有55处，同名沿袭者仅3处，相比之下，后者达前者8倍之多。事实上，在两汉以"聚"名之的聚落，除《汉书·地理志》和《后汉书·郡国志》中的记载以外，在《史记》《水经注》等史籍，以及《汉书》《后汉书》的其他部分之中亦不乏记载，除去重复，专称的聚名有近百处之多。《论衡·书虚》云："天下郡国且百余，县邑出万，乡亭聚里，皆有号名"。从上述文献中所见的聚名来看，其大概有几种情况：一是以姓来命名，如刘聚、唐聚、褚氏聚、杨氏聚等。从以姓为"聚"名的情况来看，"聚"带有明显的族群的血缘性质；二是以江湖山水来命名，如圣聚、霍阳聚、彭泽聚等；三是以特色物产来命名，如桃丘聚、桃聚、杏聚等；四是以故邑、故国来命名，如上程聚、鼓聚、阳人聚、惮狐聚、鄹聚等；五是以历史人物及重大事件来命名，如秦聚、垓下聚、细柳聚、小修武聚、澶渊聚、黄淳聚、射犬聚、菟裘聚、夕阳聚、彭亡聚等。其中，有些"聚"的规模比较大，《汉书·史丹传》载，成帝鸿嘉元年（公元前20年）诏令云："夫褒有德，赏元功，古今通义也。左将军丹往时导朕以忠正，秉义醇一，旧德茂焉。其封丹为武阳侯，国东海郯之武强聚，户千一百。"这显然是一个超大型的聚。《汉书·王莽传》中载：哀帝建平二年（公元前5年），"太皇太后诏莽就第，朕甚闵焉。其以黄邮聚户三百五十益封莽"。再结合《史记》中所云"一年而所居成聚，二年成邑，三年成都"的表述，似乎可以认为"聚"属于形成较早、规模较大一类的自然聚落，并可以得知，邑和都是以聚为基础建设而成的。

考诸文献，还发现先秦两汉的文献往往将聚与邑连用。"邑"的本义是"国"，《说文解字》曰："邑，国也。"邑也指城郭或国都。《尔雅》曰："邑外谓之郊。"郭璞注云："邑，国都也。"先秦文献中亦有"十室之邑""百室之邑"的说法，这里的"邑"即为普通一类的聚落。聚与邑连用的表述，如《史记·商君传》云："筑冀阙宫庭于咸阳，秦自雍徙都之。……而集小（都）乡邑聚为县，置令、丞，凡三十一县。"从这里可看出，"邑聚"即为县以下的聚落形态。《史记·西南夷列传》云："西南夷君长以什数，夜郎最大；……自滇以北君长以什数，邛都最大。此皆魋结，耕田，有邑聚。"《后汉书·王丹列传》曰："邑聚相率，以致殷富。"这几条史料表明，虽然先秦时期的商鞅变法在行政区划上把邑聚一类的普通聚落并入了县，但作为聚落的一种称谓，邑聚在汉代一些边远郡县仍有保留。

（二）落

与"聚"一样，"落"也是乡野聚落的早期形态之一。《管子·轻重》记载了桓公与管子的对话："桓公问于管子曰：'崇弟、蒋弟，丁、惠之功世，吾岁罔，寡人不得籍斗升焉，去。菹菜、咸卤、斥泽、山间㙘不为用之壤，寡人不得籍斗升焉，去一。列稼缘封十五里之原，强耕而自以为落，其民寡人不得籍斗升焉。则是寡人之国，五分而不能操其二，是有万乘之号而无千乘之用也。'"大致意思是，齐国境内的崇、蒋、丁、惠等诸侯领地以及菹菜、咸卤、斥泽、山间㙘等偏僻之地，还包括那些"强耕而自以为落"的地方，不仅没有成为齐国的征税对象，反而占据了齐国五分之二的国土。可见，这里的"落"指的是国家征税对象之外的乡野聚落。这类居民一部分属于诸侯领地的居民，前引"崇弟、蒋弟，丁、惠"即是；另一部分是那些户口逃逸之民，这部分人口是受到严格控制的。云梦秦简《魏户律》记战国晚期魏国的律令云："廿五年闰再十二月丙午朔辛亥，告相邦：民或弃邑居壄（野），入人孤寡，徼人妇女，非邦之故也。"这段话中的"民或弃邑居壄（野）"似乎说明了户口逃逸的事实。人口不断逃离并开辟新的耕地，既冲击了关系国家赋税的井田制，又影响了国家经济收入与政权的稳定，所以被认为是"非邦之故"。

秦汉文献中也常见以"落"来表示乡野聚落。汉代刘向《列女传》亦云："一年成落，三年成聚。"《广雅》曰："落，谓村居也。"《汉书·赵充国传》中见有"聚落"一词，云："兵至罕地，令军毋燔聚落刍牧田中。罕羌闻之，喜曰：'汉果不击我矣！'"这里的"聚落"指的就是罕羌的聚居之地。《汉书·沟洫志》中所载"聚落"，也是指聚居空间，其云："赵、魏亦为堤去河二十五里。虽非其正，水尚有所游荡。时至而去，则填淤肥美，民耕田之。或久无害，稍筑室宅，遂成聚落。大水时至漂没，则更起堤防以自救，稍去其城郭，排水泽而居之，湛溺自其宜也。"所谓"民耕田之……稍筑室宅，遂成聚落"，结合前引《管子》中的"强耕自以为落"的表述，可以认为，这里的"聚落"应该是为便于农耕生产而生成起来的。不仅如此，此条文献史料还隐约表达出一条信息，即这类"聚落"发展的另一结果便是城郭，理由是"大水时至漂没，则更起堤防以自救"。对于"落"这类乡野聚落，国家当然要进行管控。《史记》云："吏苛察，盗贼恶少年投缿购告言奸，置伯格长以牧司奸盗贼。"裴骃集解引徐广曰："'格'，一作'落'。古'村落'字亦作'格'。街陌屯落皆设督长也。"司马贞索隐："伯音阡陌，格音村落，言阡陌村落皆置长也。"《汉书·酷吏传·王温舒》作"伯落长"。

除了"聚落"的表述外，还有"部落""庐落""里落"等，它们大多包含聚落的意义，体现出一定的群居性特征。如《后汉书·南蛮传》云："其山有六夷七羌九氐，各有部落。"此处的"部落"应指少数民族的聚落。"庐落"可能是那些散居性比较强的乡野聚落的别称，并且有聚落中具体的构筑空间。因为"庐"一般被认为是为便于农事而建造起来的居住空间。《后汉书·应劭传》云："无君长之帅，庐落之居。"同书《仇览传》亦云："吾近日过舍，庐落整顿。"唐代李贤注曰："《广雅》曰：'落，居也。'案今人谓院为落也。""里落"则可能指属于偏远乡村的聚落空间，如《后汉书·孙期传》中云："家贫，事母至孝，牧豕于大泽中，以奉养焉。远人从其学者，皆执经垄畔以追之，里落化其仁让。黄巾贼起，过期里陌，相约不犯孙先生舍。"事实上，"里落"是秦汉基层社会中的基本形态，又称"里聚"。《史记·吴太伯世家》注引《皇览》曰："太伯冢在吴县北梅里聚，去城十里。"《汉书·武五子传》曰：宣帝即位，"下诏曰：'故皇太子在湖，未有号谥、岁时祠。其议谥，置园邑。'……以湖阌乡邪里聚为戾园。"此处的"里"可能与行政编制单元的"里"有一定的关系，但并非指城郭的里，而是乡村地域的居住空间。《说文解字》中释"里"云："从田从土。"段玉裁注："有田有土而可居矣。"

（三）庐

"庐"作为城外聚落，其原义是指农民为了便于农事而在田野之中临时建造的居所。其概念大致在先秦时期就已出现。《诗经·小雅·信南山》云："中田有庐，疆场有瓜。"东汉郑玄笺："中田，田中也，农人作庐焉，以便其田事。"唐孔颖达疏："古者宅在都邑，田于外野。农时则出而就田，须有庐舍，故言中田，谓农人于田中作庐以便其田事。""庐"出现的原因可能与便于农事密切相关。因为先秦时期的农民大多集中城居，耕种则在城郭附近。然而，由于先秦农业的耕种技术尚不发达，加之耕种需要长期照看，所以，当农田的位置超过了城居的耕作半径时，为了便于农事，便派生出了这类临时性住所——庐。《汉书·食货志》云："是以圣王域民，筑城郭以居之，制庐井以均之。"由此可见，当时的老百姓有两个居处：一个是用于长期生活的空间，位于城郭；另一个是临时性的空间，在农田附近，是为了解决生产问题。《汉书·食货志》云："在野曰庐，在邑曰里。"唐代颜师古注："庐各在其田中，而里聚居也。"《春秋公羊传·宣公十五年》，东汉何休亦有注："在田曰庐，在邑曰里，一里八十户，八家共一巷。"对此，中国村落文化研究中心考察组在湖南郴州资兴市发现的代头村，就是最好的活证。其聚居空间一般由2~3栋单体式建筑组合而成，左右连栋，前后连衢（道），排列整齐有序，秩序井然。在联排民居中，东西向宽，可供车行；南北向窄，可供人行；中间或两侧设排水沟。居住区外围两侧靠近良田处，建有专门的家禽猪牛马用厩舍，十分便于耕种。代头村这一例证，十分鲜活地说明了因"庐"成"聚"成"衢"的村落生长现象。

正因为庐的出现是为了便于农事，所以农闲时节庐一般是闲置的。《说文解字》释"庐"云："庐，寄也。秋冬去，春夏居。"在田野考察中，我们在湖南湘中双峰县青树坪镇，湘西南的城步、绥宁、通道、靖州，湘南永州勾蓝瑶寨，以及贵州黔东南地区的西江、榕江等地区，曾发现过这类既具有"庐"之古名称，又具有古代"庐"的使用功能的建筑物。它们的名字就叫"田庐"，或"庐屋""牛庄屋"，修建于田垄之中，春夏人与牛临时寄住其间，秋冬则仅贮藏来年春耕的一些生产工具，并无人居住其间。它们是与村落建筑完全不同类型的建筑，在使用功能上与上古"庐"的功能作用完全一致。

后来伴随着井田制的废除，及至授田制等相对宽松政策的推行，集中城居的形式逐渐瓦解，"庐"便有了进一步生长为长期性生活空间的可能。由庐发展为村落有两个必备条件：一方面是物质性实体空间必须有明显的聚合性特征，包括空间构成的房屋、土地和景观等；另一方面是非物质性社会空间的形成，体现为明显的聚族群体性和血缘延续性。有关于此，考诸文献，发现先秦时期的庐不仅分布在距城郭不远的周边范围，而且密集布置，聚合性特征明显。《战国策·魏策》云"地名虽小，然而庐田庑舍，曾无所刍牧牛马之地"便可说明。《左传·襄公三十年》云："田有封洫，庐井有伍。"《汉书·食货志》云："理民之道，地著为本。故必建步立亩，正其经界。六尺为步，步百为亩，亩百为夫，夫三为屋，屋三为井，井方一里，是为九夫。八家共之，各受私田百亩，公田十亩，是为八百八十亩，余二十亩以为庐舍。"《汉书·王莽传中》亦云："古者，设庐井八家，一夫一妇田百亩，什一而税。"按八家庐舍二十亩地，平均每家二亩半。尽管这种划分与井田制有关，仍不免过于理想，却说明庐舍有一定的聚合性。除历史文献的记载以外，中国村落文化研究中心在湖南江永勾蓝瑶寨考察时发现的牛庄屋这一活证可为旁证（见插图6）。牛庄屋的形式、功能类似"庐"，它是旧时居于深山的瑶民为便于农业生产而于平地近田处建起的临时住所。一到开春，为了打理农田、种植庄稼，瑶民便长住其中，春耕之后才回山寨。后来随着瑶汉关系的缓和，部分瑶民便开始居于牛庄屋，久而久之，就干脆移居平地，形成了瑶民聚居的村落。牛庄屋的布局，有成排"一"字形的，也有"回"字形的四合大院，两层结构，八面倒水，一个大门。每座庄屋被分成三十格，每格一户人居住，上面住人，隔层下面则圈养牛和放置农具。牛庄屋这一活证，结合上述文献以及《史记》中"一年而所居成聚，二年成邑，三年成都"的说法，证明在古代中国社会，特别是在井田制废除之后，"庐"发展为村落是可靠、可信的史实。

（四）丘

除上述外，还有"丘"一类的乡野聚落，它不同于临时性居所的庐，而属于长期性居住空间，即所谓"野人"的聚落。丘的甲骨文字形为，像地面上左右并立的两座小山峰，其本义为自然形成的小土山。《说文解字》解释"丘"云："一曰四方高、中央下为丘。"《玉篇·丠部》则云："丠，虚也，聚也，冢也。……丘，并同丠。"由此来看，丘作为"聚"应该属于山间谷底一类的自然聚落，在今湖南南部的江华、江永，广西的桂林、百色、凭祥等地，依然可以见到这类自然村落，也由此知这类村落的形成与自然地理条件的关系。

《尚书·禹贡》谓"桑土既蚕，是降丘宅土"。据考古学者研究发现，早期中国的聚落遗址多与丘有关，其云："在一马平川的原野上，如果远远望见高于平地的漫坡或阜丘，十之八九为遗址，又以龙山文化——商代遗址为多，且这种'堌堆'的遗址又往往呈带状分布。"丘作为乡野聚落或地方组织的指称，可能在商周时期就已出现，甲骨文中"丘"字出现频率较高，如《合集》8381—8390条中"丘"就出现了10次，有"傅丘""丘"等。《史记》中还有所谓的"犬丘"，《史记》云："文王在丰，武王在镐。"周懿王时，始自镐，迁居于此。"《世本》：'懿王徙于犬丘。'"宋衷注云："（犬丘）一曰废丘，今槐里是也。"从这里来看，丘又体现为地域组织，具有一定的行政编制意义。

《庄子·杂篇》："少知问于大公调曰：'何谓丘里之言？'大公调曰：'丘里者，合十姓百名而以为风俗也，合异以为同，散同以为异。'"由此来看，丘里应该是由数个不同族姓的居民聚居而形成的居民点，可合可散，是基于地缘关系的聚合群体。《孟子·尽心下》云："民为贵，社稷次之，君为轻。是故得乎丘民而为天子。""丘里""丘民"似乎都表明"丘"虽是乡野聚落，但仍受到国家的管控。先秦文献中还有如鲁国"作丘甲"、郑国"作丘赋"的规定，可能是以丘作为征收军赋的基本单位。《春秋左传》云：成公元年，"三月，作丘甲"。杜预注："《周礼》：九夫为井，四井为邑，四邑为丘。丘十六井，出戎马一匹、牛三头。四丘为甸，甸六十四井，出长毂一乘、戎马四匹、牛十二头、甲士三人、步卒七十二人。此甸所赋，今鲁使丘出之，讥重敛。"长沙三国吴简中亦发现有"丘"的名称，说明"丘"一类的指称一直延续到了两汉时期，且可能依然指代野外的自然聚落，只是这类"丘"已被纳入了国家征管的范围而已。从相关表述来看，此类"丘"仍不属于行政编制的单位。尽管从古代文献里没有直接找到"丘"发展成村落的载述，但从发生学的概念来理解，作为乡野聚落或地缘性组织的"丘"演变为村落是可靠的，毕竟"丘"的群居性特征较为明显，而且我们在现在丘陵山谷盆地中仍然可以见到这类村落。

以上对秦汉时期几种具有典型性或代表性的乡野聚落形态进行了简要梳理和阐释，从中可以发现，无论是聚、落，还是庐、丘等形态，都发生于先秦时期，有些甚至在商代便已出现。当然，作为聚落空间的某一指代，这些名词和概念只是人为的主观界定，它们在不同时期、不同区域、不同阶层的人那里会有不同的理解和表述。概念的理解和表述可能是主观的、动态的，但作为物质实体空间与社会活动单元高度重叠的客观对象，它是相对稳定的。所以，各类聚落名词的指代，固然有助于我们理解村落起源的各类可能情况或村落的早期形态，然而切不可认为指代不同，其内涵便会有本质上的区别。毕竟村落是实际存在的生产生活空间，除自然灾害和战争等不可抗力以外，它是不会以人的意志为转移的。根据这一理解，有关村落的称谓和指代，包括后来出现的"庄""屯""川""寨""店""堡""铺"等，它们在形态和性质上虽有不同，但在本质内涵上是大致无异和无疑的。

二、国家对乡野聚落的管控

就村落存在的形态而言，秦汉社会的现实是先秦以来国家体制之外零星或少量的散居现象渐趋增多，全国各地都不同程度地散布着不同形式、不同类型的乡野聚落，初步形成了城居与散居并存的局面，城邑与乡村的分野也随之日趋明显。考古在全国各地发现的具有村落性质的遗址，便足可为证。如辽宁辽阳三道壕遗址、河南遂平小寨汉代遗址、江苏高邮邵家沟汉代遗址、江苏张家港小山村遗址、河南内黄三杨庄汉代聚落遗址、安徽泗县刘圩遗址等，以及重庆、四川等地区发现的汉代聚落遗址。上述这些遗址一般位于地理条件优越的平原、低丘之处，近水源，由房屋、水井、厕所、畜栏、土窖等组成，遗址中农业遗存丰富，除日常生活用具以外，还有铁犁、铁铲、铁锛、铁凿、铁刀、铁匕、铁锥等农业生产工具，应该属于秦汉时期已经形成并成熟的农村村落。

文献和考古材料显示，秦汉时期的村落大概有两种。第一种是城郭之中派生出来的、先秦便已存在的"庐""丘""聚""落"等。这类大多是散居形态，体现出一定的"聚居"村落要素，应该是村落形成来源的一种重要形态。也可能正是散居达到一定的规模程度，便成了带有村居一类的"聚落"。正如《汉书》所言，"民耕田之，或久无害，稍筑室宅，遂成聚落"。《史记》中也有"一年而所居成聚，二年成邑，三年成都"的说法，虽未言之凿凿，但已经足以说明"久居成聚"的可能。"聚"在这里是"村落"的意思。第二种是与城郭平行发展的一种普通聚落。除了先秦以来便出现的自然聚落，还存在流邑之民避居后所生成的自然聚落，故其在行政上受到国家的干涉或影响相对较少。考古发现，秦汉时期的部分农耕聚落就始于先秦时期，有些甚至可以上溯到新石器时代的龙山文化时期，而且在之后的历史进程中一直有相对稳定的延续。譬如，山东章丘宁家埠聚落遗址，不仅可以追溯到龙山文化时期，而且还延续至唐宋时期；河南遂平小寨遗址，从战国晚期一直使用到东汉时期。上述两种聚落在当时的平面规模上都不大，居民住户仅有数户，这可能与秦汉国家对散居的严格管控有一定关系。秦自商鞅变法，"集小都乡邑聚为县"，"令民为什伍"，即五家为伍，十户为什，相联相保。汉承秦制，实行乡亭里制，注重什伍编排，推行"编户齐民"，力图恢复和延伸集中城居的理想。《汉书·食货志》："是以圣王域民，筑城郭以居之，制庐井以均之。"《睡虎地秦墓竹简·释文·法律答问》载："旞火延燔里门，当赀一盾；其邑邦门，赀一甲。""越里中之与它里界者，垣为'完（院）'不为？巷相直为'院'；宇相直者不为'院'。""垣"即墙垣，即里与里之间有墙垣相隔；"院"便是家与家之间的隔墙。里有"里门"，里与里、户与户之间设有墙垣，百姓的生活被限制在固定的空间范围。汉初《二年律令》的规定更为详细，其云：百姓的"欲益买宅，不比其宅者，勿许"。《杂律》云："越邑里、官市院垣，若故坏决道出入，及盗启门户，皆赎黥。其垣坏高不盈五尺者，除。"《户律》还规定："田典更挟里门籥，以时开；伏闭门，止行及作田者"。如此种种，充分说明了汉代对民及民居的严格控制。至隋唐"令人悉城居"的政令，严格程度更甚。《隋书》记大业十一年（615年）诏令云："今天下平一，海内晏如，宜令人悉城居，田随近给。"《资治通鉴》也载："帝以户口逃亡，盗贼繁多，二月，庚午，诏民悉城居，田随近给。郡县驿亭村坞皆筑城。"律令的一再强调，体现了国家对土地和户口的重视，然则也在一定程度上反映了"非城居"现象的日益频繁。

不难发现，从汉代开始，由于牛耕和铁器的普遍推广，生产力水平大幅提高，散居村落的现象呈蔓延之势。事实上，到魏晋南北朝时期，散居村落已然成为官方不得不默许的一种实际存在。因为进入汉代以后，尤其是西汉后期，土地兼并、人口流动的现象突出，加之豪族势力的膨胀，先秦以来形成的"里"制和集中城居的制度已不适应日益增长的农业物质生产需求，更不能包容新的乡村内容。其中一个最突出的表现，就是单纯作为自然聚落的"聚"的不断涌现。在秦汉乡亭里制之下，这种乡野聚落出现的直接后果，自然是聚落逐渐从国家行政单位脱离，统治者对其的控制，或许只是名存实亡。因为"聚"一旦脱离国家的行政视野，就意味着成了国家征税对象之外的群体空间。从国家层面来论，汉代统治者的理想是将作为自然聚落的"聚"与行政单元"里"结合起来，实现"里聚合一"，然而先秦以来便出现的突破国家行政编制而向郭外发展的趋势，并没有因这一设想而在事实上停滞。西汉马王堆三号墓出土《驻军图》中所标记的里，一部分旁注"不反（返）"和"今毋（无）人"的情况，似乎反映了"户口逃亡"的问题。里聚分离是事实，但这种分离是艰难的，受到了来自国家权力等各方面的严重制约。一方面，为了加强控制，统治者加强监管，尽可能限制百姓于郭外聚居；另一方面，统治者不得不承认乡野聚落这种实际存在的生产生活单位，并试图将其纳入国家管理范畴。西汉马王堆三号墓出土的《地形图》（见插图7）、《驻军图》（见插图8）分别有名里43处和41处的事实可兹说明。因为地图中所标记的里，都分散在地形复杂的山川地区，应属乡野聚落的范畴，然而又有国家赋予的"××里"的名称，这显示出这些聚落明显受制于国家的行政管辖。

汉代国家与村落互动的现象背后，实际上是国家的某种妥协和村落群体向国家的靠拢。国家对村落的实际承认，促进了村落在汉代的发展，反过来，村落的发展也稳定和巩固了汉代国家的统治。不过，到东汉末年，这种状况出现了改变，因为战争不断，社会动荡加剧，全国性的乡亭里地方行政组织遭到严重破坏，里聚分离速度进一步加快。这不仅增强了"聚"的自然聚落功能，而且加强了以血缘关系为基础的豪族庄园的独立性和军事性。

总而言之，秦汉村落作为农耕文明的产物，它的发展与变迁是传统农耕社会历史演变的缩影，也是国家与乡村之间的某些历史性互动关系的体现。在早期中国历史上，秦汉国家政权合法地垄断了全国范围内的所有资源，但似乎社会网络仍然具有过滤国家试图控制社会的某些行为的能力。因而，国家对资源的垄断实际上也是有限的，它往往需要通过下发不同的行政命令或是制定符合实际的法律法规，不断调适其与村落社会之间的关系，使底层社会为争夺生存、生活资源而发生的行为与活动限制在国家的可控范围内。秦汉国家体制下村落社会的演变就充分显示了这一点。然而，这种国家权力向地方社会的渗透，可能并不如想象中的强烈，而是若隐若现的。正因如此，不少学者认为我国古代"皇权不下县"，如马克斯·韦伯提出了"有限官制论"，认为"中华帝国正式的皇权统辖权只施行于都市地区和次都市地区。……出了城墙之外，中央权威的有效性便大大地减弱乃至消失"。我国著名社会学家费孝通先生也持类似的观点，认为皇权统治"在人民实际生活上看，是松弛和微弱的，是挂名的，是无为的"。

事实上，从秦汉国家与村落社会的互动情况来看，国家权力不仅下渗到了县以下的地方社会，而且在形式上和一定程度上体现为制度性介入，只是这种渗透和介入并非以"设置国家机构"的方式实现，而更多的是通过国家在基层的代理人这一途径体现的。譬如，村落社会中的父老、耋老，唐代的里正、村正，明清时期所谓的乡绅。可以肯定，所谓"国权不下县，县下惟宗族，宗族皆自治，自治靠伦理，伦理造乡绅"的传统乡村认识范式，可能并不能完全解释包括秦汉时期在内的古代中国国家与村落社会的关系。国家视野下，历朝历代关于基层社会的行政编制和田赋徭役制度，虽然在很大程度上影响或者限制着村落，但作为国家最基础和最基本的生活单元与社会单元，村落仍以其聚族群体性、血缘延续性和地缘一体性的特质，不仅继续发展，而且在与国家的互动关系中起到了增强民族的内聚性与心理认同，维系和巩固国家的稳定、繁荣与发展的重要功能作用。
