Section 4: Agricultural Culture in Qin-Han Villages

Agriculture is the foundation for the gestation and development of Chinese civilization, and different stages of agricultural development gestate different forms of civilization. As a custom culture closely related to production and life, and even itself originating from the daily production and life activities of the people, the agricultural culture of the Qin-Han period is a relatively broad cultural type formed by people's accumulation in long-term agricultural production since the origin of prehistoric agriculture. It naturally includes all aspects of material and non-material culture including production and lifestyle, customs and habits, spiritual beliefs, and moral and value orientation concepts. The Qin-Han unification period was an important period for the development of traditional agriculture in China. In more than 400 years, traditional agriculture experienced rapid development. Among them, cultivated land area continued to expand, agricultural technology progressed significantly, and types of agricultural production increased significantly. It was precisely with the rapid development of agriculture that the Qin-Han period formed cultural content and characteristics with historical continuity and era features, prominently manifested in many aspects such as tools related to production and life, festival customs, and belief culture.

I. Production Tools and Living Utensils

In long-term agricultural production and life, Qin-Han society produced and formed a series of related production tools and living utensils. As material culture, they reflect the production and lifestyle of people in the Qin-Han period, and also reflect their customs, values, beliefs, and spiritual beliefs, serving as strong evidence for the formation process of the Qin-Han state and the Chinese nation.

(1) Production Tools

Production tools are tools or utensils used by people for labor in the production process, hence also called labor tools. The content and form of production tools are constantly developing and changing, closely related to the development of economic production methods and science and technology. At the stage of human origin, people lived by gathering, fishing, and hunting, and the tools manufactured and used were mainly stone tools and wood tools. Later, with the emergence and development of agriculture, in the early Neolithic Age, polished stone production tools with agricultural production characteristics such as shovels, sickles, and hoe-shaped tools appeared, as well as general-purpose production tools such as chisels, adzes, axes, and spinning wheels. In the late primitive society, especially after entering class society, bronze smelting technology was invented, and bronze production tools began to appear in agricultural production. In the middle and late Warring States period, iron smelting technology developed and became popular, and iron farm tools gradually replaced other production tools to become the main tools of agricultural production, enabling further improvement of agricultural production. In the Qin-Han period, agriculture had moved from "predatory" primitive agriculture to "circular" agriculture, that is, people no longer simply relied on the fertility of the land itself, but instead fully utilized organic waste discarded or produced by people to nourish the land, achieving agricultural production. This transformation necessarily required artificial land nourishment to be refined. To achieve this, in addition to increasing human input and scientifically planting crops, it was also necessary to improve or modify production tools according to new production requirements. Therefore, the emergence and development of production tools is both an inevitable result of human development and a manifestation of human social progress.

From the nature and content of production tools, production tools in the Qin-Han period can be roughly divided into agricultural tools, textile and weaving tools, and other general-purpose tools.

Agricultural tools are further divided into several categories according to different needs of agricultural production: plowing and raking tools, harvesting tools, irrigation tools, and grain processing tools. Plowing and raking tools mainly include lei (forked plow), cha (spade), chan (shovel), chu (hoe), jue (pick), pa (rake), and li hua (plowshare).

Lei, as an agricultural tool, originated in prehistoric society and belongs to a type of tool for turning soil, generally considered the early form or predecessor of the plow. In the Han dynasty, agricultural tools called "lei" were still seen. "Yantielun - Ci Quan" says: "Therefore farmers release lei and are not diligent, common people relax like ice melting and are slack." "Huainanzi - Zhushu Xun" says: "One person treads lei to plow, no more than ten mu." The "lei" here refers to agricultural tools. The form of lei is a round wooden handle at one end, with the improved version being a curved handle, and double teeth or double points at one end. In the Han dynasty stone reliefs of the Wu Family Shrines in Jiaxiang, Shandong, there is a "Shennong holding lei" image, and the form of lei seen in the image is similar to cha.

Cha, belonging to the category of hoes, its main function is to dig and turn soil. "Han Shu - Gouxu Zhi" says: "Raising cha forms clouds, opening channels forms rain." This indicates that cha was one of the main agricultural tools for reclaiming land and repairing channels in the Qin-Han period. Archaeological discoveries such as the concave-mouth cha found in Han Tomb No. 1 at Xucungang, Qi County, Henan, have blade parts pointed-round or triangular, with vertically long bodies. Similar cha have been found in Han tombs in Guangzhou and the Western Han Nanyue King's Tomb. More different is the cha unearthed from Tomb No. 183 at Shaogou in Luoyang, which is horizontal rectangular or inverted trapezoidal, with the blade edge and both sides straight, being a straight-mouth cha. The Gucheng Site at Xiaohuangdi, Jinxi, Liaoning also unearthed cha of similar form. Some scholars point out that to distinguish lei and cha in the Qin-Han period, the key lies in whether there is an iron sleeve blade, believing that "those without metal sleeve blades are called lei, those with metal sleeve blades are called cha." The iron sleeve blade was called mou in the Han dynasty. "Shuowen Jiezi" says: "Mou, Henei calls lei head metal." "Shiming - Shi Yongqi" says: "Its board is called ye (leaf), resembling a tree leaf." The wooden board installed with mou is called "ye." This image is most typical of the iron-bladed wooden cha discovered in Han Tomb No. 1 at Mawangdui, Changsha. From these, the forms of cha in the Qin-Han period were diversified, including not only double-toothed but also single-toothed or single-board forms, among which single-board cha was more common.

Chan, as an agricultural tool mainly used for lifting soil, originated in the Neolithic Age. Bronze chan first appeared in the Shang dynasty, and iron chan appeared in the middle and late Warring States period. Although chan appeared very early, relevant documentary records about it did not begin to appear until after the Han dynasty. "Shuowen Jiezi" says: "Chan, yao (spade). Also called flat iron. From metal, chan sound." Duan Yucai annotated: "Meaning using steel to plane flat soft iron. 'Guangyun' says: chan, wood-planing tool." From this, the appearance of the character "chan" may initially have been used to express the meaning of "planing flat." It was not until later that the character "chan" was used to express the agricultural tool for lifting soil. The reason there was no documentary record of "chan" before the Han dynasty may also be related to this. But this does not affect our recognition and understanding of chan in the Qin-Han or even pre-Qin periods. As an agricultural tool for lifting soil, to facilitate weeding and loosening soil, the chan body is generally thick at the top and thin at the bottom, overall gently sloped, with square, triangular, and trapezoidal shapes being the most common. Chan in the Qin-Han period was mainly iron chan, with varying forms and sizes. Typical archaeological discoveries include 8 iron chan unearthed at Dingjia, Changwu, Shaanxi, and 2 iron chan unearthed from the Nanyue King's Tomb in Guangzhou. Tomb No. 18 at Shanjiabao, Youyu County, Shanxi also discovered 1 iron-bladed copper chan of copper-iron alloy.

The function of chu (hoe) is mainly to loosen soil and weed. The physical object was first seen in the Western Zhou period, continued to be used in the Warring States and Qin-Han periods, and after continuous improvement has been passed down to the present. The form of chu is usually a wooden handle installed horizontally, with a relatively thin chu body and wide blade part. Han dynasty iron chu can be divided into several types such as hexagonal chu and crane-head chu according to different forms. The hexagonal chu has a hexagonal chu surface, with a wide and thin body, convenient for weeding. 2 hexagonal chu were unearthed at the Dongpingling Old City in Zhangqiu District, Jinan City, Shandong, with the top, shoulders, and both sides of the chu board all curved. The crane-mouth iron chu was an improved variety in the Qin-Han period, also called goose-neck iron chu or crane-head chu. Han dynasty Liu Xi's "Shiming" says: "Chu, means to assist, removing filth to assist seedlings... the head is called crane, resembling a crane head." Archaeologically it is called curved-handle chu, that is, the chu body is trapezoidal, with a curved handle connected to the top of the chu, similar to a bent goose neck, with a socket (qiong) set behind the curved handle for installing a wooden handle. 1 curved-handle chu was unearthed in Lintong, Shaanxi. Similar to chu in form and function is "jue" (pick), which appeared earlier than chu, possibly as early as the Shang dynasty or even earlier, with a longer and larger body, having single-bevel or double-bevel blades, and multi-tooth jue also existed in the Warring States period.

Jue is a tool for digging soil, which can be divided into vertical-socket jue and horizontal-socket jue according to the direction of the jue socket. Among them, the form of vertical-socket jue is the same as a hand axe, with a narrow rectangular body, varying socket mouth forms, and the socket size equal to or wider than the blade part. For example, the jue unearthed from Tomb No. 97 at Shaogou, Luoyang, has a regular shape and is overall narrow and long. Slightly different from this are several iron jue unearthed from the Han dynasty iron casting workshop site at Zhujiatai, Sangzhi, Hunan, whose jue bodies are slightly shovel-shaped, with flat and wide blade parts forming an outer arc. The horizontal-socket jue has a rectangular or trapezoidal body, with a square or oval horizontal socket near the top. 1 jue with a shovel-shaped plane was unearthed from Tomb No. 33 at Shaogou, Luoyang, being a vertical rectangular horizontal-socket mouth; different from the form of Luoyang shovel-shaped jue, 1 jue unearthed at Tieshenggou, Gong County, Henan, has a long strip or trapezoidal plane, with the blade part forming an outer arc.

Pa (rake) is mainly used for leveling and breaking soil, raking soil, raking grass, and organizing cultivated land, and is still one of the essential agricultural tools for farmers today. Pa generally consists of a wooden handle and a rake head, with the rake head having teeth, mostly two-tooth, three-tooth, and five-tooth rakes. A two-tooth rake is a rake head equipped with two teeth, also called pants-shaped rake, with the inner and outer sides of the two teeth curved, having a horizontal socket for installing the wooden handle, with the wooden handle at right angles to the rake. 1 two-tooth rake was unearthed from the Mancheng Han Tomb in Hebei, with a flat back, pants-shaped, total length 20.5 cm. A three-tooth rake is a rake head equipped with three teeth, similar in shape to the two-tooth rake but wider horizontally. 2 three-tooth rakes were found at the Dongpingling Old City in Zhangqiu District, Jinan City, Shandong, with rake tooth cross-sections trapezoidal. A five-tooth rake is a rake head equipped with five teeth, wide horizontally. A typical example is 1 five-tooth rake unearthed at Hancheng Village, Wuyishan, Fujian, with the whole vessel nearly rectangular and rake teeth long strip-shaped. This type of rake belongs to soil-preparation tools. There is also a tool "pa" (different character) of similar nature but different function. Western Han Shi You's "Jijiupian" says: "Jun, huo, bing, ba, cha, ba, pa." Tang dynasty Yan Shigu annotated: "Toothless is ba, toothed is pa. Both are used to gather and collect grain." "Shuowen Jiezi" says: "Pa, wheat-collecting tool." From this, pa may be an agricultural tool for raking grain on the threshing ground, or a tool for gathering and cutting wheat straw in wheat fields, mostly made of wood and bamboo. To this day, pa this tool is still a commonly used production tool for farmers.

Plow (li) is the most important agricultural tool in Han dynasty agricultural production activities, mainly used for turning soil, loosening soil, and opening ditches and lifting soil. To facilitate soil entry and soil lifting, the plow structure design is quite exquisite, with its handle curved and the head triangular, oval, or diamond-shaped. Iron plows are generally composed of structures such as plowshare (li hua), plow crown (li guan), and plow moldboard (li bi), with different structures performing different functions. The plowshare is a sheet-like structure installed on the plow during plowing to break soil,呈 "V" shape, triangular, or tongue-shaped, slightly spiral, with the effect of soil being turned out to one or both sides, turning the lower soil to the surface. According to specifications and functions in actual production, plowshares can be divided into large, medium, and small shares. The large share is a large plow tool, usually requiring several oxen to pull, suitable for opening ditches and making channels. The large shares currently seen archaeologically have lengths and widths both reaching over 40 cm. 1 large iron share unearthed from the Western Han village site at Sandaohao, Liaoyang, Liaoning belongs to this form, with a length of 40.2 cm, socket width of 40.6 cm, relatively flat back, bulging front, and tongue-shaped blade at the share head. Medium shares are mostly about 30 cm long, typical examples such as 1 tongue-shaped iron share unearthed from Han Tomb No. 2 at Mancheng, Hebei, and 1 triangular iron share found at Gaolou Village, Long County, Shaanxi. Small shares are under 20 cm long, with blade parts mostly isosceles triangular, such as the small share found at Bailuyuan Zhai, Lantian, Shaanxi, only 15.7 cm long and 10 cm wide at the blade. Plow crowns are mostly "V" shaped, iron blades used by being sleeved on triangular plowshares, their function being to protect the plowshare and facilitate timely replacement after the plowshare wears out. 1 plow crown was found at the Yang Mausoleum of Emperor Jing of Han, with an obvious ridge on the front, vessel wall "V" shaped, 14 cm high, 24.2 cm wingspan width, 2.3 cm thick. Plow moldboard, also called bi tu, plow mirror, or plow ear, is generally considered a new accessory that appeared in the Western Han, an attachment installed above and behind the large plowshare, inclined to one side, its function being to turn and arrange the plowed soil to one side. The plow moldboard unearthed at Zhaojia Village, Xianyang, Shaanxi, is overall tile-shaped curved, with a "tian" (field) character cast on the back, 46 cm long, 24 cm wide; the one unearthed at Wangxiang Village, Liquan, Shaanxi, is saddle-shaped, with a nose button in the middle of the back for easy fixing, 22 cm high, 23 cm wide.

Archaeological materials provide physical materials for us to understand the true image of plows in the Qin-Han period. However, to understand the usage of plowing, we can only rely on reverse inference from the plow form, lacking intuitiveness. The image materials of ox-plowing pictures in Han dynasty carvings exactly make up for this deficiency. Images show that the plowing method in the Qin-Han period was mainly ox-plowing, commonly the two-oxen carrying-yoke style, and also single-ox pulling and one-horse-one-ox parallel plowing forms. The two-oxen carrying-yoke style shows two oxen carrying a yoke in front, one person holding the plow behind, some with one person leading the oxen in front, or someone driving the oxen beside. For example, the stone reliefs from the tomb of the first year of Yongchu of Emperor An of Eastern Han (107 CE) at Xiguanzhuang, west of Mizhi County, Shaanxi; the murals from the Wang Mang period or early Eastern Han tomb at Zaoyuan, Pinglu, Shanxi; and the Eastern Han stone reliefs from Suide collected at the Xi'an Beilin Museum in Shaanxi all belong to this form. The stone reliefs from the stone-coffin tomb at Xiangchenggu, eastern suburb of Jinxiang County, Shandong, show two oxen carrying a yoke, one person holding the plow, one person leading the oxen in front, one person driving the oxen beside, and children playing nearby, with strong sceneness, relatively truly reflecting the production scene of the Eastern Han period. Generally speaking, the plow forms in the images are all straight-shaft plows, divided into double-shaft and single-shaft, with single-shaft plows more common. A single-shaft plow achieves plowing through two oxen side by side carrying a yoke, while a double-shaft plow may be an improvement on the single-shaft plow, only needing to hang two shafts on the neck of one ox to achieve traction. In terms of operability, the latter is undoubtedly more flexible, and some places still use it today.

Harvesting tools in the Qin-Han period mainly include zhi knives (sickle knives) and sickles.

Zhi knife, as an ear-cutting tool, has an overall half-moon or rectangular plane, usually with two holes for easy grasping. 13 half-moon-shaped zhi knives were unearthed at Shibei Village, Chenggong, Kunming, Yunnan, with convex ridges on the back, arc-shaped blade parts, 9-11 cm blade width. 2 rectangular zhi knives of the same form but different sizes were unearthed from the Western Han Nanyue King's Tomb in Guangzhou, with relatively thin knife bodies, two holes on the back, thicker hand-grip parts, arc-shaped cross-section resembling flat tiles, with the back embedded in a bamboo tube.

Sickle is the most common harvesting tool in the Han dynasty, with forms including crescent-shaped, straight-bodied, etc., with relatively thin blade parts, installed with wooden handles, which are either riveted or clamped. According to whether the blade part has teeth, it can be divided into toothed-blade sickles and pointed-blade sickles. The former are toothed sickles, either long strip-shaped or bow-shaped. Long strip-shaped serrated sickles were unearthed at the Anfengtang Dam site in Shou County, Anhui, with a perforation at the handle end for fixing to a wooden handle; the toothed-blade sickle found in Tomb No. 1117 at the Guangzhou Han Tomb is bow-shaped, with a socket at the base for installing a wooden handle. The blade edge of pointed-blade sickles is generally linear, with long strip and crescent shapes, having a socket for installing a wooden handle. 1 sickle was unearthed at Lulou, Hebi, Henan, with a crescent-shaped sickle body, pointed or arc-shaped sickle blade end, total length 17.5 cm, width 2.3-3.8 cm; 7 iron sickles were found at Longquanyi, Chengdu, of the same form, with inner arc-shaped blade parts and outer arc-shaped sickle body backs; copper-iron composite sickles were unearthed at Lijiashan, Jiangchuan, Yunnan, with the socket part cast in copper and the blade part cast in iron, long strip-shaped sickle body, semicircular sickle tip, total length 26.2 cm, blade length 18.5 cm. Qin-Han sickles generally have wooden handles installed, some even with relatively long wooden handles. For example, the Han dynasty pictorial brick "Weeding and Sowing" unearthed at Deyang, Sichuan, shows a large wooden-handled sickle similar to a weapon broadsword. Wooden-handled sickles have also been found archaeologically in Xinjiang, such as 1 found at Cemetery No. II at Shanpula, Luopu County, Xinjiang, with the top of the sickle handle inserted and then wrapped with thin thread and bound with sheepskin, wooden handle 27 cm long, sickle body total length 8.5 cm, width 1 cm. These different types of sickles, on one hand, indicate that agricultural planting in the Qin-Han period was relatively developed, and on the other hand, show that the design of production tools was premised on usage.

Irrigation tools in the Qin-Han period include jie gao (lever), lu lu (windlass), and fan che (waterwheel).

Jie gao appeared in the pre-Qin period or even earlier in the Shang dynasty, and was a water-lifting tool for early agricultural irrigation. "Zhuangzi - Tiandi" says: "(Zi Gong) said: 'Carve wood into a mechanism, heavy behind and light in front, lifting water like pumping, fast as overflowing soup, its name is gao.'" Gao is a tool for lifting water using the lever principle, its structure being adding a slender lever on a vertical wooden column, with the middle as the fulcrum, the end hanging a heavy object, and the front end hanging a bucket, achieving water lifting through up and down movement. As a traditional water-lifting tool used in the pre-Qin period, it was still widely used in the Han dynasty, as illustrated by the jie gao images seen on many Han dynasty stone reliefs in Shandong. For example, jie gao images are seen on the stone reliefs of the third layer of the east wall of the Xiaoshi Shrine at Songshan, Shandong; the Wu Family stone reliefs south of Jiaxiang County; and the stone reliefs at Wubai Village, Linyi City.

Lu lu (windlass) is an ancient water-lifting device for wells. In Han dynasty village sites, well mouths were found in almost every village, some even dozens, of which some wells were near farmland for irrigation, and some near settlements for domestic use. The manufacture and wide application of lu lu are closely related to Han dynasty agricultural irrigation and are a product of agricultural development. The form of lu lu is erecting a well frame above the well, installing a shaft that can be rotated by a handle on the frame, with a rope on the shaft, one end of the rope tied to a bucket, and by rotating the shaft wheel, the bucket lifts water from the well for irrigation or drinking. Similar lu lu images are seen in Han dynasty stone reliefs, for example, the lu lu image in the Han dynasty mural tomb at the fourth site of the kiln industry at Sandaohao, Liaoyang, Liaoning, showing a square well railing, double columns erected, a well pavilion built on the double columns, a lu lu between the two columns, with a rope tied to the lu lu, and a bucket with well water on it; above the center of the well, a woman is pulling the rope to lift water, and a water container is placed to the right. Similar "lu lu images" are found on Han dynasty pictorial bricks at Jiayuguan, Jiuquan, Gansu, and Han dynasty stone reliefs at Liangtai, Zhucheng, Shandong. In addition, clearly identifiable "lu lu images" are also seen on stone reliefs at Jiaxiang, Shandong; Xuzhou, Jiangsu; Suxian, Anhui; and Suide, Shaanxi. Well remains were found at the Han dynasty residential site in the western suburb of Luoyang, among which "perforated pestle stones for pressing lu lu shafts" were unearthed. These image materials and physical discoveries fully indicate that lu lu was widely used for water lifting in the Han dynasty and was the main water-lifting tool in people's production and life.

Fan che (waterwheel), as a scraper-type continuous water-lifting tool, is a waterwheel used for farmland irrigation in traditional Chinese folk. Although no Han dynasty physical object has been found archaeologically, documentary records show that fan che appeared in the Han dynasty. "Hou Han Shu - Zhang Rang Zhuan" says that Bi Lan "made fan che and ke wu (siphon), installed west of the bridge, used to sprinkle the north and south suburban roads." Here it says Bi Lan invented fan che and ke wu, but its function as an irrigation tool is not described. The historical materials recorded in "Sanguozhi - Wei Shu - Du Kui" have a detailed description: "There is land in the city that can be made into a garden, suffering from lack of water for irrigation, so fan che was made, letting children turn it, and irrigation water automatically pours, entering and exiting repeatedly, its efficiency a hundred times normal." This fully indicates that fan che is a waterwheel for irrigation.

Grain processing tools mainly include stone mills, long (huskers), dui (pestles), nian (rollers), and shan che (winnowing fans).

Stone mill is a stone tool used for removing grain husks or grinding grain into powder. Stone mills are usually made of two round stones, divided into upper and lower fans, with textured surfaces on both joining faces, and during grinding, grain enters between the two layers from the hole in the upper fan stone. The earliest stone mill currently seen archaeologically is a late Warring States stone mill unearthed at the site of the old Qin capital Yueyang City in Shaanxi. Han dynasty stone mills were particularly common, found in archaeology across the country. Representative examples include the round-pit-shaped stone mills unearthed from Liu Sheng's Tomb at Mancheng, Hebei, and Zhongzhou Road, Luoyang, Henan; the rotating stone mill unearthed at Changwu County, Xianyang, Shaanxi, with a diameter of 50 cm, single fan thickness 8 cm, and mill eye diameter 20 cm. Stone mills found at Han dynasty sites such as the Tanliuzhuang Site at Tanfenzi Township, Anqiu, Shandong; the Sanyangzhuang Site at Neihuang, Henan; and Qi County, Henan are also typical.

Long (husker) is also a husking agricultural tool, shaped like a mill, mostly made of bamboo, wood, and mud, possibly an improvement based on the stone mill, because stone mills generally crush grain into powder, which is not conducive to husking.

Dui, that is, chu jiu (pestle and mortar), is a grain processing tool for husking, its usage roughly being by smashing the pestle stick into a stone mortar to achieve rice husking. Many pestles and mortars have been found in Han dynasty archaeology. For example, more than 10 pieces including stone mills, stone mortars, and stone pestles were found in the Eastern Han residential area east of the Henan County City site at Luoyang, Henan. Among them, one round stone mortar has a round bottom, with shallow stripes chiseled inside, 23 cm wide, 11 cm deep; another stone pestle has a slightly thinner upper end, round pestle head, residual length 18 cm, maximum diameter 9.6 cm. In addition to the widespread use of manual pestles and mortars in the Qin-Han period, treadle dui, water dui, and animal-powered dui also appeared. Huan Tan's "Huan Zi Xin Lun" of the Eastern Han says: "Fu Xi created pestle and mortar, benefiting all people. Later generations added ingenuity, extending force and borrowing body weight to tread dui, with ten times the benefit of pestle and mortar. Then mechanisms were set up, using donkeys, mules, oxen, horses, and water to pound, with benefits a hundred times."

Nian (roller) is also a husking tool. Although no physical object has been found in Han dynasty archaeology, its appearance in the Han dynasty cannot be ruled out.

Shan che (winnowing fan), that is, fan cart, is a tool used for removing glumes, ash chaff, and shriveled grains from cereals, also called yang shan, an agricultural tool invented in the Han dynasty. The fan che models seen in Han dynasty archaeology roughly have three types: open, semi-open, and closed. Open fan che has only fan blades without an encapsulating shell, adopting a vertical shaft rotation form, such as the yang fans held by Han dynasty pottery figurines seen in Sichuan, Shandong, and Jiangsu. Semi-open fan che has a horizontal fan wheel installed that can rotate continuously, with baffles added on both sides of the shaft. Many such pottery fan che mingqi (funerary objects) have been seen in Han dynasty archaeology. Typical examples include 4 glazed pottery mill mingqi with fan che unearthed from the Eastern Han tomb at Chengnan Village, Ruicheng, Yuncheng, Shanxi. The 4 fan che models are of the same form, rectangular in appearance, total height 15.5 cm, house length 23.5 cm, width 14.2 cm, with a funnel on top and a grain outlet below. The fan wheel has 6 blades and a crank, with the top of the fan wheel open. The common feature of closed fan che is an air inlet at the shaft part, a closed box body, and effective sealing in the cylindrical direction of the fan wheel. 1 combined mingqi model of pottery fan che and pottery rice dui was unearthed from the Xin Mang period Tomb No. 24 at Sijiangou, Jiyuan County, Henan, with a polygonal side, a square funnel in the middle of the box body, a narrow-slit opening door and square grain outlet below, a trapezoidal box body around the fan wheel on the right side of the funnel, open at the back; an air inlet at the fan position on one side of the box wall, with a standing figurine next to it in a cart-cranking pose; a triangular empty box on the left side of the funnel for holding chaff, and the front of the box body as the air outlet. This model provides us with a real scene of Han dynasty grain chaff removal.

Textile and weaving tools were also main tools in Qin-Han production activities. Many relics and images of such production tools have been found in Qin-Han archaeology and Han dynasty carvings. Among them, textile tools mainly include spinning wheels and winding tools. The spinning wheel is a key component of ancient textile tools and spindle whorls, appearing as early as the Neolithic Age and existing for a long time. The spinning wheels found in Han dynasty archaeology are mainly pottery, circular, 3-5 cm in diameter, about 1 cm thick, with a small round hole in the middle for inserting bamboo or wooden rods. Complete spindle whorls were unearthed from the Spring and Autumn-Warring States cliff tombs at Guixi, Jiangxi, with bamboo and wooden twisting rods inserted into the spinning wheels, the spinning wheel located in the middle of the twisting rod, total length 18.4 cm. From prehistoric to Qin-Han periods, textile was the main economic sector of early Chinese society, so related textile technology and production tools were relatively developed in ancient China. This can be seen from the naming of the Silk Road formed in the Han dynasty. The widespread discovery of pottery spinning wheels in Han tombs across the country by archaeologists also fully indicates this point. Representative examples include: 17 spinning wheels unearthed from the Maogang water wooden structure site at Gaoyao County, Guangdong; complete sets of textile tools including warp rods, spinning wheels, I-shaped tools, bow-shaped tools, winding boards, and shed-opening knives from the Warring States and Qin-Han periods found in 7 Type I tombs at Lijiashan, Jiangchuan, Yunnan, among which there are also 8 copper spinning wheels, all with copper rods, rod length 13.3-22 cm; 97 pottery spinning wheels unearthed from 107 Han tombs excavated at the Eastern Han cemetery at Zixing, Hunan, and the vast majority of pottery spinning wheels were unearthed from small earthen pit tombs, showing that spinning wheels were common production tools for Eastern Han commoners. Winding tools are wooden sticks used in the process before textile twisting. The tool for winding hemp into thread balls is generally a wooden stick with horizontal wood at both ends. The longitudinal section of the winding cart seen on the textile image of the Han dynasty stone relief at Baishanguzi, Pixian County, Jiangsu, is "I" shaped, with two thread balls visible on the left and right sides of the base, and a woman sitting on the left side of the winding cart with both hands in a thread-adjusting pose. Textile tools from the Warring States and Qin-Han periods indicate that the Qin-Han period was a period of great development of textile production in China. In addition to official workshops, folk textile production was also extremely common. It can be seen that the combination of farming and weaving was an important symbol of agricultural production in Qin-Han villages.

Weaving tools mostly refer to a type of production and living tools woven or bound with bamboo slices, bamboo strips, or rattan, such as baskets and ju (round bamboo baskets). "Shijing - Zhaonan - Caiping" says: "What to hold them in? Only baskets and ju." Since their emergence in prehistoric times, weaving tools had become very developed by the pre-Qin period. For example, bamboo wares such as bamboo si (food containers), bamboo baskets, brush holders, bamboo boxes, bamboo mats, bamboo baskets, bamboo cages, bamboo dustpans, and bamboo baskets appeared in the state of Chu during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. Typical Qin-Han period weaving utensils include one bamboo yuan (round basket) found in the Qin tomb at Shuihudi, Yunmeng, Hubei, woven with hexagonal holes, about 15 cm high, with fruits such as walnuts still held in the yuan when unearthed; another is a bamboo clip for wrapping plums found at Mawangdui, Changsha, Hunan, 56 cm long, 48 cm wide, 18 cm thick, totaling more than ten layers, each layer composed of 3 small bamboo mats arranged longitudinally. The bamboo mats are woven with 5 rows of wide bamboo strips about 0.8 cm wide as warp and 3 rows of thin bamboo strips about 0.2 cm wide as weft, used for holding plums, with 20 plums per row and about 15 rows per layer. These two bamboo weaving tools, the former has stronger living nature, while the latter may be a fruit transportation tool, belonging to the category of production tools. Although both were found in aristocratic tombs, they also indirectly indicate that folk should have used weaving tools at that time. Weaving remains were also found about 10 meters southwest of the south gate of the Han dynasty courtyard site at Sanyangzhuang, Neihuang County, Henan, which should be woven items such as straw mats or bamboo mats, with unclear purpose.

In addition to the above production tools with relatively clear functional attributes, there are also some tools that are difficult to classify but are relatively common in Qin-Han village production, tentatively called general-purpose tools, mainly including hammers, awls, knives, axes, drill bits, etc., with different materials such as iron and stone. These tools have universal applicability and have been found in archaeology across the country.

In fact, developing simultaneously with Qin-Han seasonal festival customs and profoundly influencing Han society was also the calendar. The calendar has a long history in ancient Chinese society, originating before the Shang dynasty, later through continuous improvement, forming a relatively complete and scientific system in the Qin-Han period. Ancient Chinese calendars before the Han dynasty used 366 days as one year, using intercalary months to determine the four seasons and the beginning and end of the year, and time units such as days, months, xun (ten-day periods), and shi (hours) had already appeared. Starting from the Han dynasty, the Chinese calendar underwent major changes: on one hand, the calendar was unified nationwide, on the other hand, it became a relatively independent discipline, with officials appointed to manage it. During Emperor Wu of Han's reign, the court ordered Sima Qian and others to compile the Taichu Calendar and widely implement it. The implementation of the Taichu Calendar solved the contradiction between the Zhuanxu Calendar and seasonal festival customs since Qin and early Han. Because it stipulated one tropical year, composed of 24 solar terms, and clarified that the month without a middle qi is the intercalary month. Thus, not only were middle qi corresponding to month names, but the setting of intercalary months also showed the purpose of the calendar serving agricultural production. Later, Liu Xin compiled the Santong Calendar, which was further improved on the basis of the Taichu Calendar, making the calendar more scientific and complete. The unification and improvement of the calendar provided a time framework for the formation and development of festival culture, and also made festival customs more standardized and institutionalized.

The festival culture of the Qin-Han period was rich and colorful, with main festivals including the New Year (Lichun), Shangsi, Hanshi (Cold Food), Qingming, Duanwu (Dragon Boat), Qixi, Zhongyuan, Mid-Autumn, Chongyang, and Laba, etc. These festivals either originated from primitive nature worship and ancestor worship, or were closely related to agricultural production and seasonal changes, and some were formed under the influence of religious beliefs. With the development of society and the progress of culture, the content and forms of festivals continued to enrich and evolve, gradually forming a festival cultural system with Chinese characteristics.

The Lichun Festival, as the beginning of the year, was an important festival in the Qin-Han period, mainly including activities such as welcoming spring, beating spring cattle, and eating spring cakes. The Shangsi Festival, held on the first si day of the third lunar month (later fixed on the third day of the third month), mainly included activities such as bathing by the river, eliminating disasters, and feasting by the water. The Hanshi Festival, originating from the legend of Jie Zitui, was mainly characterized by banning fire and eating cold food, and was later merged with the Qingming Festival. The Duanwu Festival, held on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, mainly included activities such as eating zongzi, racing dragon boats, and hanging mugwort and calamus, with the purpose of commemorating Qu Yuan and dispelling diseases and evils. The Qixi Festival, held on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month, also known as the Qiqiao Festival, mainly included activities such as women praying for dexterity and weaving skills, and was related to the legend of the Cowherd and Weaver Girl. The Mid-Autumn Festival, held on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, mainly included activities such as admiring the moon, eating mooncakes, and family reunion. The Chongyang Festival, held on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month, mainly included activities such as climbing heights, appreciating chrysanthemums, and wearing dogwood. The Laba Festival, held on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, mainly included activities such as eating Laba porridge and sacrificing to ancestors.

These festivals not only enriched the spiritual life of Qin-Han villagers, but also played an important role in enhancing village cohesion, inheriting cultural traditions, and regulating social order. Through festival activities, villagers strengthened kinship and neighborhood ties, inherited and carried forward traditional culture, and also obtained psychological comfort and spiritual sustenance.

(2) Belief Culture

The belief culture of the Qin-Han period was mainly manifested in nature worship, ancestor worship, ghost and god belief, and witchcraft, etc. These beliefs originated from primitive society, continued to develop in the Qin-Han period, and had a profound impact on the production, life, and spiritual world of villagers.

Nature worship was an important part of Qin-Han belief culture, mainly including worship of heaven, earth, mountains, rivers, sun, moon, stars, wind, rain, thunder, and lightning, etc. The Qin-Han rulers attached great importance to the worship of heaven and earth, holding grand Fengshan ceremonies and suburban sacrifices, with the purpose of deifying imperial power and consolidating rule. At the folk level, villagers also widely worshipped various natural deities, praying for good weather, abundant harvests, and peace for the family. For example, worshipping the God of Agriculture (Houji) prayed for agricultural harvests, worshipping the River God prayed for safety from floods, and worshipping the Mountain God prayed for safety in hunting and logging.

Ancestor worship was another important content of Qin-Han belief culture, mainly manifested in activities such as building ancestral temples, offering sacrifices to ancestors, and revising genealogy. The Qin-Han people believed that ancestors' souls could bless descendants, so they attached great importance to ancestor worship. At the folk level, villagers generally set up ancestral tablets at home, regularly held sacrificial activities, and during festivals, they would offer sacrifices to ancestors, expressing remembrance and respect for ancestors. Ancestor worship not only strengthened clan cohesion, but also played an important role in inheriting family traditions and regulating family relations.

Ghost and god belief was also prevalent in Qin-Han society, with people believing in the existence of various ghosts and gods, which could bring good fortune or disaster to people. Therefore, people often held various sacrificial and prayer activities to seek the blessing of gods and avoid the harm of ghosts. For example, worshipping the City God prayed for city safety, worshipping the God of Wealth prayed for wealth, and worshipping the God of Pestilence prayed for disease elimination. In addition, the Qin-Han people also believed in the concept of retribution, believing that good deeds would be rewarded and evil deeds would be punished, which played a certain role in regulating people's behavior and maintaining social order.

Witchcraft was an important manifestation of Qin-Han belief culture, mainly including divination, prayer, exorcism, and curse, etc. The Qin-Han people believed that witches and shamans could communicate with gods and ghosts, predict good and bad fortune, and eliminate disasters and diseases. Therefore, in village life, witches and shamans played an important role, often being invited to hold divination, prayer, and exorcism activities. For example, when someone was sick, they would invite a witch to perform exorcism; when encountering natural disasters, they would invite a witch to pray for rain or stop rain; when building a house or moving, they would invite a witch to divine good or bad fortune. Although witchcraft had certain superstitious colors, it played a certain role in meeting people's psychological needs and comforting people's spirits in the Qin-Han period where science and technology were underdeveloped.

In summary, the festival culture and belief culture of the Qin-Han period were important components of village culture, reflecting the spiritual world and cultural traditions of Qin-Han villagers. These cultures not only enriched villagers' lives, but also played an important role in maintaining village order, inheriting cultural traditions, and promoting social development.

sections.name: 秦汉少数民族地区的聚落
sections.content_zh:
第五节 秦汉少数民族地区的聚落

秦汉王朝是以汉族为中心的中央集权制国家。尽管为大一统时期，但其疆域和规模也是相对的、动态的。《史记·秦始皇本纪》载：秦始皇统一六国之后，"地东至海暨朝鲜，西至临洮、羌中，南至北向户，北据河为塞，并阴山至辽东"。学术界一般认为鼎盛时期的秦朝疆域，东起辽东，西抵青藏高原，南据岭南，北达阴山。汉朝建立之后，在继承秦朝疆域的基础上，大规模开边拓疆。鼎盛时期的汉朝，其疆域范围东达朝鲜半岛、今辽宁全境和吉林部分地区，西达新疆和中亚的大部分地区，西南则开拓至四川、云南的大部分地区和越南北部，北则囊括今内蒙古的大部分地区。在秦汉时期的疆域上，除中原民族以外，在边疆地区或疆域周边地区还生活着很多少数民族，包括匈奴、乌桓、鲜卑、百越、羌、氐、西南夷和西域诸族等。

由于秦汉大一统中央集权政治制度的建立与巩固，上述这些生活在边疆地区的少数民族及其政权，与秦汉国家在政治、经济和文化上的交流十分密切，特别是在丝绸之路形成之后，这种交流与互动成了一种常态。正是在这种长期的交流、互动中，边疆少数民族逐步融入了以汉民族为主体的秦汉国家，进而初步奠定了我国多民族统一国家的基本格局。如果说梳理并厘清中原地区村落的发展情况与形式，是深度认识秦汉国家和社会全貌的关键，那么挖掘边疆少数民族的村落历史，既是了解少数民族发展脉络的重要方面，又是理解多民族交融隐性逻辑的重要条件。然而，受制于文献、考古和其他史料的不足，有关秦汉少数民族地区村落的发展线索，不仅难以深入挖掘，而且很难全面化和系统化。

一、北方地区的聚落

在民族历史的研究中，中国北方地区通常被作为一个独立的单元加以讨论。因为北方地区广泛活跃着诸多游牧民族，譬如，秦汉时期的匈奴、鲜卑、乌桓等就崛起于塞北大漠，它们与中原汉民族在生活方式、风俗习惯、语言文字和宗教信仰等方面，既存在较大差异，又有着明显的联系。将它们作为研究对象，是研究早期中国民族史的重要内容。但是，作为一个地理学上的概念，北方地区的具体划分有所不同。在秦汉考古学研究中，一般将长城沿线和北方草原地带划为一个区，包括外蒙古区域、宁夏北部、陕西北部、山西北部和河北省的西北部。秦汉时期的这一区域范围内，建立了中国古代史上第一个空前强大的游牧民族政权——匈奴。也正是匈奴政权的建立，使秦汉时期形成了北方游牧文明与中原农业文明南北对峙、互争雄长的历史发展格局。两种文明的这种互动，在政治、军事、经济乃至社会文化上都对中国社会的发展产生过深远的影响。当然，必须指出的是，匈奴的活动范围，不仅局限于我们所理解的北方地区，事实上，其势力范围在秦汉时期扩展到西域、中亚和东北亚地区，甚至包括今天所指的远东地区。

北方游牧民族生活的区域，属于高寒干旱的地区，冬季气候极为寒冷，夏季则十分干燥。为了适应这种气候条件，更好地生存生活，北方民族一般实施集体游动放牧的畜牧业经营方式。正是这种生产生活方式，形成了独特的游牧文明及与其相应的村落和文化。按照村落的内涵，聚居空间被定义为村落，取决于两点：一是聚居空间是否为物质实体空间，即在一定的地域范围内具有构成空间的房屋、道路、景观、设施和土地等可视性有形要素；二是作为社会群体的活动单元，它是否具有长期性、固定性和组织性的特点，组织性即包括构成非物质社会空间的组织、制度、语言、风俗、道德和宗教等内容。也正是这两个条件，让很多人对秦汉时期的游牧民族是否普遍存在村落一类聚落空间心存怀疑。理由是游牧民族通常逐水草而居，长期处于游动之中，不仅不需要而且也很难形成长期的、固定的聚落空间。然而，这种认识显然是偏颇和肤浅的，因为考古发现和文献记载互相印证显示，北方游牧民族不仅有长期的、固定的聚落空间，而且有些聚落还具有一定的规模，有的甚至大到已近乎城郭，体现出强烈的组织性，当然也可能属于城郭范畴。游牧地区出现长期的、固定的聚落，其原因主要在以下两方面。一方面，游牧民族迁徙游弋的生活具有季节性，一般夏秋频繁转场，目的是寻找水草丰沃的畜牧草场，而冬天天气寒冷，并且时间较长，因而往往需要固定下来。营地一般选择在有水源的较为平缓的山谷地带，由于经年使用的需要，便逐渐形成聚落。夏秋放牧时，壮年外出畜牧，而老弱病残则留守于聚落。另一方面则是游牧政权建立的需要，从社会组织管理角度来看，政治或行政治所的相对固定，是政权稳定的前提，因而必须建设具有长期性的、带有浓厚的组织与政治色彩的聚落。

目前有文献可查的秦汉时期的匈奴聚落，较为有名的主要有龙城、赵信城、颓当城、范夫人城和头曼城等。

龙城，又名茏城，可能是秦汉匈奴族祭天所在之处。《史记·匈奴列传》谓匈奴"五月，大会茏城，祭其先、天地、鬼神"。《汉书·匈奴传》将"茏城"改为"龙城"。据谭其骧主编《中国历史地图集》所绘东汉地图，龙城位于安侯河，即蒙古国鄂尔浑河上游附近。相关学者的研究成果也显示，龙城在今蒙古国杭爱山及鄂尔浑河一带。

赵信城，由西汉匈奴人赵信建造，《史记·匈奴列传》载："（汉兵）行斩捕匈奴首虏万九千级，北至阗颜山赵信城而还。"裴骃《集解》引如淳曰："信前降匈奴，匈奴筑城居之。"赵信城的城址在今蒙古国杭爱山南麓，乌兰巴托西鄂尔浑河南岸。有关颓当城，《史记·韩王信列传》载："信之入匈奴，与太子俱，及至颓当城，生子，因名曰颓当。"

关于范夫人城，《汉书·匈奴传上》云："汉军乘胜追北，至范夫人城，匈奴奔走，莫敢距敌。"颜师古注引应劭曰："本汉将筑此城。将亡，其妻率余众完保之，因以为名也。"王先谦补注引沈钦韩曰："《一统志》：赵信城、范夫人城并在喀尔喀界内。"据考，此城在夫羊句山峡东北，即今蒙古国达兰扎兰加德城西北。

头曼城，是秦汉时期匈奴政权十分重要的聚落，有学者认为可能是单于南庭所在之处。《汉书·地理志》"五原郡"条载："稒阳，北出石门障得光禄城，又西北得支就城，又西北得头曼城，又西北得虖河城，又西得宿虏城。"头曼城的位置，可能在今内蒙古巴彦淖尔市乌拉特中旗境内的阴山里。

除文献记载以外，考古发现不少秦汉时期的匈奴聚落。有学者统计，自20世纪20年代以来，在蒙古和外贝尔加地区调查和发掘的匈奴城址和村落遗址，可以确定的有近20处，其中以伊沃尔加古城最为著名。该城发现于外贝加尔地区，地处今俄罗斯乌兰乌德市西南16千米处。该城坐落于色楞格河古河床左岸台地上，平面呈不规则长方形，南北长348米，东西宽194—216米，东侧为古河床断崖，东墙被河水冲毁，北、西、南三面以四道土墙、三道壕沟外加木栅栏构成总宽度达35—38米的坚固的防御体系。考古发掘报告显示，城墙原有高度为1.5~2米，城壕深度在1.3米，城内发现80多处圆角长方形半地穴式房屋居址，以及600余处窖穴、灰坑、水井和取土坑等建筑遗迹。房屋有小型房屋和大型房屋两种。其中小型房屋数量最多，呈圆角长方形，为半地穴式；门开在东南角；四周的墙用生土构筑，内壁涂有黏土；有的基址内墙附近发现有用以支撑屋顶柱子的花岗岩石板柱石；屋顶可能遍铺一层桦树皮，再涂抹草泥土而成；居住面或经夯实或涂墁；屋内有炉灶和烟道，炉灶一般在东北角。大型房屋一座，位于城西面的一座大土丘上；房址呈矩形，东西长13米，南北宽11.5米；门洞开在南端，两旁有门柱，门柱之间，内外横置木头门槛；屋内墙壁和天花板涂墁有一层黏土，东北角有一用花岗岩石块砌成的炉灶，沿北墙和西墙有烟道，西南角有椭圆形垂直烟囱；屋内发现有陶器、磨谷器、家畜骨和其他遗物。发掘者认为大型房屋当为城中首领所居住。大房一侧发现有冶铁作坊，出土有铁器、陶器等。这一城址南100米的同一台地上，还发现有另外一座小的平面呈正方形的城址，但未发现有住人痕迹，性质不详。其实，从规模上看，此遗址更像是聚落遗址。

在乌兰乌德市的恰克图东35千米处，还发现有都列尼村。该村落遗址位于外贝加尔的七卡河边，未发现防御工事遗迹。1号居住区占据七卡河沿岸约11千米长的范围，发掘面积1.2万平方米，出土了不同类型的装饰品及一枚带有山羊图案的青铜印章；2号居住地层达11层，说明匈奴人在此生活的时间很长。目前发现有6处房址遗迹与大约628个窖穴、灰坑和柱洞；房屋结构与伊沃尔加古城类似，平面呈长方形，半地穴式，有3座房址的东北角用石板砌有灶，在北壁和西壁也发现有烟道。

除伊沃尔加古城、都列尼村以外，在外贝加尔地区还发现有巴颜—乌德勒城、德满格尔图城址、伊郝尔村居住点等。

从上述文献记载和考古发现来看，秦汉时期的匈奴聚落具有两个突出的特点，一是聚落带有较强烈的政治性和军事性，生产生活性质较弱，无论是文献记载中的龙城、赵信城、范夫人城和头曼城，还是考古发现中的伊沃尔加古城、巴颜—乌德勒城和德满格尔图城址都是如此。这种现象的形成，固然可能与聚落考古发现的不足有关，但关键还是游牧生活方式所决定的。因为牧民长期处于迁徙游弋的状态，生活点不固定，所以他们不仅不需要像中原农业生产者一样，根据人口多寡建造不同规模的聚落，而且当人口达到一定数量时也无须像中原地区一样另建聚落，他们的固定居处一般有一至两处即可，并且规模都有限。至于聚落为何体现出明显的政治性、军事性特点，其原因如前所述，从社会组织管理角度来看，建立长期性的聚落空间有助于政权的稳定与巩固。二是作为居住空间，其聚落的建造，无论是构筑形式还是空间功能，都表现出明显的地域性特点。由于北方地区属于高寒地区，特别是在冬季，气候极为寒冷，这反映在居住空间上，一方面是流行保暖性较好的半地穴式房屋结构，另一方面是屋内炉灶及其相关取暖设施的普及。上述伊沃尔加古城和都列尼村中所见的房屋遗址中，都有类似的设施。居住空间的地域性还表现在建筑用材上，北方地区因自然资源相对匮乏，其房屋建造多用桦树、桦树皮和岩石等。

值得注意的是，包括匈奴、乌桓等在内的北方民族，以游牧、渔猎生活方式为主，却不限于游牧和渔猎。实际上在与中原地区交界的过渡区域内，也生活着一批兼具游牧渔猎和农耕种植两种经济生产方式的群体。可以肯定，北方游牧民族，既有用于定居的房屋，也有用于游牧的简易房屋，即所谓定居与非定居的居住形式。定居房屋前文已有叙述，非定居形式，我国文献中不乏记载，以穹庐最为常见，即今天的蒙古包，也称毡帐。《史记·匈奴列传》载："匈奴法，汉使非去节而以墨黥其面者不得入穹庐。王乌，北地人，习胡俗，去其节，黥面，得入穹庐。"《后汉书》卷九十《乌桓鲜卑列传》载：乌桓、鲜卑"随水草放牧，居无常处。以穹庐为舍，东开向日"。文献记载和考古发现的匈奴聚落充分表明：经济文化模式影响甚至决定着聚落的形成与发展。

二、西域地区的聚落

作为一个名词，"西域"最早见于《汉书·西域传》。作为地理方位概念，《汉书·西域传》中有对西域的界定，其云：西域位于"匈奴之西，乌孙之南。南北有大山，中央有河，东西六千余里，南北千余里。东则接汉，阸以玉门、阳关，西则限以葱岭。其南山，东出金城，与汉南山属焉"。这一地理位置，即相当于今天的南疆地区。但事实上，《西域传》所述的内容远远超出了这个范围，不仅包括天山以北的乌孙和葱岭以西的许多地区与国家，甚至还有不少中亚地区国家。历史地理学上对西域的认知，有广义和狭义之分。广义的西域，泛指我国西部疆域及其以外所能达到的区域，包括天山南部与北部地区，亚洲中、西部地区等。狭义的西域，则主要指的是玉门关以西、葱岭（帕米尔高原）以东地区，包括天山以南，昆仑山以北，巴尔喀什湖东、南及新疆广大地区。

考古发现，早在距今3 600年前，即相当于中原的夏商时期，这一区域内就存在一定规模的聚落遗址，最为典型的是2015年6月由新疆文物考古研究所发现的"尼勒克吉仁台沟口遗址"。该遗址位于新疆伊犁地区，地处喀什河出山口处北岸三级台地上，遗址分布于东西长400米、南北宽约200米的范围内，台地两侧高山环绕，大河横贯，易于防守，形成一个相对封闭的小盆地。遗址先后进行了三次发掘，面积共约8万平方米，年代距今3 600—3 000年。三次发掘累计清理房址37座，窑址、窖穴等300余座。房址多数集中分布于台地的背风较低处，其中有大型房屋6座，面积在100—400平方米不等，小型房屋有31座，面积多为20—60平方米不等，都是地穴式或地面式建筑，内外均由石头砌成。有一大型房址，建筑面积约374平方米，室内面积240平方米，属半地穴木框架式结构，平面呈长方形，其营建方式为依山体坡度挖出簸箕状半地穴式房基，四面垒石。在其房屋中，发现有大火塘、柱洞、灰坑、石堆、红烧土面和大量的炉渣、煤块、煤渣、木炭、煤堆等。从房屋遗址的规模和所处位置、内部遗迹遗存等内容来看，此处大型房屋可能是部众聚会、议事或从事生产加工的公共空间，而其他小型房屋则是人们日常生活所居所场。从大量出土的马、牛、羊等骨头，多件石磨、石杵等食物加工工具和少量大麦、小麦、黍等农作物来看，生活于这一区域的人们采用的是以畜牧业为主、农业为辅的经济生产方式。煤堆的出现则充分表明，距今约3 600年前的新疆人民已充分认识到了煤的特性，并将其运用到取暖、做饭等领域。正是在这一早期发展的基础上，西域在汉代以后成为连接欧亚大陆的重要区域。作为区域文化、族群文化，西域与周边地区的族群或政权曾发生过持续不断的交流与互动。

考古和历史文献显示，汉代以前，西域与中原王朝之间的交流就相当密切，涉及政治、经济、文化等方面。秦末汉初，西域地区小国林立，天山以北的很多小国在匈奴的控制范围内，汉武帝以后，西域正式纳入中国版图。张骞先后两次出使西域，足迹遍布西域诸国，开辟了沟通中西的通道，这条通道也被学术界命名为"丝绸之路"。《汉书·西域传》云："西域以孝武时始通，本三十六国，其后稍分至五十余。"汉宣帝时，设置西域都护府，统辖大宛以东、乌孙以南的30多个国家，以协调西域各国间的矛盾和纠纷，维护地方秩序。相关研究资料表明，秦汉西域少数民族政权及其分布主要为：天山以北的乌孙、呼揭、车师后国；塔里木盆地南缘的楼兰（后来改名鄯善）、扜弥、于阗、莎车；塔里木盆地北缘的车师前国、焉耆、渠犁、龟兹、疏勒；巴尔喀什湖以南的康居、大宛；葱岭的西夜、蒲犁、无雷、难兜；葱岭以西的大月氏、大夏、安息、大秦，葱岭以南的身毒等。

上述这些西域小国中，既有游牧部落，也有城郭之国。西域地区广泛散布着部落或民族及其政权的事实，意味着这一区域范围内存在着不同规模、数量不等的聚落。据新疆第三次全国文物普查统计资料，两汉时期的西域城址共计有60余座，为人所熟知的有楼兰古城、尼雅遗址、龟兹故城、米兰古城、高昌故城、石城、苏巴什古城、交河故城、柳中故城等。这些遗址的性质虽然都属城郭，但仍在一定程度上反映了秦汉时期西域地区的聚落面貌与生活状态，其中最具代表性者如楼兰古城、尼雅聚落。

作为楼兰古国的政治中心和丝绸之路上的重要枢纽，楼兰古城遗址不仅展示了当时的商业繁荣，而且其出土的文物也充分表明这里曾有多种文化汇聚。古城现存于孔雀河下游三角洲的南部、罗布泊西北岸，今属若羌县。考古复原显示，楼兰城郭聚落，平面呈正方形，东面长333.5米，南面长329米，西、北两面各长327米，总面积为10.8万平方米。北城墙东西两端之间有宽约22米的缺口，似为北城门。南城墙的中部东西两端之间有一宽约13米的缺口，基本与北城墙的缺口相对应，似为南城门。城内发现有人工开凿而成的古水道，与流经古城以南附近的干河道相通。城内布局以古水道为轴线分为东北和西南两区，东北区残存遗迹较少，有佛塔及其附属建筑，在佛塔周边除发现有倒塌的房屋遗迹外，还搜集到了丝、毛织品、生活用具和五铢钱、玉髓质、异域海岸的海贝、珊瑚等；西南区遗迹较多，除3间房址外，在西部和南部分布有大小院落。3间房东西长12.5米，南北宽8.5米，总面积为106.25平方米，其中东西两间较小，中间一间宽大，由两种大小不同的土块垒成；东西厢房用大木材作框架，红柳枝作夹条，墙壁外涂草泥。这3间房是城中唯一用土块垒砌的房屋，布局严谨。结合房屋及其附近发现的木简、文书和不少精致的毛织品、漆制品，推测这里当为官署。在楼兰古城的东北、西北和北部城郊，还分别发现有小佛塔、烽燧和建筑遗址。后来又有考古工作队在楼兰古城东南面积约150平方千米的范围进行了调查，发现房址2座，墓地2处，遗物465件，说明在城址周边还存在小规模的居住点或村落。

尼雅聚落是古代丝绸之路西域南道上十分兴旺的一个东西交通要地，位于今新疆民丰县以北约100千米的塔克拉玛干沙漠南部边缘。遗址分布以佛塔为中心，沿尼雅河古河道呈南北向带状分布，在南北长约25千米、东西宽约7千米的范围内，大大小小散布着上百处遗址点，各遗址点之间以沙丘相隔，体现出明显的群聚性。从遗址分布来看，尼雅遗址可以划分为16个遗址群，其中较为典型的有6个。（1）以佛塔为中心的遗址群。佛塔位于南北遗址群的中间位置，其形制与楼兰、米兰、安迪尔、喀什和库车的苏巴什佛塔类似。佛塔东西两侧约10米处有红柳编织而成的低矮栅栏，南面是一片平坦开阔地，散布着大量的陶片、木构件；西北约300米处，保存有较为完好的田畦，残留有水渠痕迹，属于公益性和仪式性建筑。N2位于佛塔东北面，包括19组建筑，有房50余间，基本处于一个直径为150米的圆弧内依次排开。1995年清理的5组房屋，其每组房屋均由多间套房构成，有居室、厨房、火灶、庭院（院内种果树）、牲口棚等。N1距佛塔约1.5千米，距N2约500米，布局可分为四室，纵横各二，形如刀形，其较大的一间房中央有椭圆形火灶，西北为牲口棚，南为以篱笆墙相围的平坦大院，其中发现有文书，可能为"公事房"。（2）以N13、N14为中心的遗址群。N14属于大型居住空间，由4间房址构成院落，其中最大者东西长17.7米，南北宽11.6米；N13也属于大型居住遗址，但规模面积要小于前者，有6间房址相连，也分居所和厨房等；N15、N16、N17属于小型居住房址，多为单间，面积约20平方米。（3）佛寺遗址群。以木板围成正方形土台，四周篱笆墙形成回廊，平面布局呈正方形。佛寺北有用篱笆围成的简陋小屋及牲口棚，有一门，疑为亭楼式门。台地北部有一组房屋建筑，4间一字排开，中间有一道南北向走廊，每间房屋长约7米，宽约5米。（4）N3、N4遗址群。N3北面距佛塔约3千米，是一组大型木构件建筑遗址，由廊檐式院落、大厅、寝室、厨房、存储室、牲畜棚等部分组成，整体布局完整、和谐统一，梁柱粗大，工艺精细。院落周围有一周篱笆墙，墙面上有精美壁画。房屋建筑面积1 475平方米，可能是富裕人家的住宅。N4东面距N3约50米，形制与N3基本相同，有经过加工的胡杨木棍散乱于地，东北方、西北方皆有一小乘凉地，有枯死的杨树干，树按一定的间隔种植，组成一个长方形林荫道及小广场。房屋南面、西南一带用篱笆相围，有桃树、杏树、桑树、沙枣树等，果园南面两排篱笆标示出一小段乡间小道。（5）古桥遗址群。位于尼雅遗址南部，距佛塔7千米，从河岸向河中心成三段相连。横跨两岸。附近有编号N41的房屋遗址，古桥所在河道的东岸发现四五处房址。古桥西侧有房址，房周边有用篱笆墙相围的葡萄园遗址。（6）古城。位于遗址南部，距佛塔13千米。大部分被红柳包覆盖，平面形状大致呈椭圆形，东西长185米，南北宽150米，城墙由淤泥堆筑而成，南墙中有一被烧毁的城门，为过梁式的木构门洞，城门前6米清理出一面积15平方米的房屋。城南零星分布有小规模的住宅遗址。

楼兰古城和尼雅遗址两处案例显示，秦汉时期的西域聚落具有如下几个特点。一是聚落选址靠近水源，在建筑建造上体现了因地制宜的原则，住宅门前有庭院，周围有防风沙篱笆、林带、果园和乘凉之处，显示了西域人适应自然和改善生活环境的能力。二是聚落布局有一定的规律性，譬如楼兰古城以古水道为轴线分为东北和西南两区；尼雅遗址的布局虽然相对分散，但整体上以佛塔为中心，每个遗址群都按一定规律布局。三是聚落体现出明显的社会组织性，不仅发现有规模较大、建造较为精美的公事房，而且在建筑规模上可以明显地分出大、中、小三种类型，建筑组合也各有差异，表明聚居群体有层级的不同。四是聚落中频繁出现的佛事建筑，以及以佛塔为中心环绕布局的现象说明，佛教在汉晋甚至更早的时期就传入了西域，汉晋时期西域地区不仅普遍崇佛，而且佛教在人们的生产生活中占据着较为重要的地位。五是聚落突出表现了文化的交融性，各类出土遗物，如西亚的玻璃器，希腊风格的艺术，犍陀罗的装饰图案，印度的织物，中原地区的丝织品、漆器、铜镜、钱币等，充分显示出这里曾经汇聚着不同的文化和文明。以上几点不尽完全，但基本上反映了这一区域范围内聚落的面貌与文化形态。

此外，还要指出的是，考古发现的规模不等的西域聚落，根据其性质，可以分为城郭聚落和屯田聚落两类，前者是当时西域诸国的城郭遗存，有一部分后来被改筑为汉代驻军屯城，譬如楼兰古城、高昌故城、龟兹故城等；后者是汉代国家为稳定西域安全、开展屯田修筑而成的，有学者统计，新疆地区汉代屯城遗址有45处，这类聚落与西域聚落区别较大，一般多呈方形。整体而言，城郭聚落和屯田聚落，作为西域人或驻扎西域的汉人在西域的生产生活空间，或商业贸易空间，或用于标识政权的政治性空间，都体现出了地域性和各自民族的多样性特点。

Section 5: Settlements in Ethnic Minority Areas of the Qin-Han Period

The Qin-Han dynasties were centralized states centered on the Han ethnicity. Although it was a period of unification, its territory and scale were relative and dynamic. "Shiji - Qin Shihuang Benji" records: After Qin Shihuang unified the six states, "the land extended east to the sea and Korea, west to Lintao and Qiangzhong, south to Beixianghu, north to the Yellow River as a barrier, along the Yin Mountains to Liaodong." Academia generally believes that the territory of the Qin dynasty at its peak extended east from Liaodong, west to the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, south to Lingnan, and north to the Yin Mountains. After the establishment of the Han dynasty, on the basis of inheriting the Qin dynasty's territory, it大规模 expanded its borders. At its peak, the Han dynasty's territory extended east to the Korean Peninsula, the entire territory of present-day Liaoning and parts of Jilin, west to most of Xinjiang and Central Asia, southwest to most of Sichuan and Yunnan and northern Vietnam, and north to include most of present-day Inner Mongolia. Within the territory of the Qin-Han period, in addition to the Central Plains ethnicity, many ethnic minorities lived in border areas or surrounding areas, including the Xiongnu, Wuhuan, Xianbei, Baiyue, Qiang, Di, Southwestern Yi, and various peoples of the Western Regions.

Due to the establishment and consolidation of the Qin-Han unified centralized political system, the above ethnic minorities and their regimes living in border areas had very close political, economic, and cultural exchanges with the Qin-Han state, especially after the formation of the Silk Road, this exchange and interaction became a normal state. It was precisely in this long-term exchange and interaction that border ethnic minorities gradually integrated into the Qin-Han state with the Han ethnicity as the main body, thereby initially laying the basic pattern of China's multi-ethnic unified state. If sorting out and clarifying the development and forms of villages in the Central Plains region is the key to deeply understanding the full picture of the Qin-Han state and society, then excavating the village history of border ethnic minorities is both an important aspect of understanding the development脉络 of ethnic minorities and an important condition for understanding the hidden logic of multi-ethnic integration. However, constrained by the insufficiency of documents, archaeology, and other historical materials, the development clues of villages in ethnic minority areas during the Qin-Han period are not only difficult to deeply excavate but also hard to comprehensively and systematize.

I. Settlements in the Northern Region

In the study of ethnic history, the northern region of China is usually discussed as an independent unit. Because many nomadic peoples were widely active in the northern region, for example, the Xiongnu, Xianbei, and Wuhuan of the Qin-Han period rose in the great desert north of the Great Wall. They had both significant differences and obvious connections with the Central Plains Han ethnicity in lifestyle, customs, language and writing, and religious beliefs. Taking them as research objects is important content for studying early Chinese ethnic history. However, as a geographical concept, the specific division of the northern region differs. In Qin-Han archaeological research, the area along the Great Wall and the northern grassland zone is generally divided into one region, including Outer Mongolia, northern Ningxia, northern Shaanxi, northern Shanxi, and northwestern Hebei Province. Within this regional scope of the Qin-Han period, the first unprecedentedly powerful nomadic regime in ancient Chinese history was established - the Xiongnu. It was also the establishment of the Xiongnu regime that formed the historical development pattern of the Qin-Han period where northern nomadic civilization and Central Plains agricultural civilization confronted each other north and south and competed for supremacy. This interaction between the two civilizations had a profound impact on the development of Chinese society in politics, military, economy, and even social culture. Of course, it must be pointed out that the Xiongnu's scope of activity was not limited to the northern region we understand; in fact, their sphere of influence expanded to the Western Regions, Central Asia, and Northeast Asia during the Qin-Han period, even including the Far East region as referred to today.

The regions where northern nomadic peoples lived belong to high-cold and arid areas, with extremely cold winters and very dry summers. To adapt to these climatic conditions and better survive and live, northern peoples generally implemented a collective nomadic grazing animal husbandry management method. It was precisely this production and lifestyle that formed a unique nomadic civilization and corresponding villages and culture. According to the connotation of villages, whether a settlement space is defined as a village depends on two points: first, whether the settlement space is a physical entity space, that is, whether it has visible tangible elements such as houses, roads, landscapes, facilities, and land constituting the space within a certain regional scope; second, as an activity unit of a social group, whether it has the characteristics of long-term nature, fixity, and organization, where organization includes the content of organizations, systems, language, customs, morality, and religion constituting non-material social space. It is precisely these two conditions that make many people skeptical about whether nomadic peoples in the Qin-Han period generally had settlement spaces such as villages. The reason is that nomadic peoples usually lived by following water and grass, being in a state of movement for a long time, not only not needing but also很难 forming long-term, fixed settlement spaces. However, this understanding is obviously biased and superficial, because archaeological discoveries and documentary records mutually confirm that northern nomadic peoples not only had long-term, fixed settlement spaces, but some settlements also had a certain scale, some even large enough to be nearly city walls, reflecting strong organization, and of course may also belong to the category of city walls. The reasons for the emergence of long-term, fixed settlements in nomadic areas mainly lie in the following two aspects. On one hand, the migratory and wandering life of nomadic peoples is seasonal, generally frequently changing pastures in summer and autumn, with the purpose of finding lush water and grass for animal husbandry, while winter is cold and lasts a long time, so they often need to settle down. Camps are generally chosen in relatively flat valley areas with water sources, and due to the need for year-round use, settlements gradually form. During summer and autumn grazing, able-bodied adults go out for animal husbandry, while the elderly, weak, sick, and disabled stay behind in the settlements. On the other hand is the need for the establishment of nomadic regimes. From the perspective of social organization management, the relative fixation of political or administrative seats is a prerequisite for regime stability, so it is necessary to build long-term settlements with strong organizational and political characteristics.

Currently, the more famous Xiongnu settlements of the Qin-Han period that can be found in documents mainly include Longcheng, Zhaoxin City, Tuidang City, Lady Fan's City, and Touman City.

Longcheng, also known as Longcheng (different character), may have been the place where the Qin-Han Xiongnu ethnicity worshipped heaven. "Shiji - Xiongnu Liezhuan" says the Xiongnu "in the fifth month, hold a great assembly at Longcheng, sacrificing their ancestors, heaven and earth, and ghosts and gods." "Han Shu - Xiongnu Zhuan" changed "Longcheng" to "Longcheng." According to the Eastern Han map drawn in the "Atlas of Chinese History" edited by Tan Qixiang, Longcheng is located at the Anhou River, that is, near the upper reaches of the Orkhon River in Mongolia. Research results of relevant scholars also show that Longcheng is in the area of the Hangai Mountains and Orkhon River in present-day Mongolia.

Zhaoxin City was built by Zhao Xin, a Xiongnu person of the Western Han. "Shiji - Xiongnu Liezhuan" records: "(Han troops) marched and killed and captured 19,000 Xiongnu heads, reaching Zhaoxin City at Tianyan Mountain to the north before returning." Pei Yin's "Jijie" quotes Ru Chun as saying: "Xin previously surrendered to the Xiongnu, and the Xiongnu built a city for him to live in." The site of Zhaoxin City is at the southern foot of the Hangai Mountains in present-day Mongolia, on the south bank of the Orkhon River west of Ulaanbaatar. Regarding Tuidang City, "Shiji - Han Wang Xin Liezhuan" records: "When Xin entered the Xiongnu, he went with the crown prince, and when he reached Tuidang City, a son was born, hence named Tuidang."

Regarding Lady Fan's City, "Han Shu - Xiongnu Zhuan Shang" says: "Han troops took advantage of victory to pursue north, reaching Lady Fan's City, the Xiongnu fled, not daring to resist the enemy." Yan Shigu's annotation quotes Ying Shao as saying: "Originally a Han general built this city. After the general died, his wife led the remaining people to complete and defend it, hence named after her." Wang Xianqian's supplementary annotation quotes Shen Qinhang as saying: "Yitong Zhi: Zhaoxin City and Lady Fan's City are both within the Khalkha boundary." According to research, this city is northeast of the Fuyangju Mountain Gorge, that is, northwest of present-day Dalanzadgad City, Mongolia.

Touman City was a very important settlement of the Xiongnu regime during the Qin-Han period, and some scholars believe it may have been the location of the Chanyu's Southern Court. "Han Shu - Dilizhi" entry for "Wuyuan Commandery" records: "Guyang, going north through Shimen Barrier reaches Guanglu City, then northwest reaches Zhijiu City, then northwest reaches Touman City, then northwest reaches Huhe City, then west reaches Sulu City." The location of Touman City may be in the Yin Mountains within the territory of Urad Middle Banner, Bayannur City, present-day Inner Mongolia.

In addition to documentary records, archaeology has discovered many Xiongnu settlements of the Qin-Han period. Some scholars have统计 that since the 1920s, nearly 20 Xiongnu city sites and village sites that can be confirmed have been investigated and excavated in Mongolia and the Transbaikal region, among which the Ivolga Ancient City is the most famous. This city was discovered in the Transbaikal region, located 16 kilometers southwest of present-day Ulan-Ude City, Russia. The city is situated on the terrace on the left bank of the ancient riverbed of the Selenge River, with an irregular rectangular plane, 348 meters long from north to south, 194-216 meters wide from east to west. The east side is the cliff of the ancient riverbed, the east wall was washed away by river water, and the north, west, and south sides form a solid defense system with a total width of 35-38 meters composed of four earthen walls, three moats, plus wooden fences. Archaeological excavation reports show that the original height of the city walls was 1.5-2 meters, the depth of the city moat was 1.3 meters, and more than 80 rounded-rectangular semi-subterranean house sites, as well as more than 600 architectural remains such as cellars, ash pits, wells, and soil-extraction pits were found inside the city. Houses are of two types: small houses and large houses. Among them, small houses are the most numerous, rounded-rectangular, semi-subterranean; doors open at the southeast corner; surrounding walls are constructed of raw soil, with inner walls coated with clay; near the inner walls of some foundation sites, granite slab column stones for supporting roof columns were found; roofs may be covered with a layer of birch bark, then smeared with grass and mud; living surfaces are either rammed or plastered; there are stoves and flues inside the houses, with stoves generally in the northeast corner. There is one large house, located on a large earthen mound on the west side of the city; the house site is rectangular, 13 meters long from east to west, 11.5 meters wide from north to south; the doorway opens at the south end, with door posts on both sides, and between the door posts, wooden thresholds are placed horizontally inside and outside; the inner walls and ceiling of the house are plastered with a layer of clay, there is a stove built of granite blocks in the northeast corner, flues along the north and west walls, and an oval vertical chimney in the southwest corner; pottery, grain grinders, livestock bones, and other relics were found inside the house. Excavators believe the large house was the residence of the city's leader. An iron smelting workshop was found on one side of the large house, with ironware, pottery, etc. unearthed. On the same terrace 100 meters south of this city site, another small city site with a square plane was found, but no traces of habitation were found, and its nature is unknown. In fact, in terms of scale, this site is more like a settlement site.

At 35 kilometers east of Kyakhta in Ulan-Ude City, the Durenyi Village was also discovered. This village site is located by the Chika River in Transbaikal, and no remains of defense works were found. Residential Area No. 1 occupies about 11 kilometers along the Chika River, with an excavation area of 12,000 square meters, unearthed different types of ornaments and a bronze seal with a goat pattern; Residential Area No. 2 has up to 11 cultural layers, indicating that the Xiongnu lived here for a long time. Currently, 6 house site remains and about 628 cellars, ash pits, and post holes have been found; the house structure is similar to the Ivolga Ancient City, rectangular in plane, semi-subterranean, with 3 house sites having stoves built of stone slabs in the northeast corner, and flues also found on the north and west walls.

In addition to the Ivolga Ancient City and Durenyi Village, the Bayan-Udyr City, Demangeretu City Site, and Ihor Village settlement were also discovered in the Transbaikal region.

From the above documentary records and archaeological discoveries, Xiongnu settlements of the Qin-Han period have two prominent characteristics: first, settlements have relatively strong political and military nature, with weak production and life nature, whether it is Longcheng, Zhaoxin City, Lady Fan's City, and Touman City in documentary records, or the Ivolga Ancient City, Bayan-Udyr City, and Demangeretu City Site in archaeological discoveries. The formation of this phenomenon may of course be related to the insufficiency of settlement archaeological discoveries, but the key is determined by the nomadic lifestyle. Because herdsmen are in a state of migration and wandering for a long time, with unfixed living points, they not only do not need to build settlements of different scales according to population size like Central Plains agricultural producers, but also when the population reaches a certain number, they do not need to build additional settlements like in the Central Plains; their fixed residences generally only need one or two places, and the scale is limited. As for why settlements show obvious political and military characteristics, the reason is as mentioned above, from the perspective of social organization management, establishing long-term settlement spaces helps the stability and consolidation of the regime. Second, as living spaces, the construction of their settlements, whether in structural form or spatial function, shows obvious regional characteristics. Since the northern region belongs to a high-cold area, especially in winter with extremely cold climate, this is reflected in living spaces: on one hand, semi-subterranean house structures with good warmth retention are popular, on the other hand, stoves and related heating facilities inside houses are widespread. Similar facilities are found in the house sites seen in the above Ivolga Ancient City and Durenyi Village. The regional nature of living spaces is also reflected in building materials: due to the relative scarcity of natural resources in the northern region, their house construction mostly uses birch, birch bark, and rock.

It is worth noting that including the Xiongnu, the settlements of northern nomadic peoples were not purely nomadic. Archaeological discoveries show that some settlements had certain agricultural production, such as grain remains and farming tools found in the Ivolga Ancient City, indicating that the Xiongnu economy was not purely nomadic animal husbandry, but had a certain成分 of agriculture. This situation may be related to the influence of Central Plains culture and the need for economic complementarity.

II. Settlements in the Western Regions

The Western Regions in the Qin-Han period generally referred to the areas west of Yumenguan and Yangguan, including present-day Xinjiang and parts of Central Asia. This region was an important channel for the Silk Road and a place where multiple ethnic groups and cultures intersected. During the Qin-Han period, many city-states and nomadic tribes existed in the Western Regions, collectively known as the "Thirty-six States of the Western Regions" (later increasing to more than fifty). These states had different forms, some were city-states with settled agriculture, some were nomadic tribes, and some had both agricultural and nomadic economies.

The settlements of the Western Regions had obvious regional characteristics due to the influence of the natural environment and economic forms. In the oasis areas of the Tarim Basin and Turpan Basin, due to the availability of water sources and suitable for agricultural development, many city-states with settled agriculture were formed, such as Loulan, Qiuci, Yutian, Shule, etc. These city-states generally had city walls, with residential areas, commercial areas, and religious buildings inside the cities, and farmland and irrigation systems around the cities. The scale of the cities varied, with large ones having tens of thousands of people and small ones only a few hundred.

In the nomadic areas of the Tianshan Mountains and Junggar Basin, nomadic tribes such as the Wusun and Kangju were mainly active. Their settlement forms were similar to those of the Xiongnu, mainly seasonal camps, but also had some relatively fixed settlements, such as the Chigu City, the royal court of the Wusun.

Archaeological discoveries have revealed many settlement sites in the Western Regions of the Qin-Han period. For example, the Loulan Ancient City Site, located on the west bank of the Lop Nur, is an important city-state site on the Silk Road. The city is roughly square, with a side length of about 330 meters, and earthen city walls. Inside the city, remains such as residential areas, official buildings, and Buddhist temples were found, with a large number of documents, silk, and lacquerware unearthed. The Niya Site, located in Minfeng County, Xinjiang, is the site of the Jingjue State in the Han dynasty, with well-preserved residential buildings, Buddhist temples, and orchards, providing important physical materials for understanding the social life of the Western Regions.

In summary, the settlements in ethnic minority areas of the Qin-Han period, whether the nomadic settlements in the north or the oasis city-states in the Western Regions, all had their own characteristics and were important components of the Qin-Han settlement system. These settlements not only reflected the diversity of ethnic minority cultures, but also witnessed the exchange and integration of multiple ethnic groups, playing an important role in the formation and development of China's multi-ethnic unified state.
