Section 4: Production and Life in Village Society

I. Development of Cao Shi (Rural Markets) and Villages

During the Eastern Jin and Southern Dynasties periods, cao shi (rural markets) had already appeared in the Jianghuai River basin, but were relatively scattered. During the Sui-Tang-Five Dynasties period, especially in the middle and late Tang, with the destruction of the fang-shi (ward-market) system and the demand for commodity economic development, folk commodity trade developed by leaps and bounds with an irresistible trend, and emerged in various forms across the country. Therefore, the Sui-Tang period was an important development stage for cao shi. During this period, cao shi completed the transformation from folk periodic markets to market towns, and became emerging units and important components of rural grassroots organizations.

(1) Development of Cao Shi in the Tang Dynasty

In the Tang dynasty, to strengthen grassroots control, while implementing the village-fang system and achieving urban-rural separate governance, the government also implemented differentiated management of economic trade in rural and urban areas to prevent population mobility and ensure sufficient agricultural labor resources. On one hand, the Tang court implemented a strict fang-shi system in cities, not only strictly regulating the establishment of fang-shi but also restricting the opening hours of fang-shi. "Tang Liudian" records: "All markets: at noon, beat the drum 300 times and people gather; at seven ke before sunset, strike the gong 300 times and people disperse." In the eleventh month of the first year of Jinglong (707 CE), this decree was reaffirmed: "All places that are not prefectures and counties cannot set up markets. Markets should beat the drum 200 times at noon for a great gathering, and strike the gong 300 times at seven ke before sunset to disperse." On the other hand, the Tang court strictly restricted the development of non-official markets in rural areas. An edict in the eighth month of the fifth year of Dazhong (851 CE) records: "Medium counties with 3,000 or more households set one shi ling (market official) and two shi (clerks); those with less than 3,000 households cannot set up market officials. If it is necessary to set up at important roads and old trade is frequent, allow setting according to the 3,000-household law, still report to the province. All counties under prefecture cities all set up market officials."

In the middle and late Tang, with the rapid development of folk cao shi, the fang-shi system was increasingly impacted and gradually collapsed. From the first year of Jinglong edict and the fifth year of Dazhong edict, it can be seen that the Tang court repeatedly declared the conditions for setting up markets in prefectures, counties, and below. But compared with the former "all places that are not prefectures and counties cannot set up markets," the latter's regulation "those with less than 3,000 households cannot set up market officials" clearly relaxed the conditions for setting up markets. This shows that the court had made certain compromises regarding the development of cao shi. But this compromise also恰好说明 that the original fang-shi system of Tang had continuously encountered challenges from folk markets, and this challenge had obviously exceeded official control, otherwise why would further regulations be made with legal provisions? From this, the prosperous development of folk cao shi can be seen.

(2) Types and Scale of Cao Shi in the Tang Dynasty

Tang cao shi had various types, such as mountain markets, water markets, fish markets, orange markets, medicine markets, periodic markets, hai markets, etc. Japanese scholar Hino Kaisaburo classified all these non-official markets as cao shi. Mr. Mou Fasong also agreed with this view. These non-official markets were either named by geographical location (such as mountain markets, water markets, or comprehensive markets of initial scale formed at fixed locations), or named by types of traded goods (such as specialized markets like fish markets, orange markets, medicine markets), or named by trading time (such as periodic markets like periodic markets and hai markets), reflecting the distribution status, types of traded goods, and trading time and frequency of Tang cao shi.

Luo Ye mentioned specialized fish markets in his poem "Nanxing" (Journey South): "Clear winter river warm, grebes fly; plum snow fragrance sticks to Yue girl's clothes. Fish markets and wine villages all familiar, short boat singing moon drunk then return." Another Tang poet Yuan Zhen said in "Xian Er Shou" (Two Leisure Poems): "River noise passing rain clouds, boat moored against head wind. Small boats collect fish markets, crows noise in reed groves." In addition to fish markets, there were also specialized markets such as medicine markets and orange markets. Such markets mainly sold local products, reflecting the characteristics of local agricultural resources. For example, Yuan Zhen mentioned orange markets in Yuezhou in "Fenghe Zhexi Dafu Li Deyu Shumeng Sishi Yun": "Fish and shrimp gather at orange markets, cranes and storks rise from pavilion banks." It should be noted that the orange market here may initially have been a market specializing in selling local oranges, or mainly selling oranges but also selling fish and shrimp and other goods, having the function of a comprehensive market, which illustrates the flexibility of such folk markets.

In addition to specialized markets, comprehensive markets were more common, and cao shi, mountain markets, water markets, etc. mostly belonged to this category. Such markets did not differ much from the goods sold in fang-shi, often gathering various goods, including both local products and goods transported from other places, to meet the daily needs of local people. In such larger-scale cao shi, trading participants included both local civilian merchants and itinerant merchants and settled merchants, and even larger ones had wine restaurants and inns. For example, "Youyang Zazu" records: "During the Baoli period, there was a Lu Shanren in Jingzhou, who often traded oar wood and lime, traveling to and from the Baifu South cao shi, occasionally revealing miracles, people could not measure him. Merchant Zhao Yuanqing was curious, wanting to travel with him, so frequently bought his goods, set out fruit and tea, falsely asking about his profit methods... Lu laughed and said: 'Now let's test, your master will have an extraordinary disaster at noon, if my words are right it can be avoided, you can tell him. Near noon, a cake maker will come carrying a bag. There will be more than 2,000 coins in the bag, and he will not intentionally cause trouble...' At that time Zhao was staying at commoner Zhang's house, so hurriedly returned to tell him. Zhang also had long considered Lu magical, so closed the door and waited. Near noon, sure enough someone as Lu described, knocked on the door asking to buy grain, angry at no response, kicked the door, Zhang defended with a heavy stick... Past noon, that person left, walked several hundred steps, suddenly fell and died... When the market coffin was carried, exactly 3,400 coins. Because of this, people flocked there like to a market."

This record about cao shi contains rich information. First, the Baifu South cao shi here is a comprehensive market. From the record, it can be seen that the goods sold at this cao shi included oar wood, lime, cakes, coffins, etc., with relatively diverse types. Second, according to the narrative, Lu who sold oar wood and lime at Baifu South cao shi was not a local person where the cao shi was located, but a Jingzhou person traveling to and from Baifu South cao shi. Where Zhao Yuanqing was a merchant is not explained in the text, but his "staying at commoner Zhang's house" also indicates he was not local. From this, it can be seen that participants in Tang cao shi included not only local people but also merchants from various places. Tang poet Wang Jian's description in "Bian Lu Ji Shi" (Events on the Bian Road): "Thousand li river smoke straight, green locust trees line banks long. End of the world same this road, people's speech each different dialect. Cao shi welcome river goods, ferry bridge tax sea merchants." vividly presents the scene of merchants from various places converging via waterways. This also illustrates the prosperity of cao shi along the river here.

From "Youyang Zazu," it can also be seen that Baifu South cao shi was not only a larger commodity trading place and trade transit point, but also had common people living there. This shows that Baifu South cao shi was no longer a simple small-scale periodic market, but a market with stable trading places and initial scale. Such markets were already relatively common in the middle and late Tang. Du Mu said in his poem "Ru Chashan Xia Ti Shuikou Caoshi Jueju" (Entering Tea Mountain, Inscribing at Shuikou Cao Shi): "Leaning on streams invading ridges many tall trees, boasting wine writing flags have small buildings." The so-called Shuikou cao shi in this poem even had wine restaurants. This situation is also described in Liu Yuxi's "Di Shang Xing San Shou" (Three Poems on the Embankment): "Wine flags face each other at great embankment head, below embankment connected masts above embankment buildings. Dusk pedestrians scramble to ferry urgently, oar sounds creaking fill midstream." "Spring embankment winding water徘徊, wine shops and flag pavilions open in sequence. Evening curtains come out to beckon merchants, tall large boats lower sails to come." These poems were written during Liu Yuxi's tenure as cishi of Kuizhou to cishi of Hezhou (second to fourth year of Changqing, i.e., 822-824 CE). The poems depict the prosperous scene of wine restaurants lining the Yangtze River and customers gathering in the Tang dynasty. This prosperous scene of folk markets was no less than fang-shi in cities.

There were many such large-scale folk cao shi. Shatou City south of Jiangling City in Jingzhou was a representative of prosperous Tang cao shi, and many Tang literary works described its prosperous scene. For example, Yuan Zhen once wrote "Fanjiang Wanyue Shi'er Yun" (Twelve Rhymes on Boating on the River and Enjoying the Moon): "Together carry wine in boats, same boat moon on river. Distant trees hang golden mirrors, deep pools invert jade banners. Waves add clean silk, cave illumination extinguishes condensed lamps. Noisy Shatou market, exquisite bamboo bank windows. Ba children sing Wu Gorge, sea guests talk divine rapids." The poem describes the lively scene of bright lights and crowded people at Shatou market seen by the author when boating leisurely on the river at night. Wang Jian also said in "Jiangling Ji Shi" (Events at Jiangling): "Miasma clouds and plum rain do not make mud, ten li ferry buildings press great embankments. Shu girls go down sand to welcome water guests, Ba children beside post sell mountain pheasants. Temples many red peonies burn people's eyes, ground enough green moss dye horse hooves. Midnight alone sleeping sorrow at distance, north looking return road separated by barbarian stream." This poem not only depicts the commercial scene of Shatou market, but "ten li ferry buildings press great embankment" also illustrates the large scale of Shatou market, not an ordinary small-scale periodic market.

Through the above examples, it can be seen that after the Eastern Jin and Southern Dynasties, Tang cao shi was fully developed, not only diverse in type but also already scaled, no longer limited to periodic markets. As some scholars said, if abandoning the various names of all kinds of cao shi, Tang cao shi can be roughly divided into two categories: periodic rural markets and market towns with initial city scale. Comparatively, the latter had become the main body of Tang cao shi.

(3) Distribution and Characteristics of Cao Shi in the Tang Dynasty

Generally speaking, markets were mostly distributed in areas with frequent population mobility and dense population or transportation hubs, such as river ferries, roadsides in villages, or suburbs of cities. Tang cao shi was the same. According to the above sorting of Tang cao shi types, it can be seen that Tang cao shi were most numerous at ferry crossings along rivers and river basins.

Generally speaking, ferry crossings along rivers and river basins, as transfer stations and hubs of water transportation routes, not only had many people coming and going, but also various goods and cargo were transmitted to surrounding areas through here. This uniquely endowed environment provided conditions for the development of folk trading markets, thus becoming the main distribution area of cao shi. The concentration of cao shi in the Jianghuai River basin during the Eastern Jin and Southern Dynasties already illustrated this point. Tang people had the saying "passes must occupy dangerous roads, markets must rely on important ferries," precisely pointing out the important role of ferry crossings for setting up markets. For example, according to "Tang Huiyao" Volume 71: "Ande County, Dezhou, crossing the Yellow River south, adjacent to Linyi County, Qizhou, has one Guajiakou cao shi." The Guajiakou mentioned here should be a ferry near Linyi County on the south bank of the Yellow River, and the cao shi was located at this ferry. Due to cao shi's identity as a non-official market, records about cao shi are rare in Tang historical books. But Tang literary works made good supplements. For example, "Tang Wen Shiyi" Volume 30 records: "Seventy li not far east of Kuaiji, there is a great marsh called Yu River, twenty li southeast of the river there is a cao shi, Yue Wudafu, south of Feng Mountain... Therefore its place gathers people of the world, sells goods of the world. South ridge of the market is Dexing Village, Dayun Temple set up a manor at the north of this market on Xinjiang Road, road connects to the market." Here it mentions a cao shi twenty li southeast of Yu River. The riverside cao shi in Wang Jian's "Bian Lu Ji Shi" cited above, Baifu South cao shi appearing in "Youyang Zazu," Shuikou cao shi in Du Mu's poem, cao shi along the Yangtze River in Liu Yuxi's poems, Jiangling Shatou market in Yuan Zhen and Wang Jian's poems, etc., all belong to this category.

In addition to ferry crossings along water transportation routes, suburban areas of cities were also main distribution areas of cao shi. Zhang Hu mentioned such cao shi in his poem "Zhongling Lubo" (Staying at Zhongling): "City street west post embankment connected, ten li Yangtze River night watching boats. Fish market moon middle people quietly pass, wine shop lamp below dog long sleeps." The fish market here is located west of Hongzhou City. Another example is Du Mu's "Runzhou Er Shou" (Two Poems of Runzhou), which also mentions cao shi located in the suburbs of Runzhou.

In addition, folk markets can also be seen distributed near some villages. For example, Gu Kuang mentioned cao shi near villages in "Qingyi Jiang" (Qingyi River): "Desolate returning mooring night, rippling waves strike stone sound. Village side cao shi bridge, moon below fisherman net." Li Jiayou's "Deng Chuzhou Cheng Wang Yilu Shili Shancun Zhulin Xiangci Jiaoying" also has descriptions of mountain village cao shi near Chuzhou City: "Ten li mountain village road, thousand peaks oak forest. Frost thick bamboo branches bend, year end reed flowers deep. Cao shi many woodcutters, fishing families enough waterfowl. Secluded residence though enviable, no way Zimu heart." The cao shi here is located near a mountain village. Due to geographical restrictions, goods in the cao shi were relatively limited, and people selling goods were mostly local woodcutters and fishermen. It can be seen that mountain villages relatively close to cities in the Tang dynasty could also enjoy the convenience brought by cao shi and conduct certain commercial exchange activities.

So did mountain village areas also have development of cao shi? Du Mu's "Shang Li Taiwei Lun Jiangzei Shu" (Letter to Grand Commandant Li on River Bandits) gives the answer. The text says river bandits sold looted property to tea mountains, and whenever tea was ripe, merchants from various places entered the mountains to trade, selling gold, silver, and fine clothes to tea mountain people. It can be seen that the tea mountains mentioned in Du Mu's text had trading markets. Another Tang poet Xiang Si's poem "Shan Xing" (Mountain Travel) can also supplement this: "Green oak forest deep also has people, one canal flowing water several families share. Mountain at noon returns peak shadows, grass with mud marks pass deer herd. Steaming tea fragrance comes from thatched cottage, silk reeling sound heard through bamboo fence. Traveling meets medicine-selling returning guest, not sparing following into island clouds." The poem records the author's experiences when traveling deep into mountains, but the author could meet people returning from selling medicine in deep mountains, indicating that there were trading markets around the local area.

Comparatively, cao shi in the southern region of Tang developed more prosperously than in the north. The large number of ferry cao shi and fish markets listed above were generally located in southern riverine and riparian areas, especially the Jianghuai River basin and its tributary waters. Some scholars once pointed out that the number of cao shi along the middle reaches of the Yangtze River was roughly similar to that of ferry crossings. Records of cao shi in the Jianghuai River basin can also be seen everywhere in other documents. For example, "Yuanhe Junxian Zhi" has records about Chibi cao shi located 80 li west of Hanyang County. Another poet Wei Zhuang recorded in "Jianchang Du Ming Yin" (Night Chant at Jianchang Ferry): "Moon shines Lin official ferry, village feelings alone vast. Birds perch Pengli trees, moon rises Jianchang boat. Market dispersed fisherman drunk, building deep merchant sleeps. Across river where flute, blows broken green willow smoke." The poem depicts the scene after the Jianchang Du cao shi in Hongzhou (present-day Jiangxi) dispersed at night. Xu Zhong's "Bo Dongting" (Mooring at Dongting) depicts fish markets along Dongting Lake: "Locust and willow not yet know autumn, lingering at post station head. Guest hearts all think of distance, timely rain mutually detains. Waves submerge goods fish market, sails high sell wine building. Night comes thinking tossing, hometown in southern prefecture." Another Zheng Gu's "Xiazhong Yuzhi Er Shou" (Two Poems of Dwelling in Gorges) depicts cao shi in the Jingzhou area: "Jingzhou not yet relieved siege, small county builds thatched cottages. Forced to smile at officials, willing to be bullied by wild cranes. River spring spreads nets wide, market late sells vegetables slow. Zimei still like this, suddenly dare not sorrow. Rumors especially uncertain, imperial carriage when returns. Customs change无常性, river clear sees old face. Night boat returns cao shi, spring steps up tea mountain. Fort general comes to ask, children compete to open gate." Fang Gan's "Yuezhong Yanshi Er Shou" (Two Poems of Events in Yuezhong, written after the eighth year of Xiantong when Lord Langya took office) describes fish markets in Zhejiang: "Hundred li lake waves gently shake moon, fifth watch military horns slowly blow frost. Sand edge merchants noisy fish market, island hermit drunk bamboo shoot manor."

It can be seen that the distribution of cao shi in the Jianghuai River basin had already become very common and achieved in-depth development. This development was not only reflected in the expansion of distribution areas but also in the充实 of cao shi volume. The volume mentioned here includes not only the physical scale of cao shi mentioned above, but also multiple aspects such as the commercial scale, financial resources, material resources, and composition of cao shi. The following two records can fully reflect the volume status of cao shi in the southern region of Tang. "Quantang Wen" Volume 751 contains Du Mu's "Shang Li Taiwei Lun Jiangzei Shu": "Humbly, Jianghuai taxes are the foundation of state expenditure. Now there is a great calamity, namely river bandits. I have only been in office nine months, daily seeking and inquiring, truly know the clues. Bandit groups, upper to three boats two boats 100 people 50 people, lower no less than 30-20 people, then willing to rob, rob and kill merchants, not sparing infants. Robbed merchants all get unusual goods, all take south across the river, enter mountains to trade for tea. Because unusual goods dare not be sold in cities, only tea mountains can accept. Because when tea is ripe, merchants from all around bring embroidered silk, gold hairpins and silver bracelets, enter mountains to trade, women and children all wear fine clothes, officials see and don't ask, people see and not alarm. Therefore bandits get unusual goods, also come here, and there are shops to store them. After getting tea, go out as ordinary people, 30-20 people carrying weapons... All thousands of groups, all sell private tea. Also have gathered followers, water robbery inconvenient, encountering cao shi, mooring boats at ferry mouth, then conduct land robbery. In broad daylight enter market, kill people take property, many also set fire, sing oars slowly leave. Last year on October 19, robbed Qingyang County market in Chizhou, killed six people, took one, cut open heart and abdomen, looked up to heaven and worshipped. Since then, frequently in neighboring prefectures, many robberies and killings, sinking boats to destroy traces, unknown number. All Jianghuai cao shi, all near water, wealthy families mostly live among them. For fifteen years, all cao shi in Jiangnan and Jiangbei by name have been robbed and killed, only those robbed again after three years, none safe for five years."

As a letter to讨伐 river bandits who常年 robbed cao shi along the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, this text at least reveals the following information about cao shi. First, it provides specific information for us to understand cao shi in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River. Southern cao shi were mostly distributed along river ferries, and the distribution was very extensive. Second, cao shi commerce had become the main source of taxes in the Jianghuai region and occupied an important position in national taxes, sufficient to show the commercial scale and financial resources of cao shi in the Jianghuai region. Third, cao shi in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River were very prosperous and wealthy. Descriptions such as "unusual goods," "embroidered silk, gold hairpins and silver bracelets," "wealthy families mostly live among them" all indicate that the cao shi here were no longer small trading markets, and resident members not only included merchants but also many wealthy families, constituting the main component of cao shi. All these seem to indicate that in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, many cao shi had gradually developed into scaled market towns with both commercial and residential nature. The Shatou market mentioned above is a representative of such large-scale, large-volume cao shi.

Chen Xi's "Pengzhou Xinzhi Tangchangxian Jiande Caoshi Xiemating Zhen Bing Tianwangyuan Deng Ji" (Record of Newly Established Jiande Cao Shi, Xiemating Town, and Tianwangyuan in Tangchang County, Pengzhou), written on May 15, the tenth year of Xiantong (869 CE), also shows such cao shi: "Because Tangchang County's middle boundary borders Daojiang Picheng, east-west stretching, no less than two she (distance units). Although there are villages, remote in desolate ponds. Formerly set up post stations, long abandoned and destroyed. Thus travelers eat wild and drink from springs, traders travel by star and return by candle. Robbers openly act, nowhere to report. Deep ditches rain rise, ancient roads bridges broken. Even steps hard to cross, hardships beyond description. Moreover corvee deadlines, tax collection has schedules. How can we blame those who delay? The official sadly thought, same day plan completed, then reported to commander, set up cao shi in its center. Using its township name, called Jiande. From then on those coming from four directions quickly meet near, those looking middle raise eyes know return. Old and young carrying, suddenly arrive. Ten thousand families laugh, together work construction, less than ten days completed. Now all goods gather, all living things not left. Market pavilions and inns, wings spread scales ordered. Elms and poplars connected, mulberry and hemp gradually prosperous. Such shepherd, can be said to change customs... That day merchants carrying goods arriving tens of thousands. Rare and delicate playthings all have, useful tools all displayed... Then travelers not only eat by day, but can also pass night. People already gather abundantly, customs already rich." The Tangchang County Jiande cao shi here was a cao shi developed from a township along transportation routes. Although the cao shi was set up due to human initiative, this was based on the condition that the place already had conditions for setting up a market: "Formerly set up post stations, long abandoned and destroyed" indicates the place was along transportation routes with many floating people; "traders travel by star and return by candle" indicates commercial activities existed in the place. Therefore, given bad weather, damaged roads, and long journeys, with travelers often bearing economic responsibilities, establishing a cao shi became necessary. From the description in the text, it can be known that after the cao shi was established, the place developed rapidly, not only with many merchants but also shops and inns lining up, merchants from all places converging here, with daily commercial goods flowing here

II. Production Tools and Living Utensils

The production tools and living utensils of Sui-Tang-Five Dynasties villages continued the traditions of previous dynasties while also showing new developments. In terms of production tools, iron farm tools were widely used, and the types and forms of tools were further improved. In terms of living utensils, pottery was still the main type, but porcelain gradually became popular, especially in the middle and late Tang, with the development of porcelain industry, porcelain utensils gradually entered ordinary people's homes.

Agricultural production tools in the Tang dynasty mainly included plows, rakes, sickles, etc. The appearance of the Quyuan plow (curved-shaft plow) was an important innovation in Tang agricultural tools. The Quyuan plow improved on the basis of the straight-shaft plow, shortening the plow shaft and adding a plow disk and plow evaluation, making plowing more flexible and labor-saving. The Quyuan plow was first used in the Jiangnan region and later gradually spread nationwide, becoming the main farm tool in Tang and later dynasties. In addition to plows, irrigation tools also developed, with the widespread use of waterwheels (tong che) and dragon-bone waterwheels, greatly improving irrigation efficiency.

Living utensils in Tang villages mainly included pottery, porcelain, wood, and bamboo. Pottery was mainly used for cooking and storage, such as pots, jars, bowls, etc. Porcelain was mainly used for eating and drinking, such as bowls, plates, cups, etc. The development of Tang porcelain industry was represented by Xing kiln white porcelain and Yue kiln celadon, with "Xing white Yue green" becoming a symbol of Tang porcelain. In addition, lacquerware and bronze ware were still used, but mainly among the upper class, while ordinary villagers mainly used pottery and porcelain.

III. Folk Organizations and Villages

In the Sui-Tang-Five Dynasties period, in addition to the official grassroots management system, various folk organizations also existed in villages, playing an important role in village social life. These folk organizations mainly included clan organizations, religious organizations, mutual aid organizations, etc.

Clan organizations were the most important folk organizations in Tang villages. With the development of the village-fang system and the strengthening of state grassroots control, the functions of clan organizations were somewhat restricted, but clans still played an important role in maintaining village order, mediating disputes, and providing relief. Large clans often had ancestral halls, clan fields, and clan schools, becoming important forces in village society.

Religious organizations were also important components of Tang village society. Buddhism and Taoism were widely spread in villages, and many villages had temples and abbeys. Monks and priests not only engaged in religious activities but also participated in village public affairs, such as building bridges, paving roads, and providing medical treatment. In addition, folk belief organizations such as incense societies and scripture societies also existed in villages, organizing villagers to carry out various sacrificial activities.

Mutual aid organizations were emerging folk organizations in Tang villages, mainly including societies for weddings and funerals, irrigation societies, and harvest societies. These organizations were spontaneously formed by villagers to help each other in production and life, reflecting the tradition of mutual assistance in Chinese rural society. For example, wedding and funeral societies helped villagers with weddings and funerals, irrigation societies organized villagers to build water conservancy facilities, and harvest societies held celebrations during harvest seasons.

IV. Cultural Education and Ethical Enlightenment

In the Sui-Tang-Five Dynasties period, cultural education in villages developed to a certain extent. On one hand, the implementation of the imperial examination system stimulated villagers' enthusiasm for learning, and some villages established private schools and clan schools. On the other hand, the government also attached importance to grassroots education, setting up village schools in some areas to teach villagers literacy and Confucian classics.

The content of village education mainly included literacy education, Confucian classics education, and vocational technical education. Literacy education was the foundation, teaching villagers to recognize characters and read. Confucian classics education mainly taught the Analects, Classic of Filial Piety, etc., cultivating villagers' ethical concepts. Vocational technical education mainly taught agricultural production techniques, handicraft skills, etc., helping villagers improve production skills.

Ethical enlightenment was an important part of Tang village governance. The government promoted Confucian ethics such as loyalty, filial piety, benevolence, and righteousness through various means, guiding villagers to abide by social ethics. The commendation of filial families and righteous families was an important means of ethical enlightenment. In addition, village elders and scholars also played a role in ethical enlightenment, educating villagers through words and deeds.

V. Religion in Villages

Religion had a profound influence on village social life in the Sui-Tang-Five Dynasties period. Buddhism, Taoism, and folk beliefs coexisted and interacted, jointly constituting the religious belief world of villagers.

Buddhism was widely spread in Tang villages, with many villages having Buddhist temples. Villagers believed in Buddhism, engaging in activities such as building statues, printing scriptures, holding fasting ceremonies, and donating to temples. Buddhist ideas of karma, reincarnation, and compassion had a profound impact on villagers' worldview and values. In addition, Buddhist temples also played a role in cultural education and social relief, becoming important cultural and social activity centers in villages.

Taoism, as a native Chinese religion, also had extensive influence in Tang villages. Taoist ideas of immortality, health preservation, and good fortune were popular among villagers, and many villages had Taoist temples and priests. Taoist priests engaged in activities such as praying for rain, exorcising evil spirits, and treating diseases, becoming important figures in village religious life.

Folk beliefs were even more widespread, including nature worship, ancestor worship, ghost and god beliefs, etc. Villagers held various sacrificial activities to pray for good weather, abundant harvests, and family peace. Temple fairs were important forms of folk belief activities, usually held on the birthdays of gods or specific festivals, with villagers gathering to offer sacrifices, trade, and entertain, becoming important social activities in villages.

In summary, the production and life of village society in the Sui-Tang-Five Dynasties period showed rich and diverse characteristics. The development of cao shi promoted rural commodity economy and social mobility; the improvement of production tools and living utensils improved villagers' production and living standards; folk organizations maintained village order and promoted mutual assistance; cultural education and ethical enlightenment improved villagers' cultural quality and moral level; religion provided spiritual sustenance and enriched village cultural life. These aspects together constituted the full picture of village social life in the Sui-Tang-Five Dynasties period, laying the foundation for the development of later village society.

sections.name: 少数民族地区的村落
sections.content_zh:
第五节 少数民族地区的村落

有唐一代，不仅中原地区的村落得到长足发展，边疆民族地区的村落也步入新的发展阶段。唐朝对归附中央王朝的边疆民族地区往往实施羁縻政策，即在其原有部落的基础上，通过设置羁縻州进行行政统治。从地理空间上来说，西北、西南及北方在唐代是少数民族集中聚居的地区，因而是唐代羁縻州的主要分布区域。一方面，在羁縻政策下唐代边疆民族地区享有特殊的自治权；另一方面，在中央王朝的统一领导下，各民族地区间的经济、文化交流日益频繁。这不仅极大地促进了边疆民族地区社会经济、文化水平的提高，而且有力地促进了这一区域内生产力与生产技术的发展，为边疆民族地区村落的发展提供了良好的条件。吐蕃地区因特殊的自然环境、生产生活方式，其村落的发展相对缓慢，但是在与东部大唐王朝的频繁交往之中，也有了一些新的变化，特别是在农业生产方面取得了一定的进步。

一、西北地区的村落

地处中原与中亚交界地带的西北地区，是沟通东亚、中亚、西亚与欧洲的交通要道，自古便是中原王朝与中亚国家竞相角逐的地区。7—9世纪，这一地区形成了中原唐王朝与吐蕃王朝、波斯王朝三股主要对峙势力。唐初，李唐王朝统一华北地区以后，又先后于贞观十四年、显庆二年（657年），统一了西北地区的高昌王国及西突厥。为了加强对西北地区的管理，唐王朝先后设立安西都护府和北庭都护府管理西域地区，将西域地区划归陇右道，并在龟兹、焉耆、于阗、疏勒四地修筑城堡，建立军镇，使之发展成为西域地区的主要城郭聚落。唐王朝统治下的西域地区，初步有了完备的行政体系。自此至安史之乱以前，唐王朝对西域地区的统治基本上保持着稳定的状态。在唐王朝对西北地区统治的百余年间，中原地区与这些民族地区的经济、文化交往明显增强。也正因如此，包括村落社会在内的西北地区得到了前所未有的发展。

1. 安西四镇的村落

安西四镇是唐代西北地区的主要城镇，因而包括其村落在内，相较其他地区，都得到较为充分的发展。羁縻政策是唐王朝对民族地区采取的管理手段，即在保留民族地区原有管理方法的基础上，派驻朝廷官员进行共同管理。但安西四镇的羁縻政策有所不同，其基层行政体制与内地基本相同。但有学者认为，即便如此，这也是随着羁縻制度的推行产生的。另有学者对其原因进行了讨论，认为唐代在四镇全面推行基层管理制度的目的在于"稳定"而非"征赋"。这是唐王朝企图对西北地区进行深入而全面统治的体现，虽然唐王朝仍然保留了四镇的王室制度，但可以将其视为正州。关于唐代的基层管理制度在安西四镇的具体推行状况，我们可以在相关历史文献中找到印证。

现存出土文书中，就有不少关于四镇村落的记载。这些记载说明村落在四镇已经得到普遍发展，且村落的管理制度也已经与中原地区没有明显的差别。斯坦因所获吐鲁番文书《开元年间某寺支出簿》中记载有"西河勃宁野乡厥弥拱村"，其对"乡—村"这一地域归属的表述方法的使用完全与内地相同。另根据刘再聪的考证，"西河"为于阗城西的一处河流，"厥弥拱村"即为位于此河流域的一个郊野村落。这在大谷文书所载龟兹都护辖区村落的相关信息中也可得到验证，如其中8044号《唐大历九年二月目胡子牒》载：

1牒，胡子薄福，不幸慈母身亡。家贫，殡葬尚犹未
2办。南界双渠村种少薄田，今着掏拓两丁，叁分交
3不支济，伏望矜量小人，已后但有駈驰，不敢违命，请
4乞商量处分。谨牒。
5大历九年二月 日 目胡子牒

这件文书中的"南界双渠村"就明显是位于城邑之外的郊野地区。另需指出的是，这件文书中提及目胡子因母丧请求免除摊负的维修渠堰的"掏拓"之役，据学者考证，这种赋役是唐代在边防建设时以村为单位摊派给村民的赋役，由武人负责催驱。这说明唐代的村制度应在安西四镇得到了彻底的执行。

2. 西州的村落

西州也是全面执行了唐代基层管理制度的地区。该地以汉魏屯戍于当地的汉人后裔为主，因此唐政府在消灭高昌王国以后，便在当地设立西昌州，后改为西州，使之成为中央政权管辖下的正州，接受同中原地区州县同样的管理。但受到当地以沙漠为主的自然环境及游牧民族众多的社会环境的影响，出于防御需要，当地居民多筑堡为城，以城为单位据城而守。据《唐会要》记载，唐政府于贞观十四年将西州设为正州时，在交河城、始昌城、田地城、东镇城、高昌城5城置县，由西州辖管，统归安西都护府，后又在5县下设24个乡。但根据部分学者的研究，西州的24个乡级行政单位下设置有里，而并未设村，当地民众皆居于县城、乡城或里城之中。这在现存史料中有所反映。目前出土文书中，乡城较为多见，如高宁城、武城城、安乐城、南平城等。

但西州地区没有村落并不意味着城外无人居住。除了这些城邑以外，郊外地区仍有聚落组织，只是这些聚落尚未因村坊制度的实施被划归为具有行政意义的村落。如据《唐开元二十二年西州高昌县申西州都督府牒为差人夫修堤堰事》记载：

1高昌县 为申修堤堰人
……
4右得知水官杨嘉恽、巩虔纯等状称：前件堤堰
5每年差人夫修塞，今既时至，请准往例处分
6者。准状，各责得状，料用人功如前者。依检案
7 □□例取当县群牧、庄坞、底（邸）店及夷、胡户
8 □□日功修塞，件检如前者，修堤夫
……

这件文书中就记载有群牧、庄坞这类郊野聚落。囿于史料缺载，我们无法对这类郊野聚落做进一步考证。但刘再聪认为，唐代相关文书中没有出现关于西州地区存在村组织的记载，是当地尚未设置村组织所致。此说法应当成立。据此我们可以做进一步推断：尽管西州地区民众以居于城郭为主，但唐政府的基层管理制度在该地已经得到实施，且其城外确实存在部分聚落，这种状况下，当地未设置村组织，或许是沙漠地区郊野聚落的体量与规模较小所致。

3. 沙洲地区的村落

与西州地区相似，沙洲地区的民众也以城居为主。但较为不同的是，沙洲地区存在不少村落。如出土土文书《甲辰年二月后沙洲净土寺东库惠安惠戒手下便物历》中就出现了"百尺东村"。另据出土土文书《周长安三年前后敦煌县牒》记载：

1乡，耕耘最少，此由社官村
2正，不存务农。即欲加决，正属
3农非，各决贰拾。
……

此件文书为政府下发的公文。其中对于社官及村正的记载，显示出当地的村落发展已经成熟，不仅已经设有村正，而且存在结社现象。这显然与同时期中原地区的村落已经没有明显差异。由于现存史料有限，我们无法对当时沙洲地区村落的分布状况做具体考证，但是根据敦煌文书的相关记载可知，沙洲地区的寺庙周边应该是村落的密集分布区之一。

敦煌文书中有不少关于沙洲地区百姓或聚落向寺院借贷的契约，一定程度上可以反映出寺院周边的村落发展状况。其中，吐蕃统治敦煌时期是敦煌地区寺院放贷最为繁盛的阶段，不少民间百姓因生活贫困选择向临近寺院借贷。如吐蕃文书中出现的从永寿寺借贷谷物的"宁宗部落之夏孜孜""悉董萨部落百姓孙清"，向榆林寺寺库借麦的某部落喀泽晟、范氏十三娘及曹玛赞等，向灵图寺借麦的"行人部落百姓张七奴纳突不办"等。还有吐蕃统治敦煌时期，汉文借贷契约中出现的向灵图寺借谷物的赵卿卿、史奉仙、马其邻，向永寿寺借谷物的吴琼岳等。有学者曾对吐蕃统治敦煌时期的部分寺院借贷契约进行过统计，在契约的债务人中，民间百姓所占比重最高，其次才为僧人、寺户和官员。这虽然是由不同群体的实际经济状况所决定的，但是也能够间接地反映当时寺院周边聚落的发展状况。可以看出，诸如永寿寺、灵图寺、榆林寺等寺院周边不仅散布有吐蕃部落，而且有汉人聚落的存在。可以推测，或是这些聚落因寺庙建造以后带来的人口汇集形成，或是寺庙因村落聚集而选址于此。但无论是哪种情况，寺庙周边是沙洲地区聚落或村落的主要分布区之一的推断，似乎毋庸置疑。这一点也可以与唐代中原内地村落中普遍建有寺院的状况做类比。

因此，可以看出，唐代西北地区的村落是得到充分发展的。但通过对安西四镇、西州、沙洲几个地区的考察来看，西北地区村落的发展除了与自然环境有关以外，也与地域的经济、文化发展程度有着密切关联。西州地区的乡村发展状况就是很好的例证。整体而言，唐代村坊制度对西北地区产生了深入的影响。

二、青藏地区的村落

吐蕃王朝兴起以前，青藏高原地区长期处于以众多氏族部落为组织单元的分散状态，这些氏族部落皆以血缘关系为纽带，多分布于自然环境相对优越的河谷地带以及地势较为平缓的高原地区，以游牧业和农业为生。青藏高原上的早期聚落遗址反映了这样的发展状态。如西藏象泉河流域的丁东遗址与穹窿银城遗址、拉萨河谷与藏北高原交界地带的加日塘遗址等游牧聚落遗址，青海地区的齐家文化、辛店文化、卡约文化、诺木洪文化及西藏卡若文化、曲贡文化等皆为例证。

吐蕃王朝兴起前夕，经过长期的分化与融合，西藏地区已经形成了数十个部落联盟。石硕先生曾根据历史文献对西藏地区早期的小邦进行过考证，可以确定名称与位置的共有9个，主要分布在西藏中南部拉萨河、年楚河流域及藏北高原。这些小邦实际上是相互独立的邦国，有自己的部族首领与独立的管理体系，建有堡寨，并以堡寨为中心分布着部落民众的聚居单元。

现存敦煌吐蕃文书及现有考古发现，均可说明青藏高原地区早期小邦及其周边寨子的分布状况，而这种寨子应该就是当时部落群众的聚居单元。如西藏噶尔县境内的穹窿银城遗址被认为是象雄王国的都城所在地，其城堡建筑遗址分布于一个东北—西南走向的长条形山顶。根据遗址可见城堡有防御墙和堡垒，堡内有居住建筑、祭祀建筑及公共建筑。山下还分布有居住遗址和墓地。其中，居住遗址错落分布于中部与南部的河流一级台阶之上，成组布局，共有几十余组。较大的组由20余间房屋构成。霍巍认为这些居住遗址的排列分布方式是经过周密规划的。这在西藏古代相关史籍中可以得到证明。《贤者喜宴》中有载，松赞干布统治时期，吐蕃七良臣中的第五位涅·赤桑央顿，其毕生最大的贡献就是将居于山上的民众迁到河谷地带，开垦土地，形成居住单位，并在高山上修建堡寨，以堡寨为基础改造出城镇。根据穹窿银城遗址可以看出，这种做法并非出现于吐蕃时期，而是早在象雄国已经出现。据此可以推断，穹窿银城遗址中位于山上的堡寨后来就逐渐发展为城，山下河谷地带的几十组建筑群即为当地早期普通民众的基本聚居单元。这种聚居单元或可与中原地区早期独立于城市之外的乡野聚落做类比。

吐蕃时期是青藏高原地区村落发展的重要时期。7世纪初，早期氏族部落的一支——雅隆部落经过长期的累积与发展，已经成为部落联盟中最具势力者。松赞干布即位以后，即着手加强军事力量，并在其祖父达布聂西及其父朗日论赞所开创的国家事业的基础上，平定内部叛乱。在松赞干布的带领下，该部落不仅吞并了象雄、苏毗，统一了西藏各部，还建立起吐蕃政权，将都城迁至拉萨。其后，吐蕃王朝进一步向外拓展疆域，兼并了青海的吐谷浑及川西北高原的党项、多弥、白兰诸羌，统治势力覆盖整个青藏高原地区，形成威胁唐朝西北边疆稳定的一股强势力量。安史之乱以后，吐蕃王朝更是占领了西域及河西陇右地区，开始了对西北地区的统治。疆域版图的扩大促使吐蕃王朝可与唐王朝、中亚、西亚、南亚地区直接沟通。加之统治阶层采取了积极的经济与文化发展政策，吐蕃王朝与周边的多个国家和地区也建立了密切的交往关系。在频繁的文化交流过程中，不仅吐蕃地区的社会生产力得到了较大的提升，农牧业经济也有了一定程度的发展，为青藏高原各地方的农牧型聚落的发展提供了有力条件。

首先，农业生产水平的提高促进了农业聚落与城市的发展。松赞干布统一青藏高原以后，同唐王朝一样，西藏地区进入一个相对安定的发展阶段。松赞干布非常重视农业的生产与发展，不仅开拓荒地，而且大力改善灌溉条件，蓄水为池，引水为渠，还建立了旱涝排设施，"定衡量之法，设阡陌之制，教民习书，为马涂彩"。此外，这一时期犁、镰、锨、手斧等铁制农具及"二牛抬杠"式犁耕已经在青藏高原农业生产区得到普遍使用。尤其是文成公主入藏，不仅携带了不少农艺、历算书籍以及适合高原地区生产的谷物种子，而且将中原地区的农业生产技术教授给当地民众。这极大地促进了当地农业生产条件的改进。如山南地区的农田开垦、种植、保苗、灌溉等精耕细作的生产方法，青海地区水磨的建造与使用方法，皆是文成公主入藏之力所成。

不同时期因不同原因迁入吐蕃地区的中原移民，也为吐蕃地区农业生产的发展做出了不小的贡献。农业生产水平的提高直接促进了农作物种类的丰富。据《旧唐书》记载，吐蕃时期青藏高原地区已经种植有青稞、小麦、荞麦、芸豆等多种农作物。可以看出，当时吐蕃的农业生产水平已经得到很大的提高。这不仅促进了吐蕃地区农业生产区域的扩大，也促进了当地农业聚落的发展。根据《西藏王统记》的记载，此时拉萨地区及雅鲁藏布江流域已经"牛羊遍野，农田弥望"，河谷地带也出现了村镇。这种分布于河谷的聚落，应该是在类似于穹窿银城遗址中山谷地带建筑群的基础上发展而来的，也正是涅·赤桑央顿对建立山城与河谷聚落建议的实施结果。由此也可以推测，吐蕃时期，青藏高原地区的河谷地带已经成为农业聚落发展的主要的分布区。

吐蕃时期的青藏高原，还出现了不少因军事屯田而产生的聚落。如贞观年间，唐军击败吐谷浑控制青藏高原北部地区之后，受到吐蕃势力北上扩张的威胁，唐政府不得不在当地以重兵驻守，其后更是在青藏高原东部、北部、西部地区以三面包围的形式安置重兵。不仅如此，唐王朝每年都要从内地征调丁男赴藏充兵，以维持军力，还在当地屯田发展农业与牧业以备军用。因此，青藏高原北部地区在唐初就成为唐王朝重要的屯田区。其中，规模最大者为黑齿常之部河源军（驻于今西宁市）的屯田，面积达5 000顷。自此至安史之乱爆发，唐王朝在青藏高原北部驻兵近80年，经过长期的发展，这些屯田区不可避免地会发展出一定规模的村落。吕温所作《经河源军汉村作》一诗，就记录了其出使吐蕃时在吐蕃王朝统治的河源地区所见的场景："行行忽到旧河源，城外千家作汉村。樵采未侵征虏墓，耕耘就破羌屯。金汤天险长全设，伏腊华风亦暗存。暂驻单车空下泪，有心无力复何言。"诗中即描述了当地因屯田形成的村落与城镇。据此，有学者推断，吐蕃时期，青藏高原北部地区已经有不少汉人，并且形成了部分汉人村落。

其次，畜牧业的发展促进了游牧聚落的发展。吐蕃王朝在推动农业生产发展的同时，也积极促进畜牧业的发展，开垦并划分牧场。这一时期，青藏高原已经形成了春夏逐水草而居、秋冬有固定牧场的随季节变化的放牧方式，后来逐渐演变为定居牧耕，不再是传统的单纯游牧。这种放牧方式的转变直接促进了牧区聚落的形成。

最后，佛教于吐蕃时期在青藏高原地区的发展，促进了以佛教寺院为中心的聚落的发展。吐蕃时期，由于吐蕃王朝统治阶层对佛教的弘扬与推崇，佛教寺院被大量建立。除了已建寺院会吸引民众聚居以外，新建寺院也通常会因寺属人口、"供养顺缘之奴隶"及寺产民户的增多引起人口的汇集，进而促使大小聚落形成。这在上述吐蕃统治沙洲时期的聚落发展状况中已经有明显的反映。对于普遍崇信藏传佛教的青藏地区而言，因寺院的大量兴建而带来的聚落大量发展，已经可以预见。有关学者的研究显示，仅赤祖德赞时期，吐蕃境内的佛教寺院已经达到1 008座。仅这一时期，千余座寺院对青藏高原地区聚落发展的影响力已不容忽视，更不必提整个吐蕃时期寺院对青藏高原地区聚落形成与发展的影响。

三、北方地区的村落

隋唐以前，突厥势力逐渐壮大，开始控制北至北海（今贝加尔湖）、东至辽海（今辽河上游）、西至西海（今里海）的广大草原及沙漠地区。至隋开皇三年（583年），突厥势力分为东、西二部。自此至唐代前期的近50年间，大漠南北地区皆在东突厥势力的控制之下。唐初，东突厥及北方反唐武装势力屡次对李唐新生政权发起挑战。唐军统一华北以后，开始对东突厥势力展开军事行动，并于唐贞观三年（629年）底击溃东突厥武装势力。次年三月，东突厥首领率部落投降。自此，唐王朝完成了平定北方地区的战争。

东突厥势力灭亡以后，唐王朝开始在当地设置行政区划。贞观四年（630年），唐政府在自幽州至灵州间的地区设置了顺州、祐州、化州、长州都督府，并分颉利可汗统治故地为六州，置定襄都督府及云中都督府统管各部。贞观二十三年（649年），唐朝又在北部沿边突厥各部设置了一批羁縻州。车鼻可汗政权灭亡以后，唐政府又设置瀚海都督府（663年改名云中都护府，移至云中，664年改名单于都护府）与燕然都护府（668年改安北都护府）分管大漠南北区域。唐王朝基本完成对北方地区的行政建制，并同对待其他民族地区一样，以羁縻政策进行行政统治。

北方地区以广阔的草原为主，自古便是游牧民族的天下，这就决定了该地区无法像中原地区那样充分发展农业生产，并形成稳定的定居聚落，而是以逐水草而居的游牧部落为主。早在汉代，西北地区已经形成了游牧民族的部落联盟，这类部落联盟多是由多个氏族部落组成，如匈奴部落联盟、鲜卑部落联盟、突厥部落联盟等。3世纪，这些部落联盟经过兼并、战争，最终形成几个草原部落大联盟。草原部落大联盟的成分较为复杂，但基本上由不同的氏族部落组成。如檀石槐时期的鲜卑草原部落大联盟，就包括宇文鲜卑、慕容鲜卑、段部鲜卑的五十多个邑落，每个邑落又由多个氏族构成。突厥草原部落大联盟的成分更为复杂，包括天山东部及漠北的九姓铁勒、九姓回纥、四十姓拔悉密、三十姓鞑靼等多个不同的氏族部落。至隋唐以前，西北地区已经存在诸多部落联盟，这些部落联盟由早期游牧部落发展而来。这些草原部落大联盟自形成至隋唐时期，虽然在不同历史阶段对西北草原地区的不同区域进行统治，但其部落基本的组织形式是相似的。

北方草原的游牧部落并不似青藏高原的农区部落，也与中原地区的乡村聚落不同，其部落形态与社会生产的组织方式都表现出游牧民族的突出特性，即流动性较强。这些部落会因放牧条件的改变流动，也会因战争等因素发生迁移，就连部落首领所在的牙帐也并非完全固定，甚至举部而迁的现象也时有发生，尤其是战争导致迁移更为频繁。如唐初东突厥灭亡以后，薛延陀即占据漠北地区，并将其牙帐迁至都尉楗山（今址不详）和独逻水以南（今蒙古国土拉河）区域。另如据颜真卿《臧怀恪碑》记载，开元初仆骨部设支部落有2 000帐归附唐政府；开元三年（715年），处罗可汗之子郁射设带领部落万余帐南迁。其迁移单位"帐"通常代表一户家庭。可以看出，这种迁移的规模是比较大的，而且流动性很强。

除了游牧部落外，北方草原也有部分地区存在农业生产，并形成固定的农业生产聚落。典型的为漠南地区。一方面，该地区因处于北方民族与中原地区的交界地带，当地的生活、生产方式较多地受到中原地区的影响。另一方面，隋唐时期因各种因素迁移至漠南地区的汉人，也对当地社会生产、生活方式的发展产生了直接的影响。隋末唐初的社会动乱，迫使不少中原地区的民众向外迁移。除了向南方及西南地区迁移外，相对安定的漠南草原也是重要的迁入地区。因而，隋唐时期当地也汇聚了不少汉人及突厥人。隋灭亡以后，东突厥政权曾立隋朝皇室杨政道为隋王，并将因躲避战争迁移至东突厥的中原百姓及官员等一万多人交由其管理，居于定襄郡。唐王朝击溃东突厥势力以后，部分中原汉人返回中原地区，漠南又成为部分战败东突厥降众的安置地。据《旧唐书》记载，在此期间，当地曾招募汉人来此垦田耕种。

武周时期，漠南地区还是唐朝犯人的主要流放地。如武则天就曾将牵连入越王谋反一事的近6 000人流放至漠南的丰州地区。这些迁移至漠南地区的汉人，必然促进了当地生产方式的转变，乃至定居聚落的形成与发展。据《新唐书》记载："丰州九原郡，下都督府。贞观四年以降突厥户置，不领县。……土贡：白麦、印盐、野马胯革、驼毛褐、毡。户二千八百一十三，口九千六百四十一。县二。九原，中下。永徽四年置。有陵阳渠，建中三年浚之以溉田，置屯，寻弃之。有咸应、永清二渠，贞元中，刺史李景略开，溉田数百顷。"从这则记载中可以明确两点：第一，丰州地区的土贡中，除了游牧民族特产的动物皮毛及相关制品以外，还有"白麦"，这充分显示了当地是存在农作物种植的。农作物种植及农业的发展必须依赖定居形式的农业聚落，这也同样说明了当地农业性质聚落的存在。第二，其中所载当地官吏所开凿的两条用于农业灌溉的水渠，一条因"置屯"而弃用，另外一条则"溉田数百顷"，这些信息都表明该地已经建立了农业聚落"屯"，而这个能拥有数百顷耕地的聚落规模应该并不小。

《新唐书》中的另一记载也可对吐蕃农业及农业聚落的发展提供例证。据载，元和年间，韩重华曾在振武、中受降城（今包头市西南）、云州（今山西大同）一带募民屯田，共垦田3 800余顷，并于当地形成了15个屯，每屯130人，每人分得耕地100亩。可见，这类随着屯田活动的开展所形成的农业生产聚落，也是具有中原特色的新兴聚落单元。这成为草原地区具有村落性质的农业聚居单元形成与发展的一个来源。

Section 5: Villages in Ethnic Minority Areas

Throughout the Tang dynasty, not only villages in the Central Plains region developed by leaps and bounds, but villages in border ethnic minority areas also entered a new stage of development. The Tang dynasty often implemented the jimi (loose rein) policy for border ethnic minority areas that submitted to the central dynasty, that is, on the basis of their original tribes, administrative rule was carried out by establishing jimi prefectures. Geographically, the northwest, southwest, and north were areas where ethnic minorities concentrated in the Tang dynasty, and thus were the main distribution areas of Tang jimi prefectures. On one hand, under the jimi policy, Tang border ethnic minority areas enjoyed special autonomy; on the other hand, under the unified leadership of the central dynasty, economic and cultural exchanges between various ethnic areas became increasingly frequent. This not only greatly promoted the improvement of social economy and cultural levels in border ethnic minority areas, but also strongly promoted the development of productive forces and production technology in this region, providing good conditions for the development of villages in border ethnic minority areas. Due to the special natural environment and production and lifestyle, the development of villages in the Tubo region was relatively slow, but in frequent exchanges with the eastern Tang dynasty, there were also some new changes, especially certain progress made in agricultural production.

I. Villages in the Northwest Region

The northwest region, located at the junction of the Central Plains and Central Asia, was a transportation hub connecting East Asia, Central Asia, West Asia, and Europe, and had been an area where the Central Plains dynasty and Central Asian countries competed since ancient times. From the 7th to 9th centuries, three main opposing forces formed in this region: the Central Plains Tang dynasty, the Tubo dynasty, and the Persian dynasty. In the early Tang, after the Li Tang dynasty unified the North China region, it successively unified the Gaochang Kingdom and Western Turks in the northwest region in the fourteenth year of Zhenguan and the second year of Xianqing (657 CE). To strengthen management of the northwest region, the Tang dynasty successively established the Anxi Protectorate and Beiting Protectorate to manage the Western Regions, placing the Western Regions under Longyou Circuit, and built castles and established military towns at four places: Qiuci, Yanqi, Yutian, and Shule, making them develop into the main city settlements in the Western Regions. Under Tang dynasty rule, the Western Regions initially had a complete administrative system. From then until before the An Lushan Rebellion, the Tang dynasty's rule over the Western Regions basically maintained a stable state. During the more than a hundred years of Tang dynasty rule over the northwest region, economic and cultural exchanges between the Central Plains and these ethnic areas significantly increased. It was precisely because of this that the northwest region, including village society, achieved unprecedented development.

1. Villages of the Four Anxi Towns

The Four Anxi Towns were the main cities in the northwest region of the Tang dynasty, so including their villages, compared with other regions, they all received relatively full development. The jimi policy was a management method adopted by the Tang dynasty for ethnic areas, that is, on the basis of retaining the original management methods of ethnic areas, sending court officials for joint management. But the jimi policy of the Four Anxi Towns was different, and its grassroots administrative system was basically the same as the interior. But some scholars believe that even so, this was also generated with the implementation of the jimi system. Other scholars discussed its reasons, believing that the purpose of the Tang dynasty's comprehensive implementation of the grassroots management system in the four towns was "stability" rather than "tax collection." This was a manifestation of the Tang dynasty's attempt to conduct in-depth and comprehensive rule over the northwest region. Although the Tang dynasty still retained the royal system of the four towns, it could be regarded as regular prefectures. Regarding the specific implementation status of the Tang grassroots management system in the Four Anxi Towns, we can find confirmation in relevant historical documents.

Among existing unearthed documents, there are many records about villages in the four towns. These records show that villages had been generally developed in the four towns, and the village management system had no obvious difference from the Central Plains region. The "Kaiyuan Period某 Temple Expenditure Book" among Turfan documents obtained by Aurel Stein records "Xihe Boningye Xiang Juemigong Village," and its use of the expression method of regional attribution of "xiang-cun" is completely the same as the interior. Additionally, according to Liu Zaicong's research, "Xihe" is a river west of Yutian City, and "Juemigong Village" is a rural village located in this river basin. This can also be verified in relevant information about villages under the jurisdiction of the Qiuci Protectorate recorded in Otani documents, such as Document No. 8044 "Mu Huzi Document, Second Month, Ninth Year of Dali":

1 Document, Huzi has poor fortune, unfortunately my loving mother passed away. Family poor, funeral not yet
2 completed. South boundary Shuangqu Village planted little thin field, now assigned two adults for canal repair, three parts
3 cannot support, humbly request to consider this lowly person, from now on if there is dispatch, dare not disobey orders, please
4 beg for discussion and disposition. Respectfully document.
5 Second month, ninth year of Dali, day, Mu Huzi document

The "Shuangqu Village in the south boundary" in this document is obviously located in the rural area outside the city. It also needs to be pointed out that this document mentions Mu Huzi requesting exemption from the "taotuo" corvee for repairing canals and weirs due to his mother's death. According to scholars' research, this type of corvee was a corvee apportioned to villagers by village during Tang border defense construction, urged by military personnel. This shows that the Tang village system should have been thoroughly implemented in the Four Anxi Towns.

2. Villages in Xizhou

Xizhou was also an area that fully implemented the Tang grassroots management system. This area was mainly populated by descendants of Han Chinese who garrisoned there in the Han and Wei dynasties. Therefore, after destroying the Gaochang Kingdom, the Tang government established Xichang Prefecture there, later changed to Xizhou, making it a regular prefecture under central government jurisdiction, receiving the same management as prefectures and counties in the Central Plains. But affected by the local natural environment dominated by deserts and the social environment with many nomadic peoples, for defense needs, local residents mostly built forts as cities, defending by city as a unit. According to "Tang Huiyao," when the Tang government established Xizhou as a regular prefecture in the fourteenth year of Zhenguan, it set up counties in five cities: Jiaohe City, Shichang City, Tiandi City, Dongzhen City, and Gaochang City, under the jurisdiction of Xizhou, all under the Anxi Protectorate, and later set up 24 townships under the five counties. But according to research by some scholars, under the 24 township-level administrative units in Xizhou, li were set up, but villages were not set up, and local people all lived in county cities, township cities, or li cities. This is reflected in existing historical materials. Among currently unearthed documents, township cities are more common, such as Gaoning City, Wucheng City, Anle City, Nanping City, etc.

But the absence of villages in Xizhou does not mean no one lived outside the cities. In addition to these cities, there were still settlement organizations in the suburban areas, only these settlements had not yet been classified as administrative villages due to the implementation of the village-fang system. For example, according to "Tang Xizhou Gaochang County Document to Xizhou Protectorate on Dispatching Laborers to Repair Dikes and Weirs, Twenty-Second Year of Kaiyuan":

1 Gaochang County, for reporting dike and weir repair laborers
...
4 Right, learned from water officials Yang Jiayun, Gong Qianchun, etc. stating: the aforementioned dikes and weirs
5 annually dispatch laborers to repair and block, now since the time has come, request disposition according to previous examples
6. According to the statement, each obtained statements, estimating labor as before. According to inspection of records
7 ... examples take this county's pastures, manor forts, inns, and Yi and Hu households
8 ... daily labor to repair and block, item inspection as before, dike repair laborers
...

This document records rural settlements such as pastures and manor forts. Constrained by the lack of historical records, we cannot conduct further research on such rural settlements. But Liu Zaicong believes that the absence of records about the existence of village organizations in Xizhou in relevant Tang documents is because village organizations had not yet been established locally. This statement should hold. Based on this, we can make further inferences: although people in Xizhou mainly lived in cities, the Tang government's grassroots management system had been implemented there, and there were indeed some settlements outside the cities. Under this situation, the local failure to establish village organizations may be due to the small volume and scale of rural settlements in desert areas.

3. Villages in Shazhou Region

Similar to Xizhou, people in the Shazhou region also mainly lived in cities. But relatively differently, there were many villages in the Shazhou region. For example, the "甲辰年二月后沙洲净土寺东库惠安惠戒手下便物历" (Loan Record under Hui'an and Huijie, East Storehouse of Jingtu Temple, Shazhou, After Second Month of Jiachen Year) among unearthed documents mentions "Baichi East Village." Additionally, according to the unearthed document "Dunhuang County Document, Around Third Year of Chang'an of Zhou":

1 Township, cultivation least, this due to she official and village
2 zheng, not emphasizing agriculture. Wanting to add punishment, exactly
3 farming season, each punish twenty.
...

This document is an official document issued by the government. The records about she officials and village zheng in it show that local village development had matured, not only having village zheng established, but also the phenomenon of forming associations. This was obviously no different from villages in the Central Plains region during the same period. Due to limited existing historical materials, we cannot conduct specific research on the distribution status of villages in the Shazhou region at that time, but according to relevant records in Dunhuang documents, it can be known that the surroundings of temples in the Shazhou region should be one of the densely distributed areas of villages.

There are many contracts about common people or settlements in the Shazhou region borrowing from temples in Dunhuang documents, which to a certain extent can reflect the development status of villages around temples. Among them, the period of Tubo rule over Dunhuang was the most prosperous stage of temple lending in the Dunhuang region, and many common people chose to borrow from nearby temples due to poverty. For example, in Tubo documents, there appear "Xia Zizi of Ningzong Tribe" and "Sun Qing, commoner of Xidongsa Tribe" borrowing grain from Yongshou Temple; certain tribe's Ka Zesheng, Fan Shisanniang, and Cao Mazan borrowing wheat from the Yulin Temple storehouse; "Zhang Qinu, commoner of Xingren Tribe, unable to pay tax" borrowing wheat from Lingtu Temple, etc. There are also Chinese loan contracts during the Tubo rule of Dunhuang mentioning Zhao Qingqing, Shi Fengxian, Ma Qilin borrowing grain from Lingtu Temple, Wu Qiongyue borrowing grain from Yongshou Temple, etc. Some scholars once statistics on part of temple loan contracts during the Tubo rule of Dunhuang, finding that among debtors in contracts, common people accounted for the highest proportion, followed by monks, temple households, and officials. Although this was determined by the actual economic conditions of different groups, it can also indirectly reflect the development status of settlements around temples at that time. It can be seen that around temples such as Yongshou Temple, Lingtu Temple, and Yulin Temple, not only Tubo tribes were scattered, but also Han Chinese settlements existed. It can be inferred that either these settlements formed due to population gathering brought about by temple construction, or temples were selected here due to village gathering. But in either case, the inference that temple surroundings were one of the main distribution areas of settlements or villages in the Shazhou region seems beyond doubt. This can also be compared with the situation where temples were commonly built in villages in the interior of the Tang Central Plains.

Therefore, it can be seen that villages in the northwest region of the Tang dynasty were fully developed. But through the investigation of several regions: the Four Anxi Towns, Xizhou, and Shazhou, the development of villages in the northwest region, in addition to being related to the natural environment, was also closely related to the regional economic and cultural development level. The rural development status in Xizhou is a good example. Overall, the Tang village-fang system had in-depth influence on the northwest region.

II. Villages in the Qinghai-Tibet Region

Before the rise of the Tubo dynasty, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau region was long in a scattered state with many clan tribes as organizational units. These clan tribes were all bonded by blood relations, mostly distributed in river valley areas with relatively superior natural environments and plateau areas with relatively flat terrain, making a living from nomadism and agriculture. Early settlement sites on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau reflect this development status. For example, nomadic settlement sites such as the Dongdong Site and Qionglong Silver City Site in the Xiangquan River basin of Tibet, the Jiaritang Site at the junction of the Lhasa River valley and the northern Tibet plateau; the Qijia Culture, Xindian Culture, Kayue Culture, Nuomuhong Culture in Qinghai, and the Karuo Culture, Qugong Culture in Tibet are all examples.

On the eve of the rise of the Tubo dynasty, after long-term differentiation and integration, dozens of tribal alliances had formed in the Tibet region. Mr. Shi Shuo once researched early small states in the Tibet region based on historical documents, and there are 9 with confirmable names and locations, mainly distributed in the Lhasa River and Nyangchu River basins in south-central Tibet and the northern Tibet plateau. These small states were actually independent kingdoms, with their own tribal chiefs and independent management systems, building fortified villages, with tribal people's settlement units distributed around the fortified villages as centers.

Existing Dunhuang Tubo documents and current archaeological discoveries can both explain the distribution status of early small states and their surrounding villages on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, and such villages should have been the settlement units of tribal masses at that time. For example, the Qionglong Silver City Site in Gar County, Tibet is considered the capital of the Zhangzhung Kingdom, with its castle building ruins distributed on a long strip-shaped mountain top running northeast-southwest. According to the site, the castle had defensive walls and forts, with residential buildings, sacrificial buildings, and public buildings inside the fort. Residential sites and cemeteries were also distributed at the foot of the mountain. Among them, residential sites were scattered on the first river terrace in the central and southern parts, arranged in groups, totaling more than几十 groups. Larger groups consisted of more than 20 rooms. Huo Wei believes that the arrangement and distribution of these residential sites were carefully planned. This can be proven in relevant ancient Tibetan historical records. "Xianzhe Xiyan" (The Scholars' Feast) records that during Songtsen Gampo's rule, the fifth of Tubo's seven good ministers, Nie Chisang Yangdun, his greatest lifelong contribution was moving people living on mountains to river valley areas, reclaiming land, forming residential units, and building fortified villages on high mountains, transforming them into towns based on fortified villages. According to the Qionglong Silver City Site, it can be seen that this practice did not appear in the Tubo period but had already appeared in the Zhangzhung Kingdom. Based on this, it can be inferred that the fortified villages on the mountains in the Qionglong Silver City Site later gradually developed into cities, and the dozens of building groups in the river valley at the foot of the mountain were the basic settlement units of early ordinary local people. Such settlement units may be comparable to early rural settlements independent of cities in the Central Plains region.

The Tubo period was an important period for village development on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. In the early 7th century, the Yarlung tribe, one of the early clan tribes, after long-term accumulation and development, had become the most powerful among tribal alliances. After ascending the throne, Songtsen Gampo set about strengthening military power, and on the basis of the state cause founded by his grandfather Tagbu Nyasi and his father Namri Songtsen, pacified internal rebellions. Under Songtsen Gampo's leadership, this tribe not only annexed Zhangzhung and Supi, unified various tribes in Tibet, but also established the Tubo regime, moving the capital to Lhasa. Thereafter, the Tubo dynasty further expanded its territory outward, annexing the Tuyuhun in Qinghai and the Dangxiang, Duomi, and Bailan Qiang in the northwestern Sichuan plateau, with ruling power covering the entire Qinghai-Tibet Plateau region, forming a powerful force threatening the stability of the Tang dynasty's northwest frontier. After the An Lushan Rebellion, the Tubo dynasty even occupied the Western Regions and the Hexi-Longyou region, beginning rule over the northwest region. The expansion of territory enabled the Tubo dynasty to directly communicate with the Tang dynasty, Central Asia, West Asia, and South Asia. Coupled with the ruling class adopting active economic and cultural development policies, the Tubo dynasty also established close exchange relations with multiple surrounding countries and regions. In the process of frequent cultural exchanges, not only was the social productive force in the Tubo region greatly improved, but the agricultural and pastoral economy also developed to a certain extent, providing strong conditions for the development of agricultural-pastoral settlements in various places on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

First, the improvement of agricultural production levels promoted the development of agricultural settlements and cities. After Songtsen Gampo unified the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, like the Tang dynasty, the Tibet region entered a relatively stable development stage. Songtsen Gampo attached great importance to agricultural production and development, not only reclaiming wasteland but also vigorously improving irrigation conditions, storing water as ponds, diverting water as canals, and also establishing drought and flood drainage facilities, "establishing measurement methods, setting field boundary systems, teaching people to learn writing, painting horses with colors." In addition, during this period, iron farm tools such as plows, sickles, shovels, and hand axes, as well as the "two-oxen carrying-yoke" style plowing, had been universally used in agricultural production areas on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Especially Princess Wencheng's entry into Tibet not only carried many agricultural and calendar books and grain seeds suitable for plateau production, but also taught local people the agricultural production techniques of the Central Plains. This greatly promoted the improvement of local agricultural production conditions. For example, the intensive farming production methods of field reclamation, planting, seedling protection, and irrigation in the Shannan region, and the construction and use methods of water mills in Qinghai, were all accomplished due to Princess Wencheng's entry into Tibet.
